concepts.name: Physics and its realm
concepts.why: Physics is concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and it is especially interested in what fundamental mechanisms underlie every phenomenon. A surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe, and that underlying order is what makes the subject worth studying.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the passage on the realm of physics; conceptual questions 7 and 9 ask where its classical branch applies. No exercise tests the definition on its own.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.why: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult or impossible to display directly, such as the planetary model of the atom. It is justified by experiment but accurate only under limited situations, and it lets us picture what we cannot see.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; conceptual questions 1, 2 and 6 ask what a model is, how it differs from a theory, and whether its validity can be limited.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.why: To a scientist a theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, supported by scientific evidence and verified many times by different groups of researchers. It should describe every aspect of any system within its domain, and an experiment that contradicts it means the theory is thrown out or modified.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; conceptual questions 2, 3, 4 and 6 turn on what makes a theory valid.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.why: A law uses concise language, often a single equation such as F = ma, to describe a generalized pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments. A law describes a single action, whereas a theory explains a whole group of related phenomena.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding asks what can be known about a new law before hearing it; conceptual question 6 compares the validity required of a law with that of a model.

concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.why: The scientific method is the process scientists follow as they inquire about the world: an observation and a question, some research, a hypothesis, an experiment to test it, and a conclusion drawn from the results. The cornerstone is observation, since science must describe the universe as it is.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the car that will not start is worked through as an example; conceptual question 5 asks how strict the criteria for believing a result must be.

concepts.name: Classical physics
concepts.why: Classical physics is the physics that developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century. It is an excellent approximation when matter moves at less than about 1% of the speed of light, when objects are large enough to be seen with a microscope, and when only weak gravitational fields such as the Earth’s are involved, which is why most of this text is devoted to it.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed limits on the laws of classical physics; conceptual questions 7 and 9 ask when classical physics applies, the second for a satellite at 7500 m/s.

concepts.name: Modern physics
concepts.why: Modern physics consists of two revolutionary theories, relativity and quantum mechanics, which deal with the very fast and the very small. Relativity must be used above about 1% of the speed of light or in a strong gravitational field, and quantum mechanics for objects smaller than can be seen with a microscope; their combination, relativistic quantum mechanics, is the best universally applicable theory we have.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for modern physics, relativity and quantum mechanics; conceptual question 8 asks when relativistic quantum mechanics is necessary.

concepts.name: Physical quantity
concepts.why: A physical quantity is defined either by specifying how it is measured or by stating how it is calculated from other measurements. Distance and time are defined by methods for measuring them, whereas average speed is defined as distance traveled divided by time of travel.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the section summary; Example 1.1 calculates average speed from a distance and a time.

concepts.name: Units
concepts.why: Measurements of physical quantities are expressed in terms of units, which are standardized values. Without them it would be extremely difficult to express and compare measured values in a meaningful way; the two major systems in use are SI units and English units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for units, SI units and English units; conceptual question 1; every problem in the section converts a value from one unit to another.

concepts.name: Fundamental units
concepts.why: The most fundamental physical quantities can be defined only in terms of the procedure used to measure them, and their units are called fundamental units. In this text they are length, mass, time, and electric current, measured in the meter, the kilogram, the second, and the ampere.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for fundamental units, second, meter and kilogram; Table 1.1; Check Your Understanding 1 asks which fundamental unit describes a hummingbird’s wingbeat.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.why: All other physical quantities, such as force and electric charge, can be expressed as algebraic combinations of length, mass, time, and current; speed, for example, is length divided by time. The units of such quantities are called derived units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 2 asks what a cubic centimeter being a milliliter says about the SI units.

concepts.name: Metric prefixes
concepts.why: The metric system is convenient for calculation because its units are categorized by factors of 10, and a standard set of prefixes lets the same unit be used over extremely large ranges of values. Distances in meters suit construction, kilometers suit air travel, and nanometers suit optical design, with no need to invent new units.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term for the metric system; Table 1.2; Check Your Understanding 1 asks for the prefix that fits a hummingbird’s wingbeat; conceptual question 1; problems 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Order of magnitude
concepts.why: The order of magnitude of a value is the power of 10 that sets its scale. The numbers 800 and 450 can both be written as a number times 10², so they are of the same order of magnitude; the diameter of an atom is of order 10⁻¹⁰ m and the diameter of the Sun of order 10⁹ m.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Table 1.3 of known lengths, masses and times; Check Your Understanding 1 asks which factor of 10 fits a measurement; the approximation problems of section 1.4 read their inputs from Table 1.3.

concepts.name: Conversion factor
concepts.why: A conversion factor is a ratio expressing how many of one unit are equal to another unit, such as 1000 meters in 1 kilometer or 60 seconds in 1 minute. Multiplying by the factor that cancels the unwanted unit leaves the desired unit in its place.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the 80 m to 0.080 km conversion in the text; Example 1.1; problems 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Convert a value from one unit to another
concepts.why: To convert, list the units you have and the units you want, find the conversion factor between them, and multiply so that the units cancel. If the factor is written upside down the units do not cancel, so checking the units of the answer is part of the method.
concepts.evidence: Example 1.1 converts an average speed to km/h and to m/s; problems 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are conversions.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.why: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the correct value for that measurement. Three measurements of 11.1, 11.2 and 10.9 inches of paper that is 11.0 inches long are accurate; a measurement of 12 inches is not.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the GPS bull’s-eye passage; conceptual question 1 asks how accuracy and uncertainty are related.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.why: The precision of a measurement system refers to how close the agreement is between repeated measurements made under the same conditions, that is, to the spread of the measured values. A measuring system can be accurate but not precise, or precise but not accurate.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the GPS bull’s-eye passage; the precision of a measuring tool decides how many digits a measurement can carry.

concepts.name: Uncertainty $A \pm \delta A$
concepts.why: Uncertainty is a quantitative measure of how much your measured values deviate from a standard or expected value, a disclaimer on the number: 45,000 miles plus or minus 500. All measurements contain some uncertainty, from the measuring device, the skill of the person, irregularities in the object, and anything else that affects the outcome.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the fevers-or-chills note; Check Your Understanding 1 asks whether a stopwatch can tell two sprint times apart; conceptual questions 1 and 2; problems 11, 15 and 17.

concepts.name: Percent uncertainty, $\%\,\text{unc} = \frac{\delta A}{A} \times 100\%$
concepts.why: One way to express uncertainty is as a percent of the measured value: the uncertainty divided by the value, times 100%. A bag of apples weighed at 5.1 lb with an uncertainty of 0.4 lb has a percent uncertainty of 8%.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Example 1.2; problems 1, 3, 9 and 11.

concepts.name: Method of adding percents
concepts.why: There is an uncertainty in anything calculated from measured quantities. When the measurements going in have small uncertainties, the percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation: a floor 4.00 m by 3.00 m, known to 2% and 1%, has an area of 12.0 m² known to 3%.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the floor-area passage; problems 11, 15 and 17 ask for the uncertainty in a rate, a volume and an area.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.why: When we express measured values we can list only as many digits as the measuring tool gave us, and the last digit written down is the first digit with some uncertainty. Counting the digits from the first measured digit on the left through the last on the right gives the number of significant figures, and zeros are significant except when they serve only as placekeepers.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the ruler and caliper passage; the rules for zeros; Check Your Understanding 2 counts the significant figures in five measurements; problems 5 and 7.

concepts.name: Significant figures in multiplication and division
concepts.why: For multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity having the least significant figures entering into the calculation. A circle whose radius is known to two figures has an area known to two figures, even though π is good to at least eight.
concepts.evidence: The area of a circle worked in the text; Check Your Understanding 3(b); problems 5, 7 and 13.

concepts.name: Significant figures in addition and subtraction
concepts.why: For addition and subtraction, the answer can contain no more decimal places than the least precise measurement. Potatoes weighed on scales good to 0.01 kg, 0.001 kg and 0.1 kg add up to a mass that can be given only to the tenth of a kilogram.
concepts.evidence: The potatoes worked in the text; Check Your Understanding 3(a) adds three bag weights.

concepts.name: Make a reasonable approximation
concepts.why: Physicists, other scientists and engineers often need approximations or “guesstimates” for a quantity, based on formulae whose inputs are known only to limited accuracy. Scaling up from a known quantity, such as the height of a person, gives an estimate good to an order of magnitude, which is enough to rule out unrealistic numbers and to guide an approach.
concepts.evidence: Examples 1.3 and 1.4 estimate the height of a building and of a trillion dollars in bills; Check Your Understanding asks for the area of a basketball court; problems 1, 3, 5 and 7.

concepts.name: Reference frame
concepts.why: A position is always given relative to something, such as the Earth, a whiteboard, or the cabin of an airplane. Choosing the reference frame is the first step in describing any motion.
concepts.evidence: Defined in the text ("position relative to a convenient reference frame"); the AP question separates position from displacement, which only makes sense once a frame is fixed.

concepts.name: Position
concepts.why: The position of an object is where it is at a particular time, given as a coordinate with a sign on the chosen axis. Every other quantity in one-dimensional kinematics is built from positions and times.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the AP question distinguishes position from distance traveled and displacement.

concepts.name: Displacement, $\kdx = \kxf - \kxo$
concepts.why: Displacement is the change in position, that is, the final position minus the initial position. It has a sign, and the sign gives the direction. In kinematics we nearly always deal with displacement rather than with the path taken.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a); problems 1 and 3 part (c); AP question.

concepts.name: Distance (magnitude of displacement)
concepts.why: Distance is the magnitude of the displacement, so it has no sign. It is easy to confuse with distance traveled, which is why the text treats the two separately.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (c); problems 1 and 3 part (b); conceptual question 2.

concepts.name: Distance traveled (path length)
concepts.why: Distance traveled is the total length of the path, and it can be much greater than the magnitude of the displacement. For example, a professor who paces 150 m during a lecture may end up only 2.0 m from where she started.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (b); problems 1 and 3 part (a); conceptual questions 1 to 3.

concepts.name: Average velocity, $\kvb = \kdx / \kdt$
concepts.why: Average velocity is displacement divided by the time of travel. It is a vector because displacement is a vector, so it has a direction, and its sign tells which way the object moved: an airplane passenger who takes 5 s to move −4 m toward the rear of the plane has an average velocity of −0.8 m/s. The average velocity says nothing about what happened between the starting point and the ending point.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed definition; Check Your Understanding (a), where the round trip makes it zero; conceptual questions 2 and 4; problems 1(b), 7(b) and 11(b); Example 1.1 of section 1.2 took average speed as given.

concepts.name: Acceleration
concepts.why: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, and the greater the acceleration, the greater the change in velocity over a given time. Because velocity is a vector, a change in velocity can be a change in magnitude or a change in direction, so a car turning a corner at constant speed is accelerating. Acceleration is a vector in the same direction as the change in velocity, and its SI unit is meters per second squared, which means by how many meters per second the velocity changes every second.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed note Acceleration as a Vector; conceptual questions 1, 2 and 3, which ask whether speed or velocity can be constant while the acceleration is not zero and whether velocity can be zero while the acceleration is not; conceptual question 3 of section 2.2.

concepts.name: Constant-acceleration model
concepts.why: In this section we assume that acceleration is constant. Then the average acceleration equals the acceleration at every instant, and the average velocity is simply the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. The kinematic equations all follow from this assumption, and many real motions can be described in pieces within which it holds.
concepts.evidence: Definition in the text ("acceleration is constant"); exercises ap-marble, p6, p18 test whether the learner knows when the model applies.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$
concepts.why: Displacement equals the average velocity multiplied by the elapsed time. This is the definition of average velocity rearranged, so it holds whether or not the acceleration is constant.
concepts.evidence: Tested directly by p7, p8; used in p11, p13, p14.

concepts.name: $\kvb = \tfrac{\kvo + \kv}{2}$
concepts.why: When acceleration is constant, velocity changes at a steady rate, so the average velocity is the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. This step turns the definition of average velocity into the equations for displacement.
concepts.evidence: Tested by p7, p8; required to derive x-quadratic and v-squared.

concepts.name: $\kv = \kvo + \ka\kt$
concepts.why: The final velocity depends on both the size of the acceleration and the time over which it acts. A modest acceleration that lasts a long time can produce a very large velocity.
concepts.evidence: Tested by cyu-rocket, ai-rel-1, p1 to p5; used in most later problems.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvo\kt + \tfrac12\ka\kt^2$
concepts.why: Under constant acceleration, the displacement grows with the square of the elapsed time. For example, a dragster starting from rest covers only one quarter of the track in the first half of its run.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-2, ap-marble, p5, p9, p10, p17.

concepts.name: $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 + 2\ka\kdx$
concepts.why: This equation relates velocity to displacement without involving time. Because the stopping distance of a car grows with the square of its speed, halving the speed reduces the stopping distance to one quarter.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-3, p11 to p16, p18.

concepts.name: Choose the equation from knowns and unknowns
concepts.why: To solve a problem, first list the quantities you know and the quantity you want to find, and then choose the equation in which the quantity you want is the only unknown. This is the skill that Putting Equations Together teaches and that multi-step problems test.
concepts.evidence: Taught explicitly as a problem-solving strategy; tested by p5, p7, p19, p20, p21.

concepts.name: Interpret the solution physically
concepts.why: The algebra can give two roots, a negative time, or a square root with two signs, but only one of these describes the motion. Deciding which solution is physically reasonable is part of solving the problem.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.13 rejects the negative time root; p10(b) and p17 ask the learner to judge whether a result makes sense.

concepts.name: Instantaneous velocity $\kv$
concepts.why: The smaller the time intervals considered in a motion, the more detailed the information, and carried to its logical conclusion this leaves an infinitesimally small interval over which the average velocity becomes the instantaneous velocity, the velocity at a specific instant. A car’s speedometer shows the magnitude of the car’s instantaneous velocity, and finding it precisely can involve taking a limit, though under many circumstances precise values can be found without calculus.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the airplane passenger’s trip cut into smaller segments in Figure 2.9; conceptual questions 3 and 5.

concepts.name: Acceleration due to gravity $\kg$
concepts.why: The acceleration of a free-falling object is called the acceleration due to gravity, and it is so important that its magnitude is given its own symbol, $\kg$, with the average value 9.80 m/s² on Earth. Its direction is downward, toward the center of Earth, and in fact its direction defines what we call vertical. Whether the acceleration $\ka$ in the kinematic equations has the value $+\kg$ or $-\kg$ depends on how we define our coordinate system: if up is positive, then $\ka = -\kg$.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed value; conceptual questions 1, 2(c), 5 and 6, the last two on the Moon, where the acceleration due to gravity is about one sixth of Earth’s; Example 2.16 measures a local value; problems 2 and 4 of section 2.4 express accelerations as multiples of $\kg$.

concepts.name: Restoring force
concepts.why: When an object is displaced from its equilibrium position, the deformation creates a force in the opposite direction, which pushes the object back. Without such a force there is no oscillation, because the object would simply move in a straight line at constant speed.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 1; the AP question on the meaning of the minus sign.

concepts.name: Force constant $\kk$
concepts.why: The force constant tells how stiff a system is. The larger $\kk$ is, the greater the restoring force for the same displacement, and the stiffer the system. It is the slope of the graph of restoring force against displacement, in newtons per meter.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; every problem in the section asks for the force constant; Check Your Understanding 1 asks how to make the ruler stiffer.

concepts.name: Hooke’s law, $\kF = -\kk\kx$
concepts.why: The simplest oscillations occur when the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement. This is Hooke’s law, and the minus sign says that the force points opposite to the displacement. Knowing the force and the displacement gives the force constant, which is what most problems in this section ask for.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.1; problems 1, 3 and 5; the AP question on the minus sign. The book names the law in section 5.3 for stress and strain; the node is introduced here and will be reinforced by 5.3 when that section is built.

concepts.name: Periodic motion
concepts.why: A motion that repeats itself at regular time intervals, such as a plucked guitar string or a mass on a spring moving up and down, is periodic. Each repetition takes the same time as the one before it, which is what makes a period and a frequency meaningful.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding asks for an event in your life that occurs regularly.

concepts.name: Period $\kT$
concepts.why: The period is the time to complete one oscillation. Its units are usually seconds, but may be any convenient unit of time. The word applies to the time for any event, repetitive or not, but here it is the time for one cycle of a periodic motion.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; the AP item; problems 1, 2 and 3.

concepts.name: Frequency $\kf$
concepts.why: Frequency is the number of events per unit time. For periodic motion it is the number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz, where one hertz is one cycle per second. A count of cycles divided by the time they took gives the frequency, whether or not the count is made over one second.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; the AP item; problems 2, 4, 5 and 6.

concepts.name: Period and frequency, $\kf = 1/\kT$
concepts.why: If one cycle takes a time $\kT$, then $1/\kT$ cycles fit into each unit of time, so the frequency is the reciprocal of the period and the period is the reciprocal of the frequency. Given either one, the other follows at once.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.3; the AP item; problems 1 to 4.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: When the net force on a system can be described by Hooke’s law and there is no damping, the system oscillates with equal displacement on either side of equilibrium. This is simple harmonic motion, the simplest and most common kind of oscillation, and the system is a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms simple harmonic motion and simple harmonic oscillator; conceptual questions 1 and 3; Check Your Understanding 1.

concepts.name: Amplitude $\kX$
concepts.why: The amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. It has the units of the displacement, meters for an object on a spring, and it is related to the energy in the oscillation. In one full period the object covers four amplitudes of ground.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding 1 and 2; the AP item on the distance covered in one period, placed here from 16.1.

concepts.name: Period of a simple harmonic oscillator, $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$
concepts.why: The period and frequency of a simple harmonic oscillator depend on the mass and the force constant alone, not on the amplitude. A stiffer system has a shorter period and a more massive one a longer period. Because the period is constant, a simple harmonic oscillator can be used as a clock.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.4; AP question 2; problems 1, 3, 6 and 9; conceptual questions 2, 4, 5 and 6; Check Your Understanding 1 for the independence of amplitude.

concepts.name: Position, velocity and acceleration in simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: The displacement in any simple harmonic motion is a cosine of time, $\kx(t) = \kX\cos(2\pi\kt/\kT)$. The velocity is a sine with maximum $\kvmax = 2\pi\kX/\kT = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$, zero at the turning points and greatest through equilibrium, and the acceleration is a cosine opposite in direction to the displacement. These are the sine waves that link simple harmonic motion to waves.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding 2; the graphs of Figure 16.12.

concepts.name: Simple pendulum
concepts.why: A simple pendulum is a small mass, the bob, hung from a light string. Displaced along its arc, it feels a net force of $-m\kg\sin\theta$ back toward the lowest point, because the tension cancels the part of the weight along the string. For small displacements it is a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; AP question 3.

concepts.name: Restoring force on a pendulum, $\kF \approx -\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$
concepts.why: For angles below about 15°, $\sin\theta$ and $\theta$ differ by 1% or less, so the restoring force $-m\kg\sin\theta$ becomes $-m\kg\theta$, and with $\ks = L\theta$ it is $-\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$. That is Hooke’s law with a force constant $\kk = m\kg/L$, which is what makes the pendulum a simple harmonic oscillator.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a 12° swing is within the small-angle range); the derivation that Example 16.5 rests on.

concepts.name: Period of a simple pendulum, $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$
concepts.why: Putting $\kk = m\kg/L$ into $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$ cancels the mass and leaves $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$. Only the length and the acceleration due to gravity affect the period; the mass does not, and the amplitude hardly does for small swings. This is why a pendulum keeps time.
concepts.evidence: Example 16.5; AP questions 2 and 3; conceptual question 1; every problem in the section.

concepts.name: Measuring $\kg$ with a pendulum
concepts.why: Squaring the period formula and solving for $\kg$ gives $\kg = 4\pi^2 L/\kT^2$. If the length is known precisely and the period is timed over many swings at a small angle, this gives the local acceleration due to gravity to several digits, which matters in geological exploration.
concepts.evidence: The section’s learning objective; Example 16.5; AP question 2; the Take-Home Experiment; problems 7 and 13.

concepts.name: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2 = \text{constant}$
concepts.why: A simple harmonic oscillator has no dissipative forces, so its energy is shared between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy with the total constant. The energy goes completely from one form to the other as the system oscillates: all potential at the turning points, all kinetic through equilibrium. Started from rest at $\kx = \kX$, the total is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.
concepts.evidence: The AP item on the internal energy of a 1 kg oscillator; AP question 4 of section 16.3 (the energy at the centre), placed here; conceptual question 1; problem 2(b); problem 1(b), with gravity.

concepts.name: Speed in simple harmonic motion, $\kv = \pm\kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$
concepts.why: Solving the conservation of energy for the velocity gives the speed at every position, greatest at equilibrium and zero at the turning points, with $\kvmax = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$. The maximum velocity is proportional to the amplitude, greater for stiffer systems, and smaller for larger masses.
concepts.evidence: The section’s learning objective; Example 16.6; Check Your Understanding 1 and 2; problem 1(a) through the frequency.

concepts.name: The projection of uniform circular motion is simple harmonic motion
concepts.why: A point moving round a circle at constant angular velocity $\kw$ has a projection on a fixed axis at $\kx = \kX\cos\kw\kt$, and with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$ this is exactly the position of a simple harmonic oscillator. The shadow of a ball on a turntable therefore moves in simple harmonic motion, and the speed and the period of any simple harmonic oscillator can be read off the circle: the similar triangles give $\kv = \kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$, and one revolution gives $\kT = 2\pi\kX/\kvmax = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding; the section summary. The AP item on the range of $x = A\sin\omega t$ is unkeyed and left out.

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.why: A vector is any quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as a displacement, a velocity of 90 km/h east, or a force of 500 newtons straight down. In one-dimensional motion its direction is given simply by a plus or minus sign, and on paper it is drawn as an arrow whose length is proportional to its magnitude and which points in the same direction as the vector.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding, where speed is a scalar because it does not change when the direction changes; conceptual questions 1 to 4 ask whether a speed, an acceleration and a temperature are vectors or scalars.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.why: A scalar is any quantity that has a magnitude but no direction. A temperature of 20 ºC, the 250 kilocalories in a candy bar, a 90 km/h speed limit and a distance of 2.0 m are all scalars, and a scalar can be negative, in which case the minus sign indicates a point on a scale rather than a direction. Scalars are never represented by arrows.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Check Your Understanding; conceptual questions 1, 2 and 4, the last on a temperature of −5 ºC.

concepts.name: Assign a coordinate system
concepts.why: To describe the direction of a vector you must designate a coordinate system within the reference frame, which for one-dimensional motion is a single coordinate line. Motion to the right or upward is usually taken as positive, but it can be more convenient to make downward positive for a falling object or left positive for runners heading left. It does not matter as long as the system is clear and consistent, and once you assign a positive direction and start solving a problem, you cannot change it.
concepts.evidence: The section’s second learning objective; the AP item on how to set up the coordinates for a dropped feather; the choice of positive direction that every example of sections 2.4 and 2.7 begins with.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.why: In physics the definition of time is simple: time is change, or the interval over which change occurs. Every measurement of time involves measuring a change in some physical quantity, whether a number on a digital clock, a heartbeat or the position of the Sun in the sky, and the amount of change is calibrated by comparison with a standard such as the second.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; conceptual question 1 asks for a device that measures time and for the change in it that indicates a change in time.

concepts.name: Elapsed time, $\kdt = \ktf - \kto$
concepts.why: We are usually interested in the elapsed time for a particular motion, which is found by noting the time at the beginning and the end of the motion and subtracting the two. Life is simpler if the beginning time is taken to be zero, as when we use a stopwatch, and in this text motion starts at $\kto = 0$ and the symbol $\kt$ is used for elapsed time unless otherwise specified.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the lecture that runs from 11:00 to 11:50; the stopwatch convention that every later kinematic equation assumes.

concepts.name: Instantaneous speed
concepts.why: Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, so it is a scalar with no direction. A passenger with an instantaneous velocity of −3.0 m/s toward the rear of the plane has an instantaneous speed of 3.0 m/s, and a shopper moving at 40 km/h due north has an instantaneous speed of 40 km/h.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; conceptual questions 3 and 5 ask how a speedometer’s reading and the instantaneous velocity are related.

concepts.name: Average speed, distance traveled divided by elapsed time
concepts.why: Average speed is the distance traveled divided by the elapsed time. Because the distance traveled can be greater than the magnitude of the displacement, the average speed can be greater than the magnitude of the average velocity: a half-hour drive to a store and back that puts 6 km on the odometer has an average speed of 12 km/h and an average velocity of zero. Average speed is therefore not simply the magnitude of average velocity.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the trip to the store in Figure 2.10; Check Your Understanding (b); conceptual questions 2 and 4; problems 1(a), 5 and 7(a); Example 1.1 of section 1.2 calculated one.

concepts.name: Average acceleration, $\kab = \kdv / \kdt$
concepts.why: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time over which it changes, that is, the final velocity minus the initial velocity over the elapsed time. Its sign follows the sign of the change in velocity rather than the direction of motion: a train slowing from a negative velocity to rest has a positive average acceleration.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the boxed definition; Example 2.1, the racehorse leaving the gate; Examples 2.4, 2.5 and 2.7 for the subway train; problems 1 and 3.

concepts.name: Instantaneous acceleration $\ka$
concepts.why: Instantaneous acceleration is the acceleration at a specific instant in time, obtained by considering an infinitesimally small interval, as for instantaneous velocity. Using only algebra we choose an average acceleration that is representative of the motion: when the acceleration varies only slightly, the average over the whole interval will do, and when it varies greatly it is best to consider smaller time intervals and choose an average acceleration for each.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the two graphs of instantaneous acceleration against time in Figure 2.17; the section summary.

concepts.name: Deceleration
concepts.why: Although acceleration is in the direction of the change in velocity, it is not always in the direction of motion. When an object slows down, its acceleration is opposite to the direction of its motion, and this is called deceleration. Deceleration always reduces speed.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the subway train arriving at a station in Figure 2.13; Examples 2.5 and 2.7; Check Your Understanding, the airplane landing while traveling east; conceptual questions 4 and 5.

concepts.name: The sign of the acceleration against the sign of the velocity
concepts.why: Negative acceleration is acceleration in the negative direction of the chosen coordinate system, and it may or may not be a deceleration: a negative acceleration will increase a negative velocity, and a positive acceleration slows a train that is moving to the left. If the acceleration has the same sign as the velocity, the object is speeding up, and if it has the opposite sign, the object is slowing down.
concepts.evidence: The Misconception Alert on deceleration against negative acceleration and the four cars of Figure 2.14; the passage Sign and Direction; Example 2.7; Check Your Understanding; conceptual questions 4 and 5; the AP item on the book pushed across a table with each direction taken as positive.

concepts.name: Calculate an average acceleration from two velocities and a time
concepts.why: To find an average acceleration, draw a sketch and assign a coordinate system, identify the initial and final velocities with their signs and the elapsed time, find the change in velocity as the final velocity minus the initial velocity, and divide by the time. When the units are mixed, as with a velocity in kilometers per hour and a time in seconds, convert everything into meters and seconds before dividing.
concepts.evidence: The section’s second learning objective; Example 2.1 and the subway Examples 2.4, 2.5 and 2.7, with Example 2.6 finding an average velocity by the same steps; problems 1 and 3.

concepts.name: The six problem-solving steps
concepts.why: While there is no simple step-by-step method that works for every problem, six general procedures make problem solving easier and more meaningful: examine the situation to determine which physical principles are involved and draw a sketch with a positive direction marked on it; make a list of what is given or can be inferred, the knowns; identify exactly what needs to be determined, the unknowns; find an equation or set of equations that contains only one unknown; substitute the knowns with their units and obtain a numerical solution complete with units; and check whether the answer is reasonable. The steps are often taken in a different order or several at once, and with practice they become almost automatic.
concepts.evidence: The six numbered steps and the section summary; conceptual questions 1 and 2, on what is needed to choose an equation and on what to do last; every worked example of sections 2.5 and 2.7 follows the steps.

concepts.name: Recognize an unreasonable result and find its cause
concepts.why: Physics must describe nature accurately, and some problems have results that are unreasonable because one premise is unreasonable or because the premises are inconsistent with one another. A runner who accelerates at 0.40 m/s² for 100 s would reach 40 m/s, about 89 mph, which is four times faster than a person can run. To check a result, solve the problem in the usual way, ask whether the answer is too large or too small or has the wrong sign or the wrong units, and if it is unreasonable look for the premise that caused it, here the time of 100 s. Checking builds intuition about nature as well as uncovering errors.
concepts.evidence: The passage Unreasonable Results with its three steps and the runner; conceptual question 2; the Unreasonable Results problems of sections 3.4 and 3.5.

concepts.name: Free fall
concepts.why: The most remarkable fact about falling objects is that, if air resistance and friction are negligible, all objects at a given location fall toward the center of Earth with the same constant acceleration, independent of their mass, as a hammer and a feather did together on the Moon. An object falling without air resistance or friction is in free fall, and that assumption opens a broad class of situations to the kinematic equations.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the hammer and the feather of Figure 2.37; the note that every problem of the section assumes air resistance is negligible; conceptual question 4 asks what changes when it is not.

concepts.name: Kinematic equations for free fall, $\ky = \kyo + \kvo\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$
concepts.why: For straight up and down motion with no air resistance, the motion is one-dimensional with a constant acceleration of magnitude $\kg$, so the kinematic equations apply with $\ky$ for the vertical position and $\ka = -\kg$ when up is positive: $\kv = \kvo - \kg\kt$, $\ky = \kyo + \kvo\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ and $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$. The same equations describe a rock thrown up, a rock thrown down and an object simply dropped; only the initial velocity differs.
concepts.evidence: The boxed equations; Examples 2.14 and 2.15; Check Your Understanding, the ice falling 30.0 m; problems 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 and 17.

concepts.name: At the highest point the velocity is zero and the acceleration is still $-\kg$
concepts.why: A rock thrown upward slows, stops for an instant at its highest point and falls back. At that point its velocity is zero, but its acceleration is still −9.80 m/s², as it is for the whole trip, while the rock is moving up and while it is moving down. Knowing that $\kv = 0$ at the top is what lets us find the maximum height from the initial velocity, or the initial velocity from the height reached.
concepts.evidence: The discussion of Example 2.14, where the rock is highest at 1.33 s; conceptual questions 1 and 2; problems 3, the basketball player’s takeoff velocity, and 5, the height of the dolphin’s jump.

concepts.name: The speed of a falling object depends only on its initial speed and its height
concepts.why: Because only the acceleration due to gravity is acting, the speed of a falling object depends only on its initial speed and its vertical position relative to the starting point, not on whether it was thrown up or down. A rock thrown up at 13.0 m/s passes its starting point again at −13.0 m/s, and 5.10 m below it is moving at −16.4 m/s, exactly the velocity it has when thrown straight down at 13.0 m/s. At any height on the way up and at the same height on the way down the speeds are equal and the velocities opposite.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.15 and its discussion; conceptual questions 3 and 4; problems 7(b) and 9.

concepts.name: Find $\kg$ from the distance and the time of a fall
concepts.why: The precise acceleration due to gravity at a place can be found from data taken in an introductory laboratory: an object for which air resistance is negligible is dropped, and the time it takes to fall a known distance is measured. With $\kvo = 0$ the position equation gives $\ka = 2(\ky - \kyo)/\kt^2$, so a fall of 1.0000 m in 0.45173 s gives $\kg = 9.8010$ m/s², more precise than the average value because the data are precise. Two velocities at two heights serve as well, through $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$.
concepts.evidence: The section’s learning objective on the effects of gravity; Example 2.16; the Take-Home Experiment on reaction time; the AP item on the spacecraft falling toward an asteroid.

concepts.name: Slope and intercept of a straight-line graph, $y = mx + b$
concepts.why: When two physical quantities are plotted against one another, the horizontal axis is usually the independent variable and the vertical axis the dependent variable, and a straight-line graph has the general form $y = mx + b$. Here $m$ is the slope, the rise divided by the run, and $b$ is the $y$-intercept, the point at which the line crosses the vertical axis. Reading a slope and an intercept off a graph of motion is how the motion equations appear in graphical form.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for independent variable, dependent variable, slope and $y$-intercept; Figure 2.44; the jet car’s graph of position against time, whose slope and intercept give $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$.

concepts.name: The slope of a graph of $\kx$ against $\kt$ is the velocity
concepts.why: On a graph of position against time the rise is a change in position and the run is a change in time, so the slope is $\kdx / \kdt$, the velocity. A straight line means constant velocity, and its slope is the average velocity between any two points; a curve means the velocity is changing, and its steepness at each point is the velocity there. The intercept is the position at time zero, so the graph gives $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note The Slope of $x$ vs. $t$; Example 2.17; problems 1(a), 2, 3(a) and 6; conceptual questions 1 and 2.

concepts.name: The slope of a graph of $\kv$ against $\kt$ is the acceleration
concepts.why: On a graph of velocity against time the rise is a change in velocity and the run is a change in time, so the slope is $\kdv / \kdt$, the acceleration. A straight line means the acceleration is constant, and with the intercept $\kvo$ the graph gives $\kv = \kvo + \ka\kt$, the same relationship that was derived algebraically. When the line curves, the acceleration is changing, and it can be read from the slope at each point.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note The Slope of $v$ vs. $t$; Example 2.19; problems 1(b), 3(b), 4 and 7(c); conceptual questions 3 and 4.

concepts.name: Find an instantaneous slope from a tangent line
concepts.why: The slope of a curve at a point is equal to the slope of a straight line tangent to the curve at that point. To find it, draw the tangent, read the coordinates of two widely separated points on it, and divide the change in the vertical quantity by the change in time; any error in reading data from the graph is proportionally smaller when the interval is larger. Done at every point of a position graph this gives the velocity graph, and done on the velocity graph it gives the acceleration.
concepts.evidence: Examples 2.18 and 2.19; problems 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, each of which asks for the slope of a curve at a given time.

concepts.name: Derive one motion graph from another
concepts.why: A graph of position against time can be used to generate a graph of velocity against time, and a graph of velocity against time a graph of acceleration against time, by finding the slope of the graph at every point. Where a graph is linear the slope is the same everywhere and the derived graph is flat; where it bends, the derived graph rises or falls. The reverse also holds: a flat velocity graph means a straight position graph, and a sloping one means a curve.
concepts.evidence: The section’s fourth and fifth learning objectives; Figure 2.46, where the velocity graph is built from the tangents of the position graph; Check Your Understanding (b); conceptual questions 2, 4, 5 and 6; problems 5 and 8; the AP item of section 2.4 on the book sliding to a stop.

concepts.name: Read a motion from its graph
concepts.why: A graph, like a picture, is worth a thousand words, and a graph of motion can be read for the motion itself: where a position graph is steepest the velocity is greatest, where it is flat the velocity is zero, and where it falls the velocity is negative; where a velocity graph is flat the acceleration is zero, and where it falls the object is slowing. A ship whose velocity graph is level, then drops steeply, then drops more gently moves at constant velocity, decelerates hard, then decelerates gently until it stops.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a), the ship coming into harbor; conceptual questions 1, 2 and 4, which ask when the velocity or the acceleration is greatest, zero and negative; problem 7, which reads a sprinter’s average velocity, instantaneous velocity, acceleration and race time off a velocity graph.

concepts.name: Perpendicular displacements add by the Pythagorean theorem
concepts.why: A walk of 9 blocks east followed by 5 blocks north covers 14 blocks, but the straight-line distance between the two points is only 10.3 blocks, because the two legs of the trip and the straight-line path form a right triangle and the Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse. This is one example of a general characteristic of vectors: the total displacement is the sum of its perpendicular parts, and its magnitude comes from the theorem. Vectors that are not perpendicular cannot be added this way.
concepts.evidence: The walk in the city and Figures 3.3 to 3.5; problem 1 of section 3.2 and problem 4 of section 3.3, where two perpendicular legs are added.

concepts.name: Horizontal and vertical components of a vector
concepts.why: For two-dimensional motion, the path of an object can be represented with three vectors: one shows the straight-line path between the initial and final points of the motion, one shows the horizontal component of the motion, and one shows the vertical component. The horizontal and vertical components add together to give the straight-line path, and each is affected only by the motion in its own direction.
concepts.evidence: The three vectors of Figure 3.5; the glossary term component in section 3.2; problems 3 and 11 of section 3.2, which ask for the components of a displacement and of a velocity.

concepts.name: Independence of perpendicular motions
concepts.why: The horizontal and vertical components of two-dimensional motion are independent of each other: any motion in the horizontal direction does not affect motion in the vertical direction, and vice versa. A ball dropped from rest and a ball thrown horizontally at the same instant from the same height are at the same vertical position at every flash of a stroboscope, while the thrown ball covers the same horizontal distance between flashes because nothing accelerates it horizontally. This is the key to analyzing projectile motion, which is resolved into motions along perpendicular directions.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note Independence of Motion; the two baseballs of Figure 3.6; the three AP items, on the acceleration of a thrown ball, on the graph of the vertical acceleration of a ball launched horizontally, and on the experiment with three balls; conceptual question 4 of section 3.4, the two coins flicked and nudged off a table.

concepts.name: A vector in two dimensions: magnitude and direction
concepts.why: In two dimensions the direction of a vector is specified relative to a reference frame by an angle, and the vector is drawn as an arrow with a length proportional to its magnitude, its tail at the starting point and its head at the pointed end. In this text a vector is written in boldface, its magnitude in italics and its direction by an angle, such as the total displacement $\mathbf{D}$ of 10.3 blocks at 29.1º north of east.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for magnitude, direction, head and tail; the boxed note Vectors in this Text; Figures 3.8 and 3.9; conceptual questions 1, 2, 3 and 5.

concepts.name: Resultant vector
concepts.why: The resultant is the sum of two or more vectors, drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last. Its magnitude is at most the sum of the magnitudes, when the vectors point the same way, and at least their difference, so two nonzero vectors add to zero only when they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for resultant and resultant vector; conceptual questions 6 and 8; conceptual question 1 of section 3.3, on the greatest and the smallest magnitude a resultant can have.

concepts.name: Add vectors graphically by the head-to-tail method
concepts.why: To add vectors graphically, draw the first as an arrow using a ruler and protractor, place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first and continue for every vector to be added, then draw the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last and measure its length with a ruler and its angle with a protractor. The method is valid for any number of vectors and is limited in accuracy only by the precision with which the drawing can be made and the precision of the measuring tools.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the six numbered steps and Figure 3.10; Example 3.1, the woman who takes a walk; problems 1, 5, 7 and 9.

concepts.name: Vector addition is commutative, $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{A}$
concepts.why: The resultant is independent of the order in which the vectors are added: adding the same displacements in a different order ends at the same point. This is true in every case and is an important characteristic of vectors, just as you get the same result whether you add 2 + 3 or 3 + 2.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the discussion of Example 3.1 and Figure 3.18; problem 5 of section 3.3, which adds the same two legs in the other order.

concepts.name: Vector subtraction, $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A} + (-\mathbf{B})$
concepts.why: The negative of a vector has the same magnitude but the opposite direction, and subtracting a vector is defined to be adding its negative. A sailor who follows the second leg of her directions in the opposite direction arrives at $\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}$ instead of at $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$, a very different place from the dock, and the graphical method of subtraction is the head-to-tail method with $-\mathbf{B}$ in place of $\mathbf{B}$.
concepts.evidence: Figure 3.19; Example 3.2, the woman sailing a boat; problems 7 and 9; problem 7 of section 3.3.

concepts.name: Multiplying a vector by a scalar
concepts.why: When a vector is multiplied by a scalar $c$, its magnitude becomes the absolute value of $c$ times the original magnitude; if $c$ is positive the direction does not change, and if $c$ is negative the direction is reversed. Walking three times as far on a leg of 27.5 m at 66.0º north of east means walking 82.5 m in the same direction, and division is multiplication by a scalar between 0 and 1.
concepts.evidence: The passage Multiplication of Vectors and Scalars and the section summary; conceptual question 7 asks why a scalar cannot be added to a vector.

concepts.name: Resolve a vector into perpendicular components
concepts.why: In many cases we need the opposite of addition: to take a single vector and find what other vectors added together produce it, usually its components along perpendicular axes such as north and east. Knowing that a total displacement is 10.3 blocks in a direction 29.0º north of east, we can find how many blocks east and north had to be walked, graphically with a ruler and protractor or analytically with the right triangle the components form.
concepts.evidence: The passage Resolving a Vector into Components; problems 3 and 11, which ask for the components of a displacement and of a velocity; problems 3 and 9 of section 3.3.

concepts.name: Components from magnitude and direction, $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$
concepts.why: If a vector is known by its magnitude $\kA$ and its angle $\theta$ from the $x$-axis, its components along the axes are the two legs of a right triangle, $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$. The component vectors add to the vector, but their magnitudes do not add to its magnitude: 3 m east and 4 m north make 5 m, not 7 m, and no component can be greater than the magnitude of the vector itself.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note Determining Vectors and Vector Components with Analytical Methods; Figures 3.25 and 3.26; conceptual questions 2, 3 and 4; problems 3 and 9.

concepts.name: Magnitude and direction from components, $\kA = \sqrt{\kAx^2 + \kAy^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kAy / \kAx)$
concepts.why: If the perpendicular components of a vector are known, the vector can be found analytically: its magnitude is $\sqrt{\kAx^2 + \kAy^2}$, which is just the Pythagorean theorem for the right triangle the components form, and its direction relative to the $x$-axis is $\tan^{-1}(\kAy / \kAx)$. For components of 9 and 5 blocks this gives 10.3 blocks at 29.1º, as in the walk in the city.
concepts.evidence: The boxed note Determining Vectors and Vector Components with Analytical Methods; Figure 3.27; the last two steps of Example 3.3; problems 1, 4, 5 and 11.

concepts.name: Add and subtract vectors by components
concepts.why: To add vectors analytically, identify the $x$- and $y$-axes, find the components of each vector with $\kAx = \kA\cos\theta$ and $\kAy = \kA\sin\theta$, add the components along each axis to get $\kRx = \kAx + \kBx$ and $\kRy = \kAy + \kBy$, and then find the magnitude $\kR = \sqrt{\kRx^2 + \kRy^2}$ and the direction $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kRy / \kRx)$ of the resultant. Components along the same axis add like ordinary numbers, which is what makes the method work. Subtraction is identical, since the components of $-\mathbf{B}$ are the negatives of the components of $\mathbf{B}$. Analytical methods are more concise, accurate and precise than graphical methods, which are limited by the accuracy of a drawing.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term analytical method; the four numbered steps; Example 3.3; problems 1, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 11; every velocity problem of section 3.5.

concepts.name: Projectile motion
concepts.why: Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown or projected into the air, subject only to the acceleration of gravity; the object is called a projectile and its path is called its trajectory. Because gravity is vertical, the horizontal and vertical motions are independent, and the key to analyzing a projectile is to break its curved path into a horizontal motion with no acceleration and a vertical motion with $\kay = -\kg$. Air resistance is taken to be negligible, and the trajectory is then a parabola.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for projectile, projectile motion, trajectory and air resistance; conceptual questions 1 and 2, on the velocity and the acceleration during the flight; the AP items of section 3.1 on a thrown ball.

concepts.name: Horizontal motion of a projectile, $\kx = \kxo + \kvx\kt$ with $\kvx$ constant
concepts.why: With air resistance negligible there is no acceleration along the horizontal axis, so the horizontal component of the velocity stays at its initial value $\kvx = \kvo\cos\theta_0$ and the horizontal displacement is simply $\kvx\kt$. The horizontal motion continues at this constant velocity for as long as the vertical motion keeps the projectile in the air.
concepts.evidence: The boxed Horizontal Motion equations and Figure 3.35(b); Example 3.4(c); problems 1, 3(b) and 17; the AP item on graphing the horizontal and vertical velocities of a ball launched horizontally, and the AP items of section 3.2 on the same tables.

concepts.name: Vertical motion of a projectile, $\kvy = \kvoy - \kg\kt$ and $\ky = \kyo + \kvoy\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$
concepts.why: Along the vertical axis a projectile is in free fall with the initial vertical velocity $\kvoy = \kvo\sin\theta_0$, so the kinematic equations apply with $\kay = -\kg$ when up is positive: $\kvy = \kvoy - \kg\kt$, $\ky = \kyo + \kvoy\kt - \tfrac{1}{2}\kg\kt^2$ and $\kvy^2 = \kvoy^2 - 2\kg(\ky - \kyo)$. The vertical velocity decreases as the object rises, is zero at the highest point and grows again downward as it falls. The time a projectile is in the air is governed by its vertical motion alone, and time is the one variable the two motions share.
concepts.evidence: The boxed Vertical Motion equations and Figure 3.35(c); Examples 3.4(a), 3.4(b) and 3.5(a); problems 1, 3(a), 3(c), 13 and 15; the AP items on the tables of heights, held from section 3.2.

concepts.name: Solve a projectile problem by resolving and recombining
concepts.why: To analyze projectile motion, resolve the initial velocity into components along the horizontal and vertical axes, treat the motion as two independent one-dimensional motions linked only by the time, solve for the unknowns in each, and recombine the components with $\ks = \sqrt{\kx^2 + \ky^2}$ and $\kv = \sqrt{\kvx^2 + \kvy^2}$ and the angles $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\ky / \kx)$ and $\theta_v = \tan^{-1}(\kvy / \kvx)$ when the total displacement or velocity is wanted. The vertical equation is often a quadratic in the time, and the root that describes an event before the launch is discarded.
concepts.evidence: The four numbered steps and the boxed Total displacement and velocity equations; Examples 3.4 and 3.5; problems 3(d), 5, 13, 15, 17 and 21.

concepts.name: Maximum height of a projectile, $\kh = \kvoy^2 / 2\kg$
concepts.why: The highest point in any trajectory, called the apex, is reached when the vertical velocity is zero, and solving $\kvy^2 = \kvoy^2 - 2\kg\ky$ at that point gives the maximum height $\kh = \kvoy^2 / 2\kg$. It depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity, so any projectile with a 67.6 m/s initial vertical component of velocity rises 233 m, whatever its horizontal velocity.
concepts.evidence: Example 3.4(a) and the passage that follows it; the section summary; problems 9(b) and 23; the Critical Thinking item on the heights reached by two launchers, which the book prints with section 3.5 and this section takes.

concepts.name: Range of a projectile on level ground, $\kR = \kvo^2 \sin 2\theta_0 / \kg$
concepts.why: On level ground the range is the horizontal distance a projectile travels, $\kR = \kvo^2\sin 2\theta_0 / \kg$ when air resistance is negligible. The greater the initial speed the greater the range, the maximum range for a given speed is obtained at 45º, and for every other angle there is a second angle, its complement, that gives the same range with a different maximum height. The range also depends on $\kg$, which is why a golf ball travels so far on the Moon, and when the range is large the Earth curves away beneath the projectile, until at a great enough speed it goes into orbit.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Figure 3.38; conceptual question 3 on the archer’s choice of angle; problems 5, 7, 9, 11, 19, 21 and 23; problem 25 derives the equation.

concepts.name: Relative velocity
concepts.why: A velocity is always relative to some reference frame, and an object such as a boat on a river or a plane in a crosswind has a velocity relative to the medium while the medium has a velocity relative to an observer on solid ground. The velocity of the object relative to the observer is the vector sum of the two, so the boat moves diagonally to the shore and the plane does not move in the direction in which it is pointed. In one-dimensional motion velocities add like ordinary numbers: a ball driven at 30 m/s by a player running at 5 m/s moves at 35 m/s relative to the goalkeeper.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; Figures 3.40 and 3.41; conceptual questions 1 and 2; problems 1, 3 and 13, the last on galaxies receding from one another.

concepts.name: Add velocities by components
concepts.why: Velocity is a vector, so the rules of vector addition apply to it: the components are $\kvx = \kv\cos\theta$ and $\kvy = \kv\sin\theta$, and the magnitude and direction come back from $\kv = \sqrt{\kvx^2 + \kvy^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kvy / \kvx)$. Choosing a coordinate system with one axis parallel to one of the velocities makes the mathematics easier, as it does for a boat heading straight across a river, and when the total velocity is known, the same components give the unknown velocity of a wind or a current.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term vector addition; the four boxed equations; Examples 3.6 and 3.7; problems 1, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 15.

concepts.name: Classical relativity
concepts.why: Relativity is the study of how different observers moving relative to each other measure the same phenomenon, and classical relativity, first discussed correctly by Galileo and Newton, is limited to speeds below about 1% of the speed of light. Binoculars dropped from the mast of a moving ship fall straight down to an observer on the ship and along a curved path to an observer on shore, yet both see them strike the deck at the base of the mast; a coin dropped in an airliner falls at 5.42 m/s to the passenger and at 260.06 m/s, almost horizontally, to an observer on the ground. To get the correct description, it is crucial to specify the velocities relative to the observer.
concepts.evidence: Glossary terms for relativity and classical relativity; Figures 3.45 and 3.46; Example 3.8; conceptual questions 3, 4 and 5; problem 13, the galaxies receding from one another.

concepts.name: Dynamics
concepts.why: Kinematics describes how an object moves, and says nothing about why it moves that way. Dynamics is the study of the forces that cause objects and systems to move, and Newton’s laws of motion are its foundation, so the rest of the chapter rests on knowing what question dynamics asks.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by naming dynamics as the study of the forces that cause motion, the chapter introduction sets it against kinematics, and the section summary states it again.

concepts.name: Force
concepts.why: A force is a push or a pull, and it has both a magnitude and a direction, so it is a vector and adds as the vectors of the previous chapter add. Every later idea in the chapter is stated in terms of forces, so the working definition comes first.
concepts.evidence: The section defines force as a push or a pull with magnitude and direction, Figure 4.3 adds the forces of two skaters head to tail, and the conceptual question asks what properties allow forces to be classified as vectors.

concepts.name: External force
concepts.why: Only the forces that act on a body from outside it change its motion, so before any law can be applied the forces have to be sorted into those that come from outside and those that act between parts of the body. A body cannot push itself along.
concepts.evidence: The section defines an external force as one that originates outside the object or system, the free-body diagram of Figure 4.3 shows only external forces, and two AP items ask whether a body can exert a force on itself and what exerts the force that moves a rowed boat.

concepts.name: Draw a free-body diagram
concepts.why: A free-body diagram draws the body as a single point and every external force acting on it as an arrow from that point, so the forces can be added without the picture of the situation getting in the way. It is the drawing every problem in this chapter starts from.
concepts.evidence: The section names Figure 4.3(b) as the first free-body diagram of the book and defines the technique, and the diagrams are drawn again in the worked examples of 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and 4.7.

concepts.name: Standard unit of force
concepts.why: A force can be measured only against some force that can be produced again and again, just as a distance is measured against a standard distance. The stretched spring gives such a standard, and the magnitude of any other force can then be stated as a multiple of it.
concepts.evidence: The section takes the restoring force of a spring stretched a fixed distance as a standard, Figure 4.4 shows a spring scale reading six units, and the conceptual question asks the reader to propose a different standard that can produce the same force repeatedly.

concepts.name: Newton’s first law of motion
concepts.why: A body at rest remains at rest, and a body in motion remains in motion at a constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on it. The law says that a change in velocity has a cause, so a sliding object that stops has been stopped by something, and friction is that something.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law in a box, argues it from a block sliding on a surface made smoother and smoother, and both conceptual questions and the whole of 4.3 rest on it.

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.why: Inertia is the property of a body that keeps it at rest or keeps it moving at a constant velocity, which is why Newton’s first law is also called the law of inertia. Some bodies have more of it than others, and that difference is what mass measures.
concepts.evidence: The section defines inertia and names the first law the law of inertia, the boulder and the basketball show that bodies differ in it, and a conceptual question asks how inertia and mass are related.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.why: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, and it is how much inertia the body has. Unlike weight, mass does not vary with location: a body has the same mass on Earth, in orbit and on the Moon, and masses are found in practice by comparison with the standard kilogram.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mass as the quantity of matter and the measure of inertia, the Check Your Understanding box asks whether a kilogram of cotton balls or a kilogram of gold has more mass, and a conceptual question asks which of weight and mass is the intrinsic property.

concepts.name: Define the system of interest
concepts.why: Which forces count as external depends on where the boundary of the system is drawn, so the boundary has to be chosen before Newton’s second law can be written down. The wagon and its rider make one system; the wagon alone makes another, and the two give different net forces.
concepts.evidence: The section defines a system by its boundaries and works the wagon of Figure 4.5 both ways, a conceptual question asks how the choice of system affects which forces must be considered, and the first problem on the two children pushing a wagon asks for the system before it asks for the acceleration.

concepts.name: Net external force
concepts.why: The net external force is the vector sum of all the external forces acting on a system, found head to tail or by components as any other vectors are. It is the single force that stands in for all of them, and it is what the second law relates to the acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the net external force and adds the forces of the wagon in Figure 4.5(b), the rocket sled example writes it as four thrusts minus friction, and the problems ask for it directly.

concepts.name: Newton’s second law of motion, $\kFnet = m\ka$
concepts.why: The acceleration of a system is directly proportional to the net external force on it and in the same direction, and inversely proportional to its mass. This is the equation the rest of the chapter and much of the book is worked with, and it is a relation among three quantities that can each be measured on their own, not a definition.
concepts.evidence: The section builds the law from the two proportionalities, states it in a box in three forms, and applies it to the lawn mower and the rocket sled; a dozen problems ask for a force, a mass or an acceleration from the other two.

concepts.name: The newton, $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$
concepts.why: The SI unit of force is defined from Newton’s second law: one newton is the force that accelerates a one-kilogram system at one metre per second squared. Substituting the units is also what turns an answer in newtons per kilogram into an acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the newton under its own heading, the lawn mower example substitutes kilogram metres per second squared for newtons to get its answer, and the problems are all set in newtons.

concepts.name: Weight, $\kwgt = m\kg$
concepts.why: The weight of an object is the gravitational force on it, and Newton’s second law applied to a falling object gives its magnitude as the mass times the acceleration due to gravity. Weight is a force and is measured in newtons, and it changes with the body the object is near.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the equation in a box, works out that a 1.0 kg object weighs 9.8 N on Earth and about 1.7 N on the Moon, and the problems on the astronaut on the Moon and the lunar module turn on it.

concepts.name: Mass against weight
concepts.why: Mass is the quantity of matter and does not change with place; weight is the gravitational force on that mass and does. The two words are used interchangeably in everyday language, and separating them is what makes the Moon problems and the bathroom-scale questions come out right.
concepts.evidence: The section sets the two against each other in the Common Misconceptions box and the Take-Home Experiment on bathroom scales, and the problem on the astronaut on the Moon asks for the weight on Earth and the mass in both places.

concepts.name: Friction
concepts.why: Friction is a force that opposes the motion past each other of objects that are touching, and it appears in almost every free-body diagram of the chapter. Naming it as an external force is what lets the first law account for a sliding object slowing down.
concepts.evidence: The section defines friction where the wagon of Figure 4.5 is analysed, the rocket sled example subtracts 650 N of it from the thrust, and the problems on the mower, the motorcycle and the wagon all give a friction force.

concepts.name: Newton’s third law of motion
concepts.why: Whenever one body exerts a force on a second body, the first body experiences a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force it exerts. Forces always occur in pairs, and no body can exert a force on another without experiencing one itself.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law in a box, shows it in the swimmer pushing off the wall in Figure 4.9, and the AP items on the ball hitting the ceiling, the skaters and the Earth and the Moon all turn on it.

concepts.name: The two forces of a pair act on different bodies
concepts.why: The two forces of a third-law pair look as though they should cancel, and they do not, because they act on different systems. The wall pushes on the swimmer’s feet and the swimmer’s feet push on the wall, and only the first of those is an external force on the swimmer.
concepts.evidence: The section makes the point with the swimmer of Figure 4.9 and lists the walking professor, the car’s drive wheels, the rocket and the bird, and a conceptual question asks the football lineman how he can out-push an opponent who pushes back just as hard.

concepts.name: Internal forces cancel and do not enter the second law
concepts.why: A force between two parts of one system is matched by its equal and opposite partner inside the same system, so the two add to nothing and the net external force is unchanged. That is why the professor’s push on the cart does not appear when the professor and the cart are taken as one system.
concepts.evidence: The section works the professor and cart of Figure 4.10 twice, once as System 1 and once as System 2, and the discussion states that internal forces cancel; a conceptual question asks how the choice of system decides whether a pair cancels.

concepts.name: Thrust
concepts.why: A rocket moves forward by throwing gas backward: it pushes hard on the gas, and by the third law the gas pushes just as hard forward on the rocket. That forward reaction force is called thrust, and it is what drives rockets, aeroplanes and cars.
concepts.evidence: The section defines thrust where the rocket and the helicopter are discussed, and the rocket sled of 4.3 and the rocket problems of 4.6 and 4.7 are worked with it.

concepts.name: Normal force $\kN$
concepts.why: Whatever supports a load must push up on it, and where that support is perpendicular to the surface of contact it is called the normal force. A table sags under a bag of dog food until its restoring force is as large as the weight, and on a level surface that makes the normal force equal to the weight; on an incline, or when the object accelerates, it is not.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the normal force with the dog food of Figure 4.11, the summary states that it equals the weight on a level surface, the skier example finds it from the perpendicular equation, and the toboggan and kite AP items are drawn with it.

concepts.name: Weight on an incline, $\kwpar = m\kg\sin\theta$ and $\kwperp = m\kg\cos\theta$
concepts.why: On a slope the convenient axes are along and across the surface, and the weight is the one force that lies along neither, so it is resolved into a component parallel to the slope, which drives the object down it, and a component perpendicular to it, which the normal force balances.
concepts.evidence: The section resolves the skier’s weight in the boxed note Resolving Weight into Components and Figure 4.13, the skier example uses both components, and the car on the 20º slope in the AP items is worked the same way.

concepts.name: Acceleration down a frictionless incline, $\kapar = \kg\sin\theta$
concepts.why: Dividing the parallel component of the weight by the mass cancels the mass, so every object slides down a frictionless incline of the same angle with the same acceleration, just as every object falls with the same acceleration in the absence of air resistance.
concepts.evidence: The section derives it in part (a) of the skier example and states in the discussion that the result holds regardless of mass, and part (b) shows how friction reduces it.

concepts.name: Tension
concepts.why: A tension is a force carried along the length of a flexible connector such as a rope, a cable or a tendon. A connector can only pull, never push, so the force it carries is always parallel to its length, and where there is no friction the tension is the same everywhere along it.
concepts.evidence: The section defines tension, shows the rope of Figure 4.14 pulling equally on the hand and the mass, and follows the same tension round the corners of a tendon and a bicycle brake cable in Figure 4.15; the traction conceptual questions and the spider-web and gymnast problems turn on it.

concepts.name: Tension in a rope supporting a weight, $\kTf = m\kg$
concepts.why: A mass hanging at rest from a rope has no acceleration, so the net force on it is zero and the tension must equal the weight. Once the tension is known at one point of a frictionless connector it is known everywhere along it.
concepts.evidence: The section proves it from Newton’s second law for the 5.00 kg mass of Figure 4.14 and gets 49.0 N, and the gymnast, spider web and baby-scale problems and the cable AP item ask for a tension the same way.

concepts.name: Tension from a perpendicular force, $\kTf = \kFperp / (2\sin\theta)$
concepts.why: Pushing sideways at the middle of a connector that is nearly straight creates a tension far larger than the push, because only the small vertical component of each half supports it. That is how a car is pulled out of the mud with a chain, and it is why no connector can be exactly horizontal.
concepts.evidence: The section extends the tightrope result to a perpendicular force and applies it to the chain and the car of Figure 4.18, a problem asks the reader to show the relation, and another asks for the force needed at 2.00º and at 7.00º.

concepts.name: Inertial frame of reference
concepts.why: Newton’s laws take the simple forms of this chapter only in a frame that is neither accelerating nor rotating. In an accelerating frame an observer sees forces with no physical origin, such as the westward push on a satellite seen from a rotating Earth, and those fictitious forces are an artefact of the frame.
concepts.evidence: The section distinguishes real from fictitious forces under Extended Topic: Real Forces and Inertial Frames, defines the inertial frame in the glossary, and states that every phenomenon in the text is considered in one.

concepts.name: The four steps for a problem about forces
concepts.why: A problem about forces is worked in the same four steps every time: sketch the situation and draw every force as an arrow, list the knowns and unknowns and choose the system of interest, draw the free-body diagram and apply Newton’s second law, and check that the answer and its units are reasonable.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the four steps with Tarzan on his vine in Figure 4.20 and restates them in the summary, and a dozen problems ask the reader to show explicitly how the steps are followed.

concepts.name: Net force along each axis, $\kFnetx = m\ka$ and $\kFnety = 0$
concepts.why: Before the force equations are written, decide in which directions the system accelerates. Where there is no acceleration along an axis the net force along that axis is zero, and where there is, the net force along it is the mass times that acceleration; the two axes are then two one-dimensional problems.
concepts.evidence: The section states both equations in the boxed note Applying Newton’s Second Law, the AP items on the toboggan and the elevator are answered from them, and the nurse’s cart and the snow-saucer problems use them along both axes.

concepts.name: Resolve forces onto convenient axes
