concepts.why: A two-dimensional force problem becomes a pair of one-dimensional problems as soon as the forces are projected onto a well-chosen pair of axes: one axis along the direction of motion, or along an incline, saves most of the work.
concepts.evidence: The section says in step 3 that a two-dimensional problem is broken down by projecting the forces onto axes chosen for convenience, and the snow-saucer sled, the braces on a tooth and the pair of forces adding to a total in Figure 4.25 are all worked this way.

concepts.name: Two wires at different angles carry different tensions
concepts.why: When an object hangs from two wires the horizontal components of the tensions must cancel and the vertical components must add to the weight. The two tensions are equal only when the two angles are equal; the wire that is nearer the vertical carries the greater share.
concepts.evidence: The section works the traffic light of Figure 4.22 and finds 108 N and 132 N, the discussion states when the tensions are equal, and the problem on the person pulled from a burning building is keyed with two unequal tensions.

concepts.name: What a scale reads, $\kFs = m\ka + m\kg$
concepts.why: A bathroom scale reads the force it pushes up with, not the weight. In an elevator accelerating upward it reads more than the weight, at any constant velocity it reads the weight exactly, and in free fall it reads zero and the person appears weightless.
concepts.evidence: The section works the 75.0 kg man of Figure 4.23 and gets 825 N while accelerating and 735 N at constant speed, the conceptual questions on the aircraft flown at g and the hat in the elevator turn on it, and an Unreasonable Results problem asks for the reading again.

concepts.name: Drag force
concepts.why: A drag force is the frictional force a fluid such as air or water exerts on an object moving through it, and like any friction it opposes the motion. Here it is the one unknown in Newton’s second law: subtract the mass times the acceleration from the applied force and what is left is the drag.
concepts.evidence: The barge example names the drag force, draws it opposite to the applied force in Figure 4.21 and finds it to be 7.5 × 10⁴ N, less than a six-hundredth of the weight of the ship.

concepts.name: Join kinematics to Newton’s laws in one problem
concepts.why: Forces produce accelerations, and an acceleration is what the kinematic equations are written in, so a problem can be worked from a force to a distance or from a distance back to a force. Identify which principles are involved, then use each chapter’s own strategy in turn.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the two steps and works the soccer player from a change in velocity to an average force, and eight problems marked Integrated Concepts ask for a speed, a height or a force in the same way.

concepts.name: The four basic forces
concepts.why: Only four distinct forces account for every known phenomenon: the gravitational, the electromagnetic, the weak nuclear and the strong nuclear force. Everything we feel directly except gravity is electromagnetic, and the two nuclear forces act only over the size of a nucleus or less.
concepts.evidence: The section names the four forces and tabulates their relative strengths, ranges and carrier particles in Table 4.1, the AP items ask which force explains a normal force and a rope’s tension, and the problems ask for ratios of their strengths.

concepts.name: Force field
concepts.why: All forces act at a distance, so something must carry them between objects. A force field surrounds the object that creates it and is a characteristic of that object alone; a test object placed in the field experiences a force that depends on where it is.
concepts.evidence: The section defines a force field, uses Earth’s gravitational field as the example that gives the weight at the surface, and Figure 4.24 draws the electric field between two charges.

concepts.name: Carrier particle
concepts.why: Fields leave open what actually carries a force, and the proposal that has held since Yukawa is that every force is transmitted by the exchange of an elementary particle, as two people passing a basketball push each other apart without touching.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the basketball and the exchanged meson in Figure 4.25, Table 4.1 lists the carrier particle of each of the four forces, and a conceptual question asks for an example in which an exchange gives an attractive force.

concepts.name: Kinetic friction
concepts.why: When two surfaces in contact are moving relative to one another, the friction between them is called kinetic friction. It is the force that slows a hockey puck sliding on ice, and it is the one that behaves simply enough to be written as a single product.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, and the skiing example, the incline problems and the AP item on a block sliding across a floor are all about the friction on something already moving.

concepts.name: Static friction
concepts.why: When the surfaces are not moving relative to one another, static friction can act between them. It is a responsive force, growing to be equal and opposite to whatever you push with, up to a limit, which is why a heavy crate can be pushed harder and harder and still not move.
concepts.evidence: The crate on the concrete floor is the section's first worked argument, the glossary defines the term, and the AP item on a 20 N push against a 40 N box and the conceptual question on letting up on the brake pedal both turn on it.

concepts.name: Coefficient of friction
concepts.why: The coefficient of friction is the number that carries what the two materials are. It has no units, its magnitude is usually between 0 and 1.0, and for the same pair of surfaces the kinetic coefficient is smaller than the static one, which is why a crate is easier to keep moving than it was to start.
concepts.evidence: Table 5.1 lists both coefficients for thirteen pairs of materials, the text works a 100 kg crate through both of them, and the AP item that asks whether a coefficient is greater than 0.5 tests nothing else.

concepts.name: Magnitude of static friction, $\kfs \le \mu_{\text{s}}\kN$
concepts.why: Static friction has a minimum and a maximum, and the maximum is the coefficient of static friction times the normal force. The inequality is the whole content of the result: the friction is whatever it needs to be, until the applied force passes that maximum and the object moves.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the equation, the text uses it to find the 440 N needed to start a 100 kg crate, and the problems on the wooden crate, the utility truck and the block of ice all ask for the force at which motion begins.

concepts.name: Magnitude of kinetic friction, $\kfk = \mu_{\text{k}}\kN$
concepts.why: Once an object is moving, the friction on it is the coefficient of kinetic friction times the normal force. A system in which this holds is described as one in which friction behaves simply, and it is the form every problem of the section uses.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the equation, the skiing example solves it for the coefficient, and the problems on the steel spatula, the piston, the knee joint and the freight train are all this one product.

concepts.name: Friction on a slope, $\kfk = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg\cos\theta$
concepts.why: On a slope the normal force is not the whole weight but only the component of it perpendicular to the surface, so the friction is the coefficient times mg cos θ. This is where the components of Chapter 3 and the friction of this section meet, and it is why every object slides down a given slope with the same constant acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The skiing example resolves the weight on a 25º slope, the take-home experiment with a coin on a tilted book measures the coefficient as tan θ, and the problems on the snowboarder, the skier and the car on a 6º slope all follow the same steps.

concepts.name: The atomic origin of friction
concepts.why: Friction is proportional to the normal force but not to the total area in contact, and that is only explained by looking at the surfaces closely: they touch at their high spots, the actual area of contact grows as they are pressed together, and they warm because the rubbing sets their atomic lattices vibrating.
concepts.evidence: Figure 5.5 draws the actual area of contact under a small and a large normal force, Figure 5.6 shows a probe tip deformed as it is dragged, the Making Connections note describes the research, and two of the AP items ask for the direction of friction and for where the heat comes from.

concepts.name: Drag force, $\kFD = \tfrac{1}{2}C\rho A\kv^2$
concepts.why: For a large object that is not moving too slowly, the drag force is proportional to the square of the speed, and the constant in front gathers the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. Doubling the speed of a car therefore multiplies the drag on it by about four.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the equation, Table 5.2 lists drag coefficients from an airfoil to a circular flat plate, and the problems on the Camry and the Hummer and on the factor by which drag grows between 65 and 110 km/h use it directly.

concepts.name: Drag coefficient
concepts.why: The drag coefficient is the dimensionless number that carries the shape of the object. It is determined empirically, usually in a wind tunnel, and it is why aerodynamic shaping matters: a Toyota Camry has a coefficient of 0.28 and a Hummer H2 one of 0.64, and a skydiver's own coefficient changes with the position they fall in.
concepts.evidence: Table 5.2 lists twelve values from an airfoil to a circular flat plate, Figure 5.8 shows the wind tunnel they are found in, the passage on body suits and shaved legs is about reducing them, and the conceptual question on body suits asks for the pros and the cons.

concepts.name: Terminal velocity
concepts.why: A falling body speeds up until the drag force has grown equal to its weight. The net force is then zero, so by Newton's second law the acceleration is zero and the speed stays where it is. Terminal velocity is what free fall becomes once the air is no longer neglected.
concepts.evidence: The skydiver is worked through in the text, the example finds the terminal velocity of an 85 kg skydiver falling spread eagle, and the take-home experiment with nested coffee filters measures it.

concepts.name: Terminal velocity, $\kvt = \sqrt{2m\kg/\rho C A}$
concepts.why: Setting the drag force equal to the weight and solving for the speed gives the terminal velocity in terms of the mass, the drag coefficient, the area facing the fluid and the density of the fluid. It is why a 75 kg skydiver falls at about 350 km/h head first and at about 200 km/h spread eagle.
concepts.evidence: The text works the 75 kg skydiver through it, the example repeats it for 85 kg, and the problems on the 80 kg skydiver, on two skydivers of different masses and on the falling squirrel are all this equation.

concepts.name: Stokes' law, $\kFs = 6\pi r\eta\kv$
concepts.why: When the object is very small, is going very slowly, or is in a medium denser than air, the drag is proportional to the speed itself rather than to its square, and the force is 6πrηv. This is the drag that a bacterium, a grain of pollen or a dust particle feels.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the law, the text gives the terminal velocities of bacteria and of sediment settling in a lake, and the problems on the spherical bacterium and on the ball bearing dropped in motor oil use it in both directions.

concepts.name: Size and terminal velocity
concepts.why: Divide an animal's length, breadth and height each by ten and its weight falls to a thousandth while its surface falls only to a hundredth, so the smaller animal meets relatively ten times the resistance. That is why a squirrel can fall from a tree and walk away and a person cannot.
concepts.evidence: Haldane's paragraph is quoted in full, the text compares the squirrel's terminal velocity with the skydiver's, the conceptual question asks why the squirrel is unharmed, and the Critical Thinking item on two beads compares their radii from their fall times.

concepts.name: Deformation
concepts.why: A change in shape due to the application of a force is a deformation. Even very small forces are known to cause some deformation, and for small ones two things are observed: the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed, and the size of the deformation is proportional to the force.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on a bulldozer pushing a car into a wall, the glossary defines the term, and the conceptual questions on whether your height depends on the time of day and on the stress needed to deform a spider's web are about nothing else.

concepts.name: The elastic region, permanent deformation and tensile strength
concepts.why: The proportionality between force and deformation holds only so far. Past the straight part of the graph the deformation is still elastic, past that the object is permanently deformed, and at the tensile strength it fractures. Bones are brittle, so their elastic region is small and the fracture abrupt.
concepts.evidence: Figure 5.11 draws all of the regions of the graph of deformation against applied force, the glossary defines tensile strength, and the tendon's curve in Figure 5.15 shows a material with a toe region, a linear region and a failure region.

concepts.name: Change in length, $\kdL = \frac{1}{\kY}\frac{\kF}{A}\kLo$
concepts.why: The change in length of a wire or rod is proportional to the force and to the original length and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, and the constant that carries the substance is Young's modulus. A long guitar string stretches more than a short one, and a thick one stretches less than a thin one.
concepts.evidence: Table 5.3 lists Young's modulus for twenty materials, Figure 5.12 shows one weight stretching three strings by three different amounts, and the examples on the ski-lift cable and on the femur, together with eight of the problems, all solve this equation.

concepts.name: Stress
concepts.why: The ratio of force to area is defined as stress, measured in newtons per square meter. Writing the force in this way is what lets one number describe a material rather than one particular rod, since the same force on a thinner wire is a larger stress.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the tendon's curve is plotted against tensile stress, and the bulk modulus example works with a force per unit area of 5.00 × 10⁷ N/m² at a depth of 5.00 km.

concepts.name: Strain
concepts.why: The ratio of the change in length to the original length is defined as strain, and it is a unitless quantity. Most materials behave elastically while the strain is less than about 0.1%, and a support tendon such as the ones in your leg can change its length by as much as ten percent.
concepts.evidence: The book boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, Figure 5.15 plots the tendon's stress against its strain, and the water-compression example gives its answer as the fractional change in volume.

concepts.name: Stress and strain, $\text{stress} = \kY \times \text{strain}$
concepts.why: Rearranged, the equation for the change in length says that the stress is Young's modulus times the strain. In this form it is Hooke's law again, with stress in place of force and strain in place of deformation, which is why one shape of statement covers a stretched wire, a sheared bookcase and a compressed cube.
concepts.evidence: The book states the form in words and boxes it under Strain, derives the force constant k = YA/L₀ from it, and plots the tendon's stress against its strain in Figure 5.15.

concepts.name: Shear deformation, $\kdx = \frac{1}{\kS}\frac{\kF}{A}\kLo$
concepts.why: A force applied perpendicular to the length and parallel to the cross-sectional area shears the object sideways, and the constant is the shear modulus. The equation is logical: it is easier to bend a long thin pencil than a short thick one, and both bend more easily than a steel rod of the same size.
concepts.evidence: Figure 5.16 shears a bookcase, the book boxes the expression, the example finds the mass of a picture from the 1.80 μm flex of the nail it hangs on, and the problems on a vertebra, on a disc between vertebrae and on a pencil eraser use it.

concepts.name: Change in volume, $\Delta V = \frac{1}{\kBb}\frac{\kF}{A}V_0$
concepts.why: An object squeezed evenly on all its surfaces changes its volume rather than its length, and the constant is the bulk modulus. Gases compress easily because their molecules are far apart, while liquids and solids are extraordinarily difficult to compress, which is why seawater five kilometers down has lost only 2.3% of its volume.
concepts.evidence: Figure 5.18 draws a cube compressed on every face, Table 5.3 gives bulk moduli for five liquids, the example computes the fractional decrease in the volume of seawater, and the problems on the capped bottle of grape juice and on freezing water run the equation backwards to a force per unit area.

concepts.name: Work
concepts.why: In science, work is not effort but a transfer of energy. A force does work on a system only when the system is displaced and the force has a component along that displacement, and the work is the product of that component and the distance the force acts through. Everything the rest of the chapter says about energy is stated in terms of it.
concepts.evidence: The section defines work, boxes the definition again under What is Work?, sets five cases of a force and a displacement side by side in Figure 7.2, and works Example 7.1, the lawn mower pushed 25.0 m. The mule-and-barge AP item held from 7.6 asks for the work a 1200 N force at 20º does over 10 km.

concepts.name: The sign of the work
concepts.why: The angle between the force and the displacement decides the sign. The work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of the motion, zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion or when there is no displacement at all, and negative when the force opposes the motion and so removes energy from the system.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.2(b) to (e) work through the cases, the section shows that a person holding a briefcase and a person carrying one on level ground both do no work on it, and all three conceptual questions ask for a situation in which a force does no work.

concepts.name: The joule
concepts.why: Work and energy have the units of force times distance, and in SI that is the newton-meter, which is given the name joule. One joule is not a large amount of energy; it would lift a small 100-gram apple a distance of about 1 meter.
concepts.evidence: The section names the newton-meter and the joule and gives 1 J = 1 N·m = 1 kg·m²/s², Example 7.1 converts its answer to kilocalories and compares it with a day's food, and the supermarket problem asks for its answer in joules and in kilocalories.

concepts.name: Calculate the work done by a constant force
concepts.why: Most of the chapter's problems begin by putting a force, a distance and an angle into the definition of work and reading off the energy transferred. Doing that once, and then setting the answer beside the energy a person eats in a day, is what makes the joule a size the reader can hold.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.1 finds the work done pushing a lawn mower 25.0 m with 75.0 N at 35.0º below the horizontal, and the problems ask for the work done on a can of soup, on an elevator car by its cable and by the gravitational force, on a crate pushed up a ramp, and on a grocery cart pushed against friction.

concepts.name: Work transfers energy
concepts.why: Work done on a system puts energy into it, and work done by a system takes energy out of it. Where that energy goes depends on the situation: friction carries it off as heat, while the work done carrying a briefcase up stairs is stored in the briefcase-Earth system and can be recovered at any time.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by asking what happens to the work done on a system, gives the building of the pyramids as energy stored by doing work, and sets two conceptual questions, one on when a lawn mower gains or loses energy and one asking for an example of work putting energy in and taking it out.

concepts.name: Net work
concepts.why: The work that changes a system's motion is the work done by the net external force, and it is also the sum of the work done by each force separately. A force perpendicular to the displacement, such as the weight or the normal force on a package sliding along a belt, does no work and drops out of the sum.
concepts.evidence: The section defines net work and writes it as the net force times the distance times the cosine of the angle, Figure 7.4 shows the package with its four forces, and Example 7.3 finds the net work twice, once from the net force and once by adding the work done by each of the four.

concepts.name: Work is the area under the force-distance graph
concepts.why: Plot the component of the force along the motion against the distance and the work is the area beneath the line. That is plain when the force is constant, and it stays true when the force varies, since the area can be cut into strips and each strip is the work done over its own small distance.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.3 draws both cases, 7.4 uses the same area to get the potential energy of a spring, the crane AP item held from 7.1 asks for the total work as a force ramps up, holds and winds down over 60 m, and the Critical Thinking item held from 7.9 compares a constant force with one that grows linearly.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy, $\kKE = \tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$
concepts.why: The quantity the net work changes is one half the mass times the speed squared, and it is given the name translational kinetic energy: the energy a body has by reason of its motion. Because the speed is squared, a car travelling at 100 km/h carries four times the kinetic energy it carries at 50 km/h, which helps explain why high-speed collisions are so devastating.
concepts.evidence: The section defines kinetic energy, Example 7.2 finds 3.75 J for a 30.0-kg package moving at 0.500 m/s, and the problems compare a truck with an astronaut in orbit and ask how fast an elephant must move to match a sprinter.

concepts.name: The work-energy theorem, $\kWnet = \tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}m\kvo^2$
concepts.why: Put Newton's second law and the constant-acceleration relation between speed and distance into the net work and the distance cancels, leaving the net work equal to the change in the kinetic energy. It was derived here for a constant force along the motion, but it holds in general, even for forces that vary in direction and magnitude.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the theorem and boxes it, Examples 7.4 and 7.5 use it to find the speed of the package and then how far it coasts, the problems on the car, the bumper, the boxing glove and the sprinter all turn on it, and the rocket-payload AP item held from 7.1 asks for the force from the distance and the final velocity.

concepts.name: Find a speed, a force or a distance from work and energy
concepts.why: Once the net work and the kinetic energies are known, the unknown of a problem can be any one of the three: the final speed, the force that caused the change, or the distance over which it acted. Solutions that go through energy are generally shorter and easier than those that use kinematics and dynamics alone.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.4 finds the speed of the package at the end of the push and Example 7.5 how far it coasts afterwards; the problems ask for the force that stops a car in 120 m, the force a bumper exerts as it collapses 0.200 m, the force a boxing glove exerts, and the force a sprinter pushes back on the track with.

concepts.name: Potential energy
concepts.why: Work done against a force that can give the energy back is not lost; it is stored in the system as potential energy. Potential energy is a property of a system rather than of a single body, since it belongs to the arrangement of the parts: lifting a mass stores energy in the mass-Earth system, and the system gives it back when the mass comes down.
concepts.evidence: The section defines gravitational potential energy as the energy put into the object-Earth system by lifting, explains why the word system is used, and shows the cuckoo clock in Figure 7.5 storing the energy on the way up and spending it on the way down.

concepts.name: Gravitational potential energy, $\kdPEg = m\kg\kh$
concepts.why: Lifting a mass at constant speed takes a force equal to its weight, so the work done in raising it through a height is the weight times the height. That work is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the object-Earth system, and it is the same whether the mass is lifted or lowered, with the sign of the height carrying the difference.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the expression and works the 0.500-kg cuckoo-clock weight raised 1.00 m to 4.90 J; the problems ask for the energy stored in a lake behind a dam and in the Great Pyramid of Cheops, and the pendulum-clock AP item held from 7.4 asks how much energy three masses give up in dropping 1.3 m.

concepts.name: Only differences in potential energy matter
concepts.why: Gravitational potential energy depends on relative position, so a level has to be chosen at which it is called zero. Earth's surface is the usual choice, but the choice is arbitrary: what relates to the work done, and so what has physical significance, is the difference between two positions. The rise between the first two rungs of a ladder is worth the same as the rise between the last two.
concepts.evidence: The section says the reference point is arbitrary and that only the difference matters, and gives the two pairs of rungs; the AP item on the flying baseball keys the potential energy as unknown, since no height is given.

concepts.name: The work done against gravity does not depend on the path
concepts.why: The change in gravitational potential energy is the weight times the change in height for any path between two points, not only for a straight lift, as long as the height change is small compared with the radius of Earth. That is what makes the idea worth having: multiplying mass, gravity and height is far easier than working out the work done along a complicated path.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.6 carries one television up the stairs and lifts another straight up with a pulley and finds the same change; the section states that the expression holds for any path, and the conceptual question asks whether the work done lifting a book onto a shelf depends on the path, the time, the height or the mass.

concepts.name: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy, $-\kdPEg = \kdKE$
concepts.why: Release a raised mass and gravity does work equal to the potential energy given up, so the kinetic energy grows by exactly that amount. When friction is negligible, the speed of a falling body then depends only on its initial speed and on the change in height, and not on its mass or on the path it takes.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.7 finds the roller coaster's speed at the bottom of a 20.0 m hill, from rest and then from 5.00 m/s, and notes that the mass cancels; the toy-car and downhill-ski problems repeat it, and the conceptual question asks why a coaster that rolls up and back returns at its starting speed.

concepts.name: Find the force that stops a fall from the energy and the stopping distance
concepts.why: A body that lands has kinetic energy that must be taken away by the work the ground does on it, and that work is the stopping force times the distance the body travels while stopping. Because the distance sits in the denominator, stopping in half a centimetre takes a force hundreds of times the body's weight, and bending the legs to stop over half a metre cuts that force a hundredfold.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.6 finds 3.53 × 10⁵ N on the knee joints of a 60.0-kg person who lands stiffly from 3.00 m, and the discussion sets that against a kangaroo's hopping; the same reckoning returns in 7.8's problems on jumping from a ledge and on a jogger's leg.

concepts.name: Conservative force
concepts.why: A conservative force is one for which the work done by it or against it depends only on where the motion starts and where it ends, and not on the path between. Gravity is one and the force of an ideal spring is another, and it is exactly this property that lets a potential energy be defined for the force, so that the work need never be calculated along the path at all.
concepts.evidence: The section defines a conservative force and boxes the definition, names gravity and the spring as examples, and sets the conceptual questions What is a conservative force? and What is the relationship of potential energy to conservative force?

concepts.name: Potential energy of a spring, $\kPEs = \tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2$
concepts.why: The force needed to stretch a spring grows from zero to the force constant times the stretch, so its average is half of that, and the work done is one half the force constant times the stretch squared. The same quantity is the area of the triangle under the graph of force against stretch, and because the spring force is conservative that work is stored and can be fully recovered.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.10 stretches the spring and shades the triangle, Example 7.8 launches a toy car from a spring compressed 4.00 cm, the subway-bumper problem asks for the force constant that stops a train in 0.400 m, and the dart-gun and pogo-stick items ask what compressing twice as far costs.

concepts.name: Mechanical energy
concepts.why: The total kinetic plus potential energy of a system is called its mechanical energy. Writing it as one quantity is what lets a problem be answered by comparing two configurations, since in a system with only conservative forces the energy changes only in form, moving between kinetic energy and the various kinds of potential energy while the total stays put.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energy and keeps a glossary row for it, and the conceptual question asks the reader to define it and to say what happens to it when only conservative forces act.

concepts.name: Conservation of mechanical energy, $\kKEi + \kPEi = \kKEf + \kPEf$
concepts.why: If only conservative forces act, the work-energy theorem says the change in kinetic energy is the work done by those forces, and that work is minus the change in potential energy. The two changes therefore cancel, so the kinetic and potential energies of the system add to a constant and the values at the start equal the values at the end.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the principle from the work-energy theorem and boxes both of its forms, and Example 7.8 uses it twice on the toy car, once for the speed at the bottom and once for the speed at the top of the slope.

concepts.name: Solve a problem by comparing two configurations
concepts.why: The way to use conservation of mechanical energy is to write every kind of energy the system has at the start and at the end, strike out the terms that are zero by choosing the heights and the moments well, and solve for the one that is left. The details of the path in between never enter, which is what makes the method so much shorter than following the forces.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.8 works both parts of the toy car this way, taking the initial height as zero so that most terms vanish; the pogo-stick problem asks for the maximum height a child can reach on the energy in a spring, and the catapult and water-tower AP items ask the same question of a rock and of a tank of water.

concepts.name: Nonconservative force
concepts.why: A nonconservative force is one for which the work done depends on the path taken, and friction is the plain example: the longer the route between two points, the more work is done against it. Because the work depends on the path, no potential energy can be defined for such a force, and the work it does has to be counted directly.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.13 erases a happy face along two paths between the same two points and rubs out more along the longer one, the section defines the term and keeps a glossary row for it, and the rug-and-floor AP item asks which of two routes costs more work against friction.

concepts.name: Friction turns mechanical energy into thermal energy
concepts.why: The work done by a nonconservative force adds mechanical energy to a system or removes it. Friction removes it: the energy becomes thermal energy that spreads out and leaves the system, and even where the thermal energy is caught and kept it cannot be fully turned back into work, so it is lost in that sense as well.
concepts.evidence: The section says so where it defines a nonconservative force, Figure 7.14 sets a rock dropped onto a spring, which keeps its mechanical energy, beside the same rock dropped onto the ground, which loses it to heat, sound and a dent, and the coasting-car problem asks how much thermal energy friction generated on the hill.

concepts.name: Nonconservative work changes the mechanical energy, $\kWnc = \kdKE + \kdPE$
concepts.why: Split the net work into the part done by conservative forces and the part done by nonconservative ones, and replace the conservative part by minus the change in potential energy. What is left says that the total mechanical energy changes by exactly the work the nonconservative forces do: positive work adds to it, negative work takes from it, and zero work leaves it conserved.
concepts.evidence: The section derives both forms of the relation and boxes them in the summary, Figure 7.15 shows a person pushing a crate up a ramp against friction, and the AP item on a rock falling through air resistance asks for the kinetic energy it arrives with.

concepts.name: Find a distance or a speed when friction acts
concepts.why: With friction in the problem, the work it does is the friction force times the distance, taken as negative because it opposes the motion, and it goes into the energy equation beside the kinetic and potential energies. Solving for the distance or the final speed then takes one line, where following the forces would mean combining the weight, the normal force and friction as vectors first.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.9 finds that a baseball player sliding at 6.00 m/s against 450 N of friction stops in 2.60 m and Example 7.10 that he stops in 2.31 m going up a 5.00º slope; the skier problem asks for her speed at the top of a 2.50-m rise and the coasting-car problem for the average force of friction on the hill.

concepts.name: The law of conservation of energy
concepts.why: Total energy is constant in any process. It may change in form or pass from one system to another, but the total remains the same, and writing the law down means adding to the mechanical energy and the nonconservative work one more term for every other kind of energy the system holds. In most problems all but a few of those terms are the same at the start and at the end and simply cancel.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, gives the general equation with the other energy included, and explains that the earlier examples were the case where the other energy did not change; ten AP items and the rock-from-a-bridge problem apply it, and the javelin and the bicycle conceptual questions ask for the transfers by name.

concepts.name: The forms of energy
concepts.why: Energy shows itself in many forms besides the mechanical ones: electrical energy carried by a flow of charge, chemical energy stored in the bonds of a fuel or a food, radiant energy carried by electromagnetic waves, nuclear energy released by changes inside a nucleus, and thermal energy in the random motion of atoms and molecules. Any of them can be converted into any other and any of them can do work.
concepts.evidence: The section names and defines each form and keeps a glossary row for each, Table 7.1 sets the energies of the Big Bang, a gallon of gasoline and a mosquito on one ladder, and a conceptual question asks the reader to list four forms and a conversion from each.

concepts.name: The transformation of energy
concepts.why: The changing of energy from one form into others is happening all the time, and most chains run through several forms: the chemical energy in coal becomes thermal energy in steam, which becomes the mechanical energy of a spinning turbine, which becomes electrical energy. Sunlight on a solar cell becomes electricity and then the motion of a motor.
concepts.evidence: The section walks both chains, Figure 7.19 shows the solar-powered aircraft that runs on the second, and the conceptual questions ask for the transformations along a javelin's flight, on a bicycle ride, and for a car that coasts downhill and refuels.

concepts.name: Efficiency, $\text{Eff} = \kWout/\kEin$
concepts.why: Energy is conserved in a conversion, but the useful energy or work that comes out is always less than the energy put in, and the efficiency is the ratio of the two. A coal-fired power plant turns about 40 percent of the chemical energy in its fuel into electricity, and the rest leaves as thermal energy through the flue and the cooling towers.
concepts.evidence: The section defines efficiency and Table 7.2 lists it for cycling, swimming, shovelling, engines, power plants and light bulbs; the conceptual question asks whether a device with an efficiency less than one breaks the conservation law, and 7.8's problems use the table's figures.

concepts.name: Work a problem through the energy strategy
concepts.why: The strategy is six steps: settle the system and what is asked, look at every force and ask whether its potential energy is known, use conservation of mechanical energy where every force is conservative and the general law where it is not, strike out the terms that are zero before doing any algebra, and check at the end that the signs and the size of the answer are reasonable.
concepts.evidence: The section prints the six steps as a boxed strategy and says that the chapter's examples follow them; 7.4's pogo-stick problem and 7.7's car-on-a-slope problem each ask the reader to show explicitly how they follow the steps.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.why: Power is the rate at which work is done, and since work is a transfer of energy it is also the rate at which energy is spent. A 60-W light bulb spends 60 J every second. Great power means a large amount of work done or energy spent in a short time, which is what a dragster, a volcano and a rocket have in common.
concepts.evidence: The section defines power and boxes the definition, Example 7.11 finds 538 W for a woman running up a 3.00 m flight of stairs in 3.50 s, and the conceptual question asks whether an appliance's rating depends on how long it is switched on.

concepts.name: The watt and the horsepower
concepts.why: The SI unit of power is the watt, one joule per second. The older horsepower is still used for motors and engines, and one horsepower is 746 watts, so the woman running up the stairs puts out a little less than a horsepower; a person can beat that for a few seconds, and a horse can hold it for hours.
concepts.evidence: The section gives both units and both conversions and keeps a glossary row for each, the take-home investigation asks the reader to rate their own stair climbing in horsepower, and the dragster and car problems ask for answers in watts and in horsepower.

concepts.name: Calculate a power output from the energy and the time
concepts.why: Finding a power output means first finding all the work or the energy that went into the job, kinetic and gravitational alike, and then dividing by the time it took. Doing it once shows where the effort really goes: of the woman's 538 W, climbing takes almost all of it and speeding up takes barely a fifteenth.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.11 works the stairs in full, and the problems ask for the power of a dragster reaching 110 m/s in 7.30 s, of an elevator motor lifting 2500 kg, of a car climbing a 2.00º slope at 30.0 m/s, and of people pedalling generators.

concepts.name: Energy consumed in a time, $\kE = \kP\kt$
concepts.why: Turn the definition of power around and the energy a device uses is its power times the time it runs. Electricity bills are written in kilowatt-hours, the product of a power in kilowatts and a time in hours, because household appliances draw about a kilowatt for hours at a stretch and that makes the number a convenient size.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation and names the kilowatt-hour, Example 7.12 finds 36.0 kW·h for a computer run six hours a day for a month, and the problems ask for the energy in a battery that runs a clock for 18 months and for the consumption of an appliance that uses 5.00 kW·h a day.

concepts.name: Estimate what running a device costs
concepts.why: The cost of running something is its power times the time it runs times the price of a kilowatt-hour, so it is high only when both the power and the hours are high. That is why it pays to go after water heaters and air conditioners rather than toasters, which draw a great deal for a few minutes, or electric clocks, which draw almost nothing all day.
concepts.evidence: Example 7.12 costs a computer at ＄4.32 a month, the section explains which devices are worth attacking, and the problems ask for the cost of a year of an electric clock, a month of an air conditioner, and the electricity an elevator motor uses.

concepts.name: The body as an energy converter
concepts.why: Our own bodies are energy conversion machines, and conservation of energy applies to them as it does to anything else: the chemical energy stored in food becomes work, thermal energy, or chemical energy stored in fatty tissue. How much goes to each depends on how much is eaten and on how active the person is, and anything eaten beyond what is needed goes to fat.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.23 draws the three destinations of food energy as the other-energy terms of the conservation equation, Example 7.13 finds that working off 1000 kJ takes 42 minutes of cycling or shows up as 26 g of fat, and the conceptual question compares dieting with exercise.

concepts.name: Metabolic rate and the basal metabolic rate
concepts.why: The rate at which the body uses food energy to stay alive and to do things is its metabolic rate, a power like any other. The rate at rest is the basal metabolic rate, about 85 W, and it is divided among the organs, with the liver and spleen taking the largest share and the brain the next. About 75 percent of the calories burned in a day go to these basic functions.
concepts.evidence: Table 7.4 divides the basal rate among the organs in watts and as a percentage, Table 7.5 gives the rate for activities from sleeping at 83 W to sprinting at 2415 W, and the problems ask for a person's daily energy need from a timetable of activities and for the fat gained by sitting and sleeping all day.

concepts.name: Energy use is measured by oxygen use
concepts.why: Digestion is essentially the oxidation of food, so the energy a person spends is directly proportional to the oxygen they take in: about 20 kJ of energy for each litre of oxygen consumed, whatever the food. That makes a person's power output measurable simply by measuring their breathing.
concepts.evidence: The section states the proportionality and the 20 kJ per litre, Figure 7.24 shows the pulse oxymeter that measures it, Table 7.5 lists oxygen consumption beside power for each activity, and the treadmill problem asks for a subject's efficiency from 2.00 L/min of oxygen.

concepts.name: Useful work
concepts.why: Work done by a person means work done on the outside world, such as lifting weights, climbing stairs or accelerating to a run. Internal work, such as the heart pumping blood or the muscles of a shiver pulling against one another, is not counted, even though it costs energy; the forces the body exerts are nonconservative, so they can change the mechanical energy of whatever is worked on.
concepts.evidence: The section defines useful work and keeps a glossary row for it, and the conceptual questions ask whether rubbing your hands together does work on the outside world and what the efficiency of shivering is.

concepts.name: Find the efficiency of a human activity
concepts.why: A person's efficiency is the useful work they do divided by the food energy they metabolise doing it, and for most activities it is small: a fifth at best for cycling and climbing, a fiftieth for swimming at the surface. Knowing the rate from the table and the useful work from the physics gives the ratio, and it explains why exercise burns so much food for so little lifted.
concepts.evidence: The treadmill problem puts 100 W of work against 2.00 L/min of oxygen and gets 14.3 percent, the shovelling problem asks for the useful power and the waste heat behind 800 W of metabolism, and the Great Pyramid problem asks for the efficiency of the workers who lifted the blocks.

concepts.name: Renewable energy sources
concepts.why: Renewable forms of energy are those that cannot be used up: water, wind, solar and biomass. They are still a small share of the world's supply, but they are the fastest growing part of it, and some countries already draw a large fraction of their electricity from them, as New Zealand does from hydroelectric power.
concepts.evidence: The section defines renewable forms of energy and keeps a glossary row for it, Figure 7.26 gives the shares by source, Figure 7.28 shows a field of solar arrays, and Table 7.6 sets out hydro and other renewables country by country.

concepts.name: Fossil fuels and the world's energy needs
concepts.why: About 85 percent of the world's energy comes from the nonrenewable fossil fuels, oil, natural gas and coal, and roughly a third of it from oil alone, much of that for transport. Demand has tripled in the past fifty years and may triple again in the next thirty, and the likelihood of a link between fossil fuel use and global warming has made the shift away from them urgent.
concepts.evidence: The section defines fossil fuels and gives the shares, Figure 7.26 breaks world consumption down by source and Figure 7.27 shows past and projected use, and the section sets out what coal and oil mean for China and India.

concepts.name: Energy use and economic well-being
concepts.why: In most countries a higher standard of living, measured as gross domestic product per capita, comes with a higher energy use per capita, so access to reliable energy is a condition of economic growth. Diversifying the sources changes that dependency and makes a grid quicker to bring back after a storm or a conflict, which the last twenty years of disruptions have shown.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.29 plots power consumption per capita against GDP per capita for many countries and shows the rise, Table 7.6 gives the consumption of eleven countries, and the section sets out the economic case for renewable sources.

concepts.name: Conserving energy is not the conservation of energy
concepts.why: The law of conservation of energy says the total in an isolated system never changes; the philosophy of energy conservation is about using less of it. The two are not in conflict, because the end of most energy transformations is waste heat that has been degraded: the total is still there, but its potential to do useful work has gone, and that is why resources run out even though energy does not.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the distinction at the close of the chapter and explains degradation, and both conceptual questions ask for it, one for the difference between the two ideas with examples and one for what it means to call energy conserved when a power plant is 35 percent efficient.

concepts.name: First condition for equilibrium, $\text{net}\;\kF = 0$
concepts.why: Newton's second law says that a system accelerates only when a net external force acts on it, so a system that does not accelerate has no net external force on it. That is the first condition for equilibrium, and because a force has components, it holds along every axis at once: the net external force is zero along the horizontal as well as along the vertical.
concepts.evidence: The section states the condition as its first equation and restates it by axis in the second, the free-body diagrams of the motionless person and of the car at constant velocity show the forces adding to zero, and every worked example of the chapter uses it to find a supporting force.

concepts.name: Static equilibrium
concepts.why: A system in static equilibrium is motionless, so its acceleration is zero and the first condition holds. This is the case of the desks, bridges and mountains the chapter opens with, and it is the case almost every problem of the chapter sets.
concepts.evidence: The section names the term beside the figure of the motionless person and the glossary carries it, and the first conceptual question asks the reader to tell it from dynamic equilibrium.

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium
concepts.why: A system moving at constant velocity also has zero acceleration, so it satisfies the first condition just as a motionless system does. Equilibrium is therefore not the same as being at rest, which is why a car driving steadily down a road belongs in a chapter about statics.
concepts.evidence: The section names the term beside the figure of the car, whose applied force is balanced by air friction and whose weight is supported by the normal forces on four tires, the glossary carries it, and the first conceptual question asks what can be said about the velocity of a body in dynamic equilibrium.

concepts.name: The point at which a force is applied
concepts.why: The first condition is necessary but it is not sufficient. Two equal and opposite forces applied along the same line leave an ice hockey stick motionless, and the same two forces applied at different places set it rotating, although the net external force is zero in both cases. So where a force acts decides whether equilibrium is achieved, which is what the second condition will measure.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the two hockey sticks side by side and says in so many words that the net force being zero is necessary but not sufficient, and the second conceptual question asks under what conditions a rotating body can be in equilibrium.

concepts.name: Torque, $\ktau = \krlev\kF\sin\theta$
concepts.why: Torque is the rotational equivalent of a force: it measures how effective a force is at changing a rotation. Opening a door shows what it depends on. The harder you push the faster the door opens, so torque grows with the force; pushing near the hinges barely works, so it grows with the distance from the pivot; and pushing along the door does nothing at all, so only the component of the force perpendicular to that distance counts, which is what the factor $\sin\theta$ supplies.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term and the equation after six drawings of a door pushed in different ways and at different places, the glossary carries torque and the SI unit newton-meter, the door and wrench problems ask for a torque from a force and a distance, and the first AP item asks which situation involves no torque.

concepts.name: Perpendicular lever arm, $\krperp = \krlev\sin\theta$
concepts.why: The perpendicular lever arm is the shortest distance from the pivot point to the line along which the force acts. It gathers the distance and the angle into one length, and it is often easier to see in a drawing than $r$ and $\theta$ are to measure separately.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it, draws it as a dashed line in the door figure and in the hockey stick figure, and the glossary carries the term; the AP item on five forces applied to an anchored object is answered by comparing lever arms.

concepts.name: Torque from the lever arm, $\ktau = \krperp\kF$
concepts.why: Because the perpendicular lever arm already carries the angle, the torque is simply the lever arm times the force. The two expressions for torque are equally valid, and which one to use is a matter of what the drawing makes easy to find.
concepts.evidence: The section states the equation immediately after defining the lever arm and says that both forms are equally valid, and the worked examples of 9.4 and 9.6 use this form throughout because every angle in them is 90º.

concepts.name: Torque is always taken about a chosen pivot
concepts.why: A torque has no meaning until a pivot point is named, because both the distance and the angle in its definition are measured from that point. The same force gives different torques about different points, and the point may be any point in or out of the body, whether or not the body can actually turn about it. What matters is that every torque in a problem is taken about the same point.
concepts.evidence: The section says that any point in any object may be chosen and that the object need not actually pivot about it, the hockey stick figure works the same force out about points A and B, and the discussion after the seesaw example turns on the pivot having been chosen where the supporting force acts.

concepts.name: Clockwise and counterclockwise torques
concepts.why: For rotation in a plane a torque has two possible directions, clockwise or counterclockwise about the chosen pivot, and torques in opposite directions are given opposite signs. The common convention is that counterclockwise torques are positive and clockwise torques negative, which is what lets the torques on a body be added as ordinary signed numbers.
concepts.evidence: The section states the convention after the second condition, the hockey stick figure shows the same force turning the stick one way about A and the other way about B, and the seesaw example inserts a minus sign into the second child's torque for exactly this reason.

concepts.name: Second condition for equilibrium, $\text{net}\;\ktau = 0$
concepts.why: The second condition necessary to achieve equilibrium is that the net external torque on the system is zero, so that the system has no accelerated rotation. It repairs what the first condition missed: the hockey stick pushed off centre has no net force but it does have a net torque. If the condition is satisfied for one choice of pivot it is satisfied for every other, so the pivot may be chosen freely.
concepts.evidence: The section states the condition in italics and as an equation, the two children on the seesaw satisfy it, and every worked example and nearly every problem of the rest of the chapter is solved with it.

concepts.name: Center of gravity
concepts.why: The weight of a body is spread over the whole of it, but for the purpose of torques the whole weight may be taken to act at a single point, the center of gravity. This is not an approximation, and it is what allows the distance to a child on a seesaw to be measured to one point rather than over the area the child covers.
concepts.evidence: The section makes the point in the discussion after the seesaw example and the glossary carries the term; 9.3 builds its whole account of stability on where the center of gravity lies, and every figure of 9.4 and 9.6 marks it.

concepts.name: Balancing a seesaw, $\krtwo = \krone m_1 / m_2$
concepts.why: A seesaw is the first problem that needs both conditions at once. Taking the pivot as the point about which the torques are calculated makes the supporting force's torque zero, and the second condition then gives the distance the second child must sit at; the first condition gives the supporting force afterwards. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot, which is what everyone's intuition about seesaws already says.
concepts.evidence: The section works the example through in two parts, the glossary and the discussion draw three lessons from it, and four of the chapter's problems are seesaws: two in 9.2, one in 9.3 and the unreasonable-results item of 9.6.

concepts.name: The torque a displacement produces
concepts.why: What decides the kind of equilibrium a body sits in is the torque its own weight produces once the body is displaced. Tilt a pencil standing on its eraser and the pivot moves to the edge of its base while the weight still acts through the center of gravity, so the weight now has a lever arm and turns the pencil one way or the other. Whether that torque points back towards equilibrium or further away from it is the whole of this section.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the pencil upright, tilted a little and tilted too far, and then the same pencil balanced on its point, and reads the direction of the torque off each drawing; the AP item on the traffic cone asks for the same reasoning in words.

concepts.name: Stable equilibrium
concepts.why: A system is in stable equilibrium if, when displaced, it experiences a net force or torque in the direction opposite to the displacement, so that it is driven back where it came from. A marble at the bottom of a bowl and a pencil standing on its eraser are both stable, and most systems are stable at least for small displacements.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term, the glossary carries it, the pencil on its eraser is drawn returning to the vertical, and the keyed AP item asks why a traffic cone on its base is stable.

concepts.name: Unstable equilibrium
concepts.why: A system is in unstable equilibrium if, when displaced, it experiences a net force or torque in the same direction as the displacement, so that it accelerates away from where it started. A ball resting on the crest of a hill and a pencil balanced on its point are both unstable, although both conditions for equilibrium are satisfied while they stand.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term, the glossary carries it, the pencil balanced on its point is drawn toppling, and the keyed AP item asks why a traffic cone on its tip is unstable.

concepts.name: Neutral equilibrium
concepts.why: A system is in neutral equilibrium if its equilibrium does not depend on where it has been displaced to. A marble on a flat table and a round pencil lying on its side simply stay where they are put, because the center of gravity remains directly above the point of support wherever the body is moved. A body may be of one kind in one direction and another kind in another, as a marble on a saddle is.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term and the glossary carries it, the figure of the sphere and the pencil on its side shows both, and the first conceptual question asks about the stability of that pencil along its length.

concepts.name: Base of support
concepts.why: A body standing on a surface stays in stable equilibrium only while its center of gravity is above its base of support; once the center of gravity passes beyond the base, the torque from the weight changes direction and the body topples. That is why stability is increased by spreading the feet, which widens the base, and by bending the knees, which lowers the center of gravity, and why a chicken, whose center of gravity is below its hips and between two broad feet, is far more stable than a person.
concepts.evidence: The section compares the standing person with the chicken and explains canes, crutches and the stance of a football player, the take-home experiment asks the reader to touch their toes with their heels against a wall, and the problems on the leaning horse, the braced wall and the chicken in the wind all turn on it.

concepts.name: The problem-solving strategy for static equilibrium
concepts.why: Statics is a special case of Newton's laws, so the strategies of Chapter 4 still apply, and this section adds four steps of its own: decide that the system really is in static equilibrium, draw a free body diagram and label every force with its magnitude, direction and point of application, apply either or both conditions for equilibrium, and check that the answer is reasonable in magnitude, direction and units.
concepts.evidence: The section prints the four steps as a boxed strategy, the worked example on the pole vaulter follows them, and two problems of the chapter ask the reader explicitly to show how they follow the steps.

concepts.name: Choosing the pivot to simplify the problem
concepts.why: Because the second condition holds for any choice of pivot, the pivot may be chosen to make the work easy. The useful choices are the ones that make the torques of unknown forces zero: a force applied at the pivot has no lever arm, and a force acting along a line through the pivot makes an angle of zero. Choosing the elbow, the hip or the hand a problem is asking about is what turns two unknowns into one.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rule as step 3 of the strategy, the pole vaulter example chooses the left hand so that the left hand's torque drops out, and both examples of 9.6 choose the joint for the same reason.

concepts.name: Symmetric supports share the weight, $\kFR = \kFL = \kwgt/2$
concepts.why: When supporting forces are applied symmetrically about the center of gravity, each carries an equal share of the weight. Both conditions are then satisfied at once: the forces add to the weight, and, taking the center of gravity as the pivot, the weight has no lever arm and the two equal forces are equidistant from the pivot, so their torques cancel. The four legs of a uniform table each carry a quarter of its weight for the same reason.
concepts.evidence: The section works the pole vaulter's first hold this way and says the argument holds for any system supported symmetrically about its center of gravity, and part (c) of the section's second problem asks the reader to verify the second condition for a pivot other than the center of gravity.

concepts.name: Unequal supports, $\kFL + \kFR = \kwgt$
concepts.why: Move the center of gravity away from the middle and the two supports no longer share the weight equally: the support nearer the center of gravity carries more, exactly as the nearer of two people carrying a load does. The forces still add to the weight, so the first condition gives the second force once the second condition has given the first. If the center of gravity lies beyond both supports, one force reverses direction and both grow large, which is why holding a pole at one end is so much harder than holding it in the middle.
concepts.evidence: The section works the example with the center of gravity 0.600 m from the left hand and gets forces of 32.7 N and 16.3 N, then shows the third hold in which the right hand must push down; the keyed AP item on the car crossing a bridge between two piers asks the same question of a bridge.

concepts.name: Simple machines
concepts.why: A simple machine is a device that multiplies or augments the force we apply, usually at the expense of the distance through which we apply it. Levers, gears, pulleys, wedges and screws are the familiar examples. A machine does not create energy, since it cannot do more work than the work put into it; what it changes is how much force the job takes.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by naming the devices and saying that energy is still conserved for them, and the conceptual questions ask which machine scissors resemble and how a pulley lets a person lift a piano.

concepts.name: Mechanical advantage, $\text{MA} = \kFo/\kFi$
concepts.why: The mechanical advantage of a machine is the ratio of the output force to the input force. It is a pure number: a mechanical advantage greater than one means the machine gives out more force than is put in, and one less than one, as for a shovel or a car axle, means it gives out less and buys something else instead.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it in its first equation and the glossary carries the term; the nail puller, wheelbarrow and car axle problems each ask for a mechanical advantage, and the first AP item asks the reader to explain the idea in terms of torque.

concepts.name: The lever, $\kli\kFi = \klo\kFo$
concepts.why: A lever is a rigid bar pivoted at a fixed place called the fulcrum. Because the bar turns about that point, the second condition for equilibrium applies to it: while the load is not moving the torque of the input force equals the torque of the output force, so the input force times its lever arm equals the output force times its own. The nail puller, the wheelbarrow, the shovel and a seesaw are all levers, and they differ only in where the pivot sits relative to the two forces.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the second condition for the nail puller and then applies it to the wheelbarrow and the shovel, and the conceptual questions ask whether a nail puller pulling a nail at constant rate is in equilibrium.

concepts.name: Mechanical advantage of a lever, $\text{MA} = \kli/\klo$
concepts.why: Rearranging the lever's torque balance turns it into a statement about forces: the mechanical advantage of a lever is the ratio of the input lever arm to the output lever arm. The longer the handle on a nail puller, the greater the force it can exert, and the shorter the handle, the less.
concepts.evidence: The section states the equation and says it is true for levers in general, the worked example on the wheelbarrow uses it, and the nail puller, mower and wheelbarrow problems all ask for a force from a ratio of lever arms.

concepts.name: Cranks, wheels and gears, $\text{MA} = r_{\text{i}}/r_{\text{o}}$
concepts.why: A crank is a lever that can be turned through a full circle about its pivot, and a wheel driven by an axle is the same thing again. Such a machine may not look like a lever, but the physics of it is unchanged: its mechanical advantage is simply the ratio of the two radii. A crank is usually built with a large mechanical advantage, while a car axle driving a much larger wheel has one well below one.
concepts.evidence: The section works out the mechanical advantage of a crank and of a simplified car axle and finds that the axle must exert 12,000 N to put 1000 N on the road, and one of the problems asks for the mechanical advantage of an axle of 1.10 cm radius driving a tire of 27.5 cm.

concepts.name: Pulleys, $\kFo \approx n\kTf$
concepts.why: An ordinary pulley changes the direction of the force in a cord without changing its magnitude, so its mechanical advantage is one. Combinations of pulleys do multiply force: each cable that pulls directly upward on the load adds a force of about the tension, since the tension is nearly the same throughout a friction-free system, so the number of such cables is about the mechanical advantage of the system.
concepts.evidence: The section draws three combinations with mechanical advantages of about 2, 3 and 4 and counts the cables in each, a conceptual question asks how a pulley lets a person lift a piano, and two problems ask for the tension and the ceiling force for an engine hung from such a system.

concepts.name: Muscles and joints as levers
concepts.why: A limb is a lever whose fulcrum is a joint, and the muscle that moves it is attached by a tendon very close to that joint. The muscle's lever arm is therefore much shorter than the load's, so the system is a simple machine with a mechanical advantage well below one and the muscle must pull far harder than the limb pushes on the world. Muscles can only contract, which is why they come in pairs, a flexor to close the limb and an extensor to open it.
concepts.evidence: The section opens with the forearm holding a book beside the equivalent lever system and says that most skeletal muscles are attached close to joints, and the conceptual questions ask why the forces our limbs exert on the world are so much smaller than the forces inside us.

concepts.name: The force in a muscle, $\kFB = (\krtwo\kwarm + \krthree\kwbook)/\krone$
concepts.why: Taking the pivot at the joint makes the torque of the joint force zero and leaves the muscle force as the only unknown, so the second condition alone gives it: the muscle's torque must balance the torques of the weights it holds. Because the muscle's lever arm is the small one, the answer is large. The biceps holding a forearm and a 4.00 kg book exerts 470 N, which is 7.38 times the weight it is supporting.
concepts.evidence: The section works the example in full, the discussion notes that the force changes as the angle at the elbow changes, and the problems on the quadriceps, the Achilles tendon, the neck muscles, the masseter and the triceps in a push-up are all the same calculation on another joint.

concepts.name: The force in a joint
concepts.why: Once the muscle force is known the first condition gives the force in the joint, and it is large too. Because a muscle can contract but cannot push, the muscle and the joint pull in opposite directions and their forces subtract: in the forearm, the 470 N up from the biceps less the 407 N down from the humerus leaves the 63 N of weight actually supported. The same arithmetic gives 4660 N on the vertebrae of someone lifting a box with their back, five and a half times the weight lifted, and spines are relatively weak.
concepts.evidence: The section states the elbow force of 407 N in the text and sets its calculation as the section's first problem, the second worked example finds the magnitude and direction of the force on the vertebrae from its components, and the problems on the knee, the ankle and the jaw each ask for a joint force.

concepts.name: Posture and back strain
concepts.why: Stand straight and the upper body's center of gravity is directly above the pivot in the hips, so its weight has no lever arm, produces no torque, and needs no muscle action to balance it. Lean forward and the center of gravity moves in front of the hips, and the torque this produces has to be countered by the muscles of the lower back, which have very small lever arms and so must pull very hard. Lifting a load with the back rather than the legs makes the same forces several times larger again.
concepts.evidence: The section draws good and bad posture side by side, works out the 4200 N in the back muscles of someone lifting a 30.0 kg box, shows people leaning forward, sideways and backward to keep their overall center of gravity above their feet, and asks in a conceptual question why pregnant women often suffer back strain.

concepts.name: Why muscles are attached close to joints
concepts.why: Paying so much force for so little seems a poor bargain until the other side of it is counted. Because the muscle's lever arm is short, a small contraction swings the limb through a large distance in a short time, which is speed, and the arrangement leaves room for the large number of joints and the wide ranges over which they work, which is flexibility and agility. A biceps attached at the wrist could not give the arm the range of movement it has.
concepts.evidence: The section asks the question in so many words and answers it with speed, flexibility and agility, and a conceptual question asks what the advantages and disadvantages would be of attaching the biceps near the wrist instead.

concepts.name: Linear momentum, $\kp = m\kv$
concepts.why: Linear momentum is the product of a system’s mass and its velocity, and it is the quantity that says how hard a moving object is to stop. A large, fast-moving object has greater momentum than a smaller, slower one, and every result in this chapter is written in terms of it, so the definition comes first.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the worked example compares the momentum of a football player with the momentum of a thrown football, and the first four problems each ask for a momentum, a mass or a speed from the definition.

concepts.name: Calculate a momentum from a mass and a velocity
concepts.why: Momentum is a vector with the same direction as the velocity, and its SI unit is the kilogram metre per second. Reading a mass and a speed out of a problem and multiplying them, keeping the direction and the unit, is the step every later collision problem begins with.
concepts.evidence: The worked example calculates the momentum of the football player and of the football and then compares the two, and the problems ask for the momentum of a charging elephant, a tranquilizer dart, a garbage truck, a trash can and the Earth in its orbit.

concepts.name: Newton’s second law in terms of momentum, $\kFnet = \kdp / \kdt$
concepts.why: Newton stated his second law as the net external force equals the change in momentum of a system divided by the time over which it changes. This is the more general statement, because it holds for a system whose mass changes, such as a rocket, as well as for one whose mass is constant.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the statement and the glossary carries it as the second law of motion, the Venus Williams example finds the average force on a tennis ball from its change in momentum and the contact time, and the AP item on a baseball struck by a bat asks for the same thing.

concepts.name: The familiar $\kFnet = m\ka$ as the constant-mass case
concepts.why: When the mass of the system does not change, the change in momentum is the mass times the change in velocity, and dividing by the time gives the acceleration. The form of the second law you already know is therefore a special case of the momentum form, and knowing which one to reach for is what makes the momentum form worth having.
concepts.evidence: The section derives $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ from $F_{\text{net}} = \Delta p / \Delta t$ in three steps and prints the words “when the mass of the system is constant” in italics, and the discussion of the tennis example says the problem could also have been solved by first finding the acceleration.

concepts.name: Change in momentum $\kdp$
concepts.why: The change in momentum is the difference between the final and the initial momentum, and for a constant mass it is the mass times the change in velocity. It is the quantity a force acting for a time produces, and it is what is conserved in the sections that follow, so it is named on its own.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term and the glossary carries it, the billiard-ball example works out the change in momentum of each ball in components, and two AP items ask for the magnitude and direction of a puck’s change in momentum.

concepts.name: Impulse, $\kdp = \kFnet\kdt$
concepts.why: Rearranging Newton’s second law shows that the change in momentum equals the average net external force multiplied by the time this force acts, and that product is called the impulse. Impulse is the same as the change in momentum, so the effect of a force depends on how long it acts as well as on how great it is.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the equation under the heading Impulse: Change in Momentum and the glossary carries the term, the section summary states it again, and most of the section’s sixteen problems ask for a force, a time or a velocity change from it.

concepts.name: A longer collision time means a smaller force
concepts.why: The change in momentum a stop requires is fixed by the mass and the speed, so if the stop is spread over a longer time the force is smaller. This is why a car has a padded dashboard, an airbag and parts that crumple, and why you roll on landing rather than land stiff-legged.
concepts.evidence: The section spends three paragraphs on dashboards, airbags, crumpling racing cars and jumping onto a soft mat, the conceptual questions ask about padding and about trampolines, and the problems compare the force on a passenger stopped by a dashboard with the force on one stopped by an airbag.

concepts.name: Average effective force $\kFeff$
concepts.why: A real force is not constant over the brief time of a collision, but you can always find an average effective force that produces the same result. On a graph of force against time, the area under the actual curve is the impulse, and the rectangle of the effective force over the same interval has the same area.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.2 draws the actual force and the effective force on one pair of axes and the caption says the areas under the two curves are equal, and two AP items give a graph of force against time and ask for the change in momentum it represents.

concepts.name: Find an average force from a change in momentum and a contact time
concepts.why: Most of what impulse is used for is one calculation: take the mass and the velocities before and after, form the change in momentum, and divide by the time of contact. Doing it carefully, with the direction kept and the milliseconds converted, is what the section’s problems and AP items ask for again and again.
concepts.evidence: The problems ask for the force on a bullet in a barrel, on a passenger held by a seat belt, on a leg slapped by a hand, on a spacecraft window struck by a paint chip and on a pier struck by a cruise ship, and the AP items ask for the force on a ball of putty, on a bouncing ball and on a car hitting a wall.

concepts.name: The two changes in momentum cancel, $\Delta \kpone + \Delta \kptwo = 0$
concepts.why: The two cars push on each other for the same length of time, and Newton’s third law makes the two forces equal and opposite. The impulses are therefore equal and opposite, so the momentum one car loses is the momentum the other gains, and this is the whole argument for conservation of momentum.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the result in five steps from the impulse on each car and from $F_2 = -F_1$, and Figure 8.3 draws the two cars before and after the bump with the momentum of each labelled.

concepts.name: Conservation of momentum, $\kptot = \kptotprime$
concepts.why: The total momentum of an isolated system is constant, whatever happens inside it and however many objects it holds. Momentum is one of the few quantities nature conserves, and every collision in the rest of the chapter is solved by writing the total momentum before the collision equal to the total momentum after it.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the conservation of momentum principle and the glossary carries it, the section summary states it again, and the problems find the final velocity of coupled train cars, of a clay koala, of a car that hits a deer and of a falcon that catches a dove.

concepts.name: Isolated system, $\kFnet = 0$
concepts.why: An isolated system is one for which the net external force is zero, and that is exactly the condition momentum needs in order to be conserved. Before you can use conservation of momentum you have to choose a system large enough that the forces that matter are internal to it.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the text points out that the two-car system conserves momentum while each one-car system does not, and two AP items ask which of four collisions is an example of an open system.

concepts.name: Recoil
concepts.why: The backward momentum felt by a body that exerts a force on another is called a recoil. When a football player runs into the goalpost the Earth recoils too, and because the Earth is so much more massive its recoil is immeasurably small, though it is real nevertheless.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the player and the goalpost and names the recoil, and problems in this and the following sections ask for the recoil velocity of a ship firing a shell, of a rifle and of a performer catching a cannon ball.
