concepts.name: Momentum can be conserved along one direction and not another
concepts.why: The three directions in space are independent, so momentum can be conserved along one of them while it is not conserved along another. For a projectile with negligible air resistance the horizontal forces are zero and the horizontal momentum is unchanged, while the vertical force of gravity is not zero and the vertical momentum is not conserved.
concepts.evidence: The section states it and Figure 8.4 draws a space probe separating in flight, with the net horizontal force still zero and the net vertical force not, and a conceptual question asks what the angle between the two directions is and for an example.

concepts.name: Momentum of subatomic particles
concepts.why: Conservation of momentum is not a rule about billiard balls alone. Momentum is a property of every subatomic particle, massless ones such as photons included, and the analysis of what scatters from what is how the nucleus and the quarks inside a proton were found.
concepts.evidence: The section’s last passage is on subatomic collisions, Figure 8.5 shows a particle scattering straight backward from a target, and the glossary carries the term quark.

concepts.name: Elastic collision
concepts.why: An elastic collision is one that conserves internal kinetic energy as well as momentum. That second conservation law is the extra equation you need when both final velocities are unknown, so knowing whether a collision is elastic decides how you can solve it.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the conceptual question asks what an elastic collision is, and several AP items turn on whether momentum alone or momentum and kinetic energy together are conserved.

concepts.name: Internal kinetic energy $\kKEint$
concepts.why: The internal kinetic energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic energies of the objects in it. It is the quantity that is conserved in an elastic collision and changed in an inelastic one, so it is the bookkeeping that tells the two kinds of collision apart.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the discussion of the worked example asks you to check that the internal kinetic energy is unchanged at 4.00 J, and the following section computes it before and after several collisions.

concepts.name: Find both final velocities of a one-dimensional elastic collision
concepts.why: Two unknown final velocities need two independent equations, and an elastic collision supplies them: conservation of momentum and conservation of internal kinetic energy. Solving the pair gives a quadratic with two roots, and the root that repeats the initial condition describes the situation before the collision and is discarded.
concepts.evidence: The worked example solves the pair for a 0.500-kg object striking a 3.50-kg object at rest, discards the root $v'_1 = 4.00$ m/s and keeps $v'_1 = -3.00$ m/s, and the problems ask for the final relative velocity of two docking satellites and for the final velocities of a goalie and a puck.

concepts.name: Real collisions are at best nearly elastic
concepts.why: Truly elastic collisions can only be achieved with subatomic particles. Macroscopic collisions always convert some kinetic energy into heat transfer due to friction and into sound, so two steel blocks on ice or two carts with spring bumpers on an air track are treated as elastic because they are nearly so, not because they are exactly so.
concepts.evidence: The section says so in its third paragraph and names the steel blocks and the air track, the take-home investigation asks you to judge whether ice cubes flicked across a tabletop collide approximately elastically, and an AP item asks why a rubber ball rebounds to only 90 per cent of the height it was dropped from.

concepts.name: Inelastic collision
concepts.why: An inelastic collision is one in which the internal kinetic energy changes. The forces between the colliding objects do work that can turn internal kinetic energy into heat transfer, or turn stored energy into internal kinetic energy, so only momentum can be counted on here.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the definition and the glossary carries it, the conceptual question asks what an inelastic collision is, and several AP items ask which of four described outcomes is the inelastic one.

concepts.name: Perfectly inelastic collision, $m_1\kvone = (m_1 + m_2)\kvprime$
concepts.why: A collision in which the objects stick together is called perfectly inelastic, because it reduces internal kinetic energy more than any other kind of collision can while still conserving momentum. Since the two objects share one final velocity afterwards, conservation of momentum alone is enough to find it.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the term and the glossary carries it, Figure 8.7 shows two equal masses meeting at equal speeds and coming to rest together, and the problems ask for the final velocity of two skaters, of a loaded freight car and of two football players who cling together.

concepts.name: Recoil velocity, $\kvprime = m_1\kvone / (m_1 + m_2)$
concepts.why: When a moving object is caught by one that is at rest, the two move off together at the incoming velocity reduced by the ratio of the incoming mass to the total mass. A goalie who catches a puck therefore recoils only a few centimetres a second, which is why the recoil of a heavy body is so easy to miss.
concepts.evidence: The worked example derives the expression and puts 0.150 kg and 70.0 kg into it to get $7.48 \times 10^{-2}$ m/s, and the problems ask for the recoil of a battleship firing a shell, of a rifle, of a circus performer catching a cannon ball and of the Moon struck by an asteroid.

concepts.name: Find the internal kinetic energy lost in a collision
concepts.why: Once the final velocities are known you can add up the kinetic energies before the collision and after it and subtract. The difference is what was lost to thermal energy and sound, and in a perfectly inelastic collision it is nearly all of what there was to begin with.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds 91.9 J before the collision and 0.196 J after it and says the minus sign means the energy was lost, and problems ask how much kinetic energy is lost when two skaters meet, when two satellites dock and when a freight car is loaded.

concepts.name: A collision can release stored energy
concepts.why: An inelastic collision does not only remove internal kinetic energy; it can add it. When a compressed spring is released during the collision, or when exploding bolts push a satellite away from its launcher, stored energy is converted into internal kinetic energy and the system ends with more than it started with.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.9 shows two carts on an air track, one carrying a compressed spring, the second worked example finds that the internal kinetic energy increases by 5.46 J in that collision, and a problem asks for the velocities of a satellite and its launcher after exploding bolts supply 5000 J.

concepts.name: Two-dimensional collision
concepts.why: When objects scatter to the side rather than along one line, you choose a convenient coordinate system and resolve the motion into components along perpendicular axes. Resolving the motion this way yields a pair of one-dimensional problems to be solved together, which is the same approach that carried kinematics and dynamics into the plane.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by saying so, Figure 8.10 draws the coordinate system with the x-axis along the incoming velocity, and the section summary repeats the choice of axes as the first thing to do.

concepts.name: Point mass
concepts.why: Two objects that collide off centre can begin to spin, and rotation is not treated until later. A point mass is a structureless particle that cannot rotate or spin, and restricting the analysis to point masses is what keeps the collision describable by the velocities alone.
concepts.evidence: The section names the restriction in its second paragraph, using two ice skaters who hook arms as the case it rules out, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Momentum along the x-axis, $m_1\kvone = m_1\kvoneprime\cos\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\cos\theta_2$
concepts.why: With the x-axis chosen parallel to the velocity of the incoming object and the second object at rest, the whole of the initial momentum lies along x. Conservation of momentum along that axis then relates the one initial speed to the two final speeds and the two scattering angles.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the equation under the heading Conservation of Momentum along the x-axis, the section summary states it, and the worked example and the puck, cannon and bowling problems all begin with it.

concepts.name: Momentum along the y-axis, $0 = m_1\kvoneprime\sin\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\sin\theta_2$
concepts.why: Neither object has any momentum along the y-axis before the collision, so the two y-components afterwards must add to zero. This is the second of the two independent equations, and it is the one that ties the two scattering angles to each other.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the equation under the heading Conservation of Momentum along the y-axis, the section summary states it, and the worked example uses it to find the speed of the unseen object because it has the fewer terms.

concepts.name: Find an unseen object’s velocity from the scattering of another
concepts.why: Two equations can be solved for two unknowns. Taking the ratio of the two conservation equations removes the unknown speed and leaves the unknown angle, and either equation then gives the speed, so a measurement of what comes out of a collision tells you about what you could not see going in.
concepts.evidence: The worked example slides an object into a dark room and finds the velocity of the object it struck from the angle and speed at which the first object emerges, a problem asks you to confirm that the example conserves momentum along both axes, and the Rutherford problem does the same for a helium nucleus scattered by gold.

concepts.name: Equal masses colliding elastically, $\frac{1}{2}m\kvone^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\kvoneprime^2 + \frac{1}{2}m\kvtwoprime^2 + m\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$
concepts.why: For two objects of equal mass, conservation of momentum along both axes gives an expression for the initial kinetic energy that carries one extra term beyond the elastic condition. The two statements can both be true only if that extra term is zero, and what follows from that is the whole of what pool players know about angles.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the identity and leaves the algebra to the reader, a problem asks you to carry out that derivation and prints the working as its answer, and the section summary states the identity.

concepts.name: Equal masses separate at $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 90^\circ$
concepts.why: The extra term can be zero in three ways: the incoming object stops, the incoming object misses, or the angle of separation is ninety degrees. All three are familiar at a pool table, and the third is the one that lets you find the second object’s direction without any further calculation.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the three ways and says the angle between the balls is very close to ninety degrees after the collision unless a great deal of spin is put on the ball, and the air hockey problem invites you to use the result to find the velocity of the second puck.

concepts.name: Rocket propulsion
concepts.why: A rocket, a jet engine, a deflating balloon and a squid all move for the same reason: matter is forcefully ejected from the system, producing an equal and opposite reaction on what remains. The exhaust does not push on the ground, which is why a rocket’s thrust is greater in outer space than on the launch pad.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the principle and names Newton’s third law, the take-home experiment asks you to let go of a filled balloon and say which way it goes, and a conceptual question asks how a motionless astronaut in the middle of a space station could move himself.

concepts.name: Thrust, $\kFthrust = \kve\,\Delta m / \kdt$
concepts.why: The exhaust velocity multiplied by the rate at which mass leaves the rocket is a quantity with the units of newtons, and it is the force the exhaust gases exert on the rocket. The faster the rocket burns its fuel, and the faster the gas leaves, the greater the thrust.
concepts.evidence: The section names the quantity thrust and gives its units, the discussion of the Saturn V example says you can show the thrust of the engines was $3.36 \times 10^7$ N, and the keyed derivation problem works the thrust out from the force needed to accelerate a small mass of gas.

concepts.name: Acceleration of a rocket, $\ka = (\kve / m)(\Delta m / \kdt) - \kg$
concepts.why: Equating the change in momentum of the whole system over a short time to the impulse of gravity gives a good approximation for the acceleration of what is left of the rocket. It is the one equation the section’s problems are worked from, and it is the first result in the book that describes a system whose mass is changing.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the equation under the heading Acceleration of a Rocket, the worked example puts the Saturn V’s liftoff mass, burn rate and exhaust velocity into it, and the problems ask for the takeoff acceleration of an antiballistic missile, of a rocket leaving the Moon and of an ion engine.

concepts.name: The three factors in a rocket’s acceleration
concepts.why: The equation says that a rocket accelerates harder the greater the exhaust velocity, the faster it burns its fuel and the smaller its mass. The last of the three changes as the rocket flies, because most of a rocket is fuel to begin with, so the acceleration increases continuously and reaches a maximum just before the fuel runs out.
concepts.evidence: The section boxes the three factors as a list and gives the practical limit of about $2.5 \times 10^3$ m/s for the exhaust velocity of a conventional propulsion system, and the discussion of the worked example explains why the Saturn V’s acceleration grew after liftoff.

concepts.name: Final velocity of a rocket, $\kv = \kve \ln(m_0 / m_{\text{r}})$
concepts.why: Neglecting air resistance and gravity, the velocity a rocket gains depends only on the exhaust velocity and on the natural logarithm of the ratio of its initial mass to the mass that is left when the fuel is gone. Because the ratio enters through a logarithm, going faster costs a great deal more fuel than you might expect.
concepts.evidence: The section states the equation and uses it to show that escaping Earth from rest needs a mass ratio of 88, so that 98.9 per cent of the rocket is fuel, and the problems ask for the velocity increase of a space probe and for how much of a single-stage rocket can be anything but fuel.

concepts.name: Why rockets have stages
concepts.why: Once air resistance and gravity are taken into account, the mass left at burnout can only be about one hundred and eightieth of the initial mass, and it is difficult to build a rocket in which the fuel has a mass 180 times everything else. The answer is to give each stage only part of the final velocity and discard it when its fuel is spent, so that later stages can be smaller.
concepts.evidence: The section works out the mass ratio, calls it difficult to build, and gives multistage rockets as the solution, and it notes that launching from an airplane starts the rocket above zero velocity and out of most of the atmosphere’s resistance.

concepts.name: Uniform circular motion
concepts.why: Uniform circular motion is motion in a circular path at constant speed, and it is the simplest form of curved motion. Every result of this chapter, from the centripetal acceleration to the orbit of a satellite, is worked out for this case first, so the chapter begins by naming it.
concepts.evidence: The chapter introduction defines the term, 6.1 opens by saying that the study of uniform circular motion begins with two angular quantities, and the section summary states it again.

concepts.name: Arc length $\kds$
concepts.why: The arc length is the distance an object travels along a circular path, and it is the distance of Chapter 2 measured along a curve rather than along a line. Every rotation angle and every linear speed in this section is worked out from it.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it beside Figure 6.3, the odometer problem and the worn-tire problem each turn a number of revolutions into an arc length, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Rotation angle, $\Delta\theta = \kds / \kr$
concepts.why: The rotation angle is the amount of rotation, defined as the ratio of the arc length to the radius of curvature, and it is the angular quantity that stands in for linear distance. Because it is a ratio of two lengths, every point of a rotating object turns through the same rotation angle in the same time, however far from the axis it sits.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it for the pits on a CD, Figure 6.4 shows two points at different radii sweeping the same angle through different arc lengths, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Radian, $2\pi\ \text{rad} = 1\ \text{revolution}$
concepts.why: One complete revolution carries a point once round the circumference, so the rotation angle of a revolution is $2\pi r / r = 2\pi$. That result fixes the unit of the rotation angle: the radian is defined so that $2\pi$ rad is one revolution, and one radian is about 57.3º. Because a radian is a ratio of two lengths it carries no unit of its own, which is why it may be inserted into or dropped from an answer.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the unit from the circumference, Table 6.1 sets common angles in both measures, the worked example discusses why the radian may be inserted into the answer, and the microwave and truck problems ask for a conversion between revolutions and radians.

concepts.name: Angular velocity, $\kw = \Delta\theta / \kdt$
concepts.why: The angular velocity is the rate of change of the rotation angle, and it answers the question of how fast an object is rotating. It is the angular quantity analogous to linear velocity, it is measured in radians per second, and with respect to the axis of rotation it has only two directions, clockwise and counterclockwise.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it, the worked example finds the angular velocity of a car tire, the conceptual question asks which rotational quantities are analogous to distance and velocity, and five of the section's problems ask for one.

concepts.name: Linear and angular velocity, $\kv = \kr\kw$
concepts.why: A pit on a rotating CD moves an arc length $\Delta s = r\Delta\theta$ in a time $\Delta t$, so its linear speed is $v = r\omega$. Read one way, the relation says that a point on the rim moves faster than a point near the axis; read the other way, $\omega = v/r$ says that a car with small tires must spin them faster than a car with large ones to travel at the same speed.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the arc length and reads it in both directions, the worked example finds the angular velocity of a 0.300 m tire at 15.0 m/s and compares it with an earth mover's, and the pitcher, lacrosse, truck and football problems all turn on it.

concepts.name: Centripetal acceleration $\kac$
concepts.why: In uniform circular motion the magnitude of the velocity never changes but its direction changes constantly, so there is an acceleration. Taking the difference of the velocities at two nearby points shows that the change points directly toward the center of curvature, and so does the acceleration. Centripetal means center seeking, and it is what you notice as a sideways acceleration when you turn a corner in your car.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.7 draws the two velocities and their difference, the section opens on the feeling of turning a corner, the conceptual question asks whether a centripetal acceleration can change the speed of circular motion, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Centripetal acceleration, $\kac = \kv^2 / \kr$ and $\kac = \kr\kw^2$
concepts.why: The triangle formed by the two velocities and the triangle formed by the two radii are similar, and following that through gives $a_{\text{c}} = v^2/r$. Substituting $v = r\omega$ gives the second form, $a_{\text{c}} = r\omega^2$, and you may use whichever is more convenient. Because the speed enters squared, it is four times as hard to take a curve at 100 km/h as at 50 km/h, and a sharp corner, having a small radius, asks more again.
concepts.evidence: The section derives both forms from similar triangles, the two worked examples use one form each for a car on a highway curve and for an ultracentrifuge, and nine of the section's problems ask for a centripetal acceleration or for the speed or angular velocity that produces one.

concepts.name: Centrifuge
concepts.why: A centrifuge is a rotating device used to separate specimens of different densities, and it works because a high centripetal acceleration separates them far faster than gravity does and does so with small samples. An ultracentrifuge is one optimized for very high speeds, and a maximum centripetal acceleration of several hundred thousand $g$ is possible in a vacuum.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the centrifuge and the ultracentrifuge and lists what they separate, Figure 6.8(b) draws one, the second worked example finds an acceleration 472,000 times $g$ at a point 7.50 cm from the axis, and the glossary carries ultracentrifuge.

concepts.name: Quote a centripetal acceleration in multiples of $\kg$
concepts.why: A centripetal acceleration means more to the reader when it is set beside the acceleration due to gravity, so the book divides one by the other and quotes the ratio. It is how centrifuges are rated, how the tolerance of astronauts to launch and reentry is measured, and how you can tell at once whether a ride would be uncomfortable or dangerous.
concepts.evidence: Both worked examples end by taking the ratio $a_{\text{c}}/g$, and the fairground ride, the grindstone, the skater, the jet tire and the swing problems each ask for an acceleration in multiples of $g$ or for the angular velocity that produces one.

concepts.name: Centripetal force, $\kFc = m\kac$
concepts.why: Any net force causing uniform circular motion is a centripetal force. It is not a new kind of force: the tension in the rope on a tether ball, the force of Earth's gravity on the Moon, friction between skates and a rink floor, and a banked roadway's force on a car can each be the centripetal force. What makes a force centripetal is its direction, toward the center of curvature, and Newton's second law then gives its magnitude.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by listing the forces that can act as one, the glossary carries the term, and the conceptual questions ask what force makes a skater turn, what stretches the string on a rotating mass, and whether any combination of forces can be a centripetal force.

concepts.name: Centripetal force, $\kFc = m\kv^2 / \kr$ and $\kFc = m\kr\kw^2$
concepts.why: Putting the two forms of the centripetal acceleration into $F_{\text{c}} = ma_{\text{c}}$ gives two forms of the centripetal force, and you use whichever is more convenient: the first when you know the speed, the second when you know the angular velocity. The force is always perpendicular to the path and always points toward the center of curvature, because the acceleration does.
concepts.evidence: The section states both forms, the first worked example finds the 1125 N force on a 900 kg car through a 500 m curve at 25.0 m/s, and the merry-go-round, wind turbine, bobsled and centrifuge-cage problems each ask for one.

concepts.name: Radius from the centripetal force, $\kr = m\kv^2 / \kFc$
concepts.why: Solving the centripetal force for the radius shows that for a given mass and speed a large force makes a tight curve and a small force a wide one. It is the reading that tells you why a car with too little friction under it runs wide off the road rather than stopping, and why the stress in a high-speed tire depends on the tire's diameter.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rearrangement and Figure 6.9 draws the same speed taken with two different forces and two different radii, and the conceptual question on the stress in high-speed tires and the bobsled problem both turn on it.

concepts.name: Friction on a level curve, $\mu_{\text{s}} = \kv^2 / \kr\kg$
concepts.why: On a level curve the only horizontal force on the car is friction, so friction is the whole centripetal force. Setting $mv^2/r$ equal to the greatest static friction $\mu_{\text{s}}N = \mu_{\text{s}}mg$ and cancelling the mass gives the smallest coefficient of friction with which the curve can be taken at that speed. The mass cancels because friction is proportional to the normal force, so it does not matter how heavily the car is loaded.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds that a 900 kg car through a 500 m curve at 25.0 m/s needs only $\mu_{\text{s}} = 0.13$ and discusses what happens when the road offers more or less, Figure 6.10 draws the car and its free-body diagram, and the unbanked 50.0 m curve problem asks the same question of a speed that turns out to be unreasonable.

concepts.name: Banked curve and ideal banking
concepts.why: A banked curve is one whose road is sloped so that the slope helps you negotiate the curve, and the greater the angle the faster the curve can be taken. In an ideally banked curve the angle is such that the curve can be taken at a certain speed without the aid of friction at all, because the normal force alone supplies the centripetal force.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces banked curves and ideal banking before deriving the angle, Figure 6.11 draws the car on the slope with the two forces acting on it, and the glossary carries banked curve, ideal banking, ideal speed and ideal angle.

concepts.name: Ideal banking angle, $\theta = \tan^{-1}(\kv^2 / \kr\kg)$
concepts.why: On a frictionless banked curve the horizontal component of the normal force $N\sin\theta$ must supply the centripetal force and the vertical component $N\cos\theta$ must balance the weight. Dividing one by the other removes the normal force and the mass together and leaves $\tan\theta = v^2/rg$. Roads must therefore be steeply banked for high speeds and for sharp curves, and the angle does not depend on the mass of the vehicle.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the angle from the two components of the normal force and discusses how it grows with the speed and shrinks with the radius, and the 1.20 km highway curve, the bobsled turn and the icy mountain road problems each ask for an ideal angle or work back from one.

concepts.name: Ideal speed, $\kv = (\kr\kg\tan\theta)^{1/2}$
concepts.why: Reading the banking relation the other way gives the speed a curve of a given radius and bank is built for, which the book calls the ideal speed. It is the speed at which the road alone holds you on the curve, and friction then lets you take the curve at a greater or a lower speed without sliding.
concepts.evidence: The second worked example finds 45.8 m/s for a 100 m radius curve banked at 65.0º and remarks that this is about 165 km/h, and the 20.0º curve and the 15.0º icy curve problems each ask for an ideal speed.

concepts.name: Solve a circular-motion problem from a free-body diagram
concepts.why: A circular-motion problem is a Newton's second law problem in which the direction of the acceleration is known in advance: it points at the center of curvature. You draw the free-body diagram, choose axes with one of them along the radius, and set the net force along that axis equal to $mv^2/r$. Every case in the section, the level curve, the banked curve, the vertical loop and the swinging cage, is worked that way.
concepts.evidence: Both worked examples begin from a free-body diagram, Figures 6.10 and 6.11 draw one each, four of the conceptual questions ask for a free-body diagram or for the direction of the force on a rider, and the centrifuge-cage and roller-coaster problems cannot be started without one.

concepts.name: Non-inertial frame of reference
concepts.why: A non-inertial frame of reference is an accelerated frame. The car turning the corner and the rotating merry-go-round are both non-inertial, and inside such a frame Newton's laws do not hold as they stand unless forces with no physical origin are added to them.
concepts.evidence: The section names the turning car and the merry-go-round as non-inertial frames, Figures 6.12 and 6.13 draw each scene twice, once in the frame and once from the ground, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Fictitious force
concepts.why: A fictitious force is a force having no physical origin, invented so that Newton's laws can be applied inside an accelerating or rotating frame. Nothing pushes the passenger to the left as the car turns right; the passenger is going in a straight line and the car is moving to the right underneath. Either view allows us to describe nature, but the view from an inertial frame is the simplest and truest, because in it every force has a real origin.
concepts.evidence: The section works through the jet on the runway and the car turning right, Figure 6.12 draws the imagined force and the real one side by side, and the washing-machine and barrel-ride conceptual questions ask for the real forces behind a fictitious one.

concepts.name: Centrifugal force
concepts.why: The centrifugal force is the fictitious force that seems to throw you off a rotating frame, and it is not to be confused with the centripetal force, which is real and points the other way. In Earth's frame nothing throws the rider off the merry-go-round; the rider must hang on in order to go in a circle rather than travel in a straight line off the edge. A centrifuge works for the same reason: the inertia of the particles carries them along a tangent while the test tube is forced round.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the ride on the merry-go-round and the sedimentation in a centrifuge, Figures 6.13 and 6.14 draw both, the glossary carries the term, and the washing-machine and barrel-ride conceptual questions ask about it.

concepts.name: Coriolis force
concepts.why: A ball slid straight out across a rotating merry-go-round follows a straight path over the ground and a path curved to the right across the boards, and in the merry-go-round's frame that curve is explained by a fictitious force, the Coriolis force. Earth turns the same way seen from above the North Pole, so any motion in the northern hemisphere is deflected to the right and any motion in the southern hemisphere to the left. The deflection is usually negligible, but on the scale of a weather system it turns the winds flowing into a low pressure into a counterclockwise circulation, which is why hurricanes rotate one way north of the equator and tropical cyclones the other way south of it.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.15 draws the ball's two paths, Figure 6.16 shows the deflected winds round a low and a high pressure and two satellite photographs of cyclones turning opposite ways, the glossary carries the term, and the draining-sink conceptual question asks for the direction of the rotation in the northern hemisphere.

concepts.name: Newton's universal law of gravitation, $\kF = GmM/\kr^2$
concepts.why: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force along a line joining them, directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force is always attractive, it depends on nothing but the masses and the separation, and the same formula holds for a father and a baby, for Earth and the Moon, and for one galaxy and another. The magnitude of the force on each of the two bodies is the same, consistent with Newton's third law, however different the two masses are.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law in words and in symbols, Figure 6.18 draws the two masses and the equal and opposite forces, the Misconception Alert insists that the force on each is the same, and the baby-and-father, mountain and Neptune problems each ask for a force or an acceleration from it.

concepts.name: Gravitational constant $G$
concepts.why: $G$ is the proportionality factor in the universal law of gravitation, measured to be $6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ and thought to be the same everywhere in the universe. Its small size is why two 1.000 kg masses 1.000 m apart attract each other with only $6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ N, and why we are unaware that even large objects like mountains exert gravitational forces on us. Of all the fundamental constants in physics, $G$ is by far the least well determined.
concepts.evidence: The section gives its value and its units and works out the force between two 1.000 kg masses, the AP item on what $G$ represents asks for it directly, and the Cavendish passage explains how it is measured and why the measurement matters.

concepts.name: Center of mass
concepts.why: The bodies gravity acts between tend to be large, so the law is applied by assuming that each body acts as if its entire mass were concentrated at one point, its center of mass. The center of mass is the average location of the mass, and a system of objects responds to external forces as if all of its mass were concentrated there. It is between the two centers of mass that the distance $r$ in the law of gravitation is measured.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term before stating the law in symbols, Figure 6.18 marks it on both bodies, Figure 6.19 shows that for an object on Earth's surface the distance between the two centers of mass is very nearly Earth's radius, and the problem on the Earth-Moon center of mass 4700 km from Earth's center turns on it.

concepts.name: The acceleration due to gravity, $\kg = GM/\kr^2$
concepts.why: The weight of an object $mg$ is the gravitational force between it and Earth, so $mg = GmM/r^2$. The mass of the object cancels, leaving $g = GM/r^2$, and substituting Earth's mass and radius gives $9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$. This is why all masses fall with the same acceleration, and it takes Galileo's observation a step further by explaining it in terms of a force. The same expression gives $g$ on the Moon, on Mars, at the distance of the Moon, or wherever a mass and a distance are known.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the expression and works out Earth's value from its mass and radius, the worked example uses it at the distance of the Moon, three of the AP items compare the surface gravity of Jupiter, of Titan and of a newly discovered planet, and the Moon-and-Mars problem asks for two more.

concepts.name: Find a body's mass from $\kg$ and its radius, $M = \kg\kr^2/G$
concepts.why: Once $G$ is known, the relation $g = GM/r^2$ can be turned round to give the mass of the body rather than its surface gravity. This is how an accurate value for Earth's mass was finally obtained, more than a hundred years after Newton published the law, and it is one reason the measurement of $G$ mattered so much.
concepts.evidence: The Cavendish passage derives $M = gr^2/G$ and notes that every quantity on the right is known from direct measurement, the first problem of the section asks for Earth's mass from $g$ and the radius at the pole and compares it with the accepted value, and the AP item on Titan asks for the mass of a moon the same way.

concepts.name: Gravity supplies the Moon's centripetal acceleration
concepts.why: Newton's own test of his law was to ask whether the acceleration due to Earth's gravity at the distance of the Moon is the acceleration the Moon's orbit needs. Working out $GM/r^2$ at $3.84 \times 10^8$ m gives $2.70 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$, and working out $r\omega^2$ from the Moon's 27.3-day period gives $2.72 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m/s}^2$. The two differ by less than one per cent, and the clear implication is that Earth's gravitational force causes the Moon to orbit Earth.
concepts.evidence: The worked example does the two calculations and compares them, the section records that Newton found the two accelerations agreed pretty nearly, and the problem on the Earth-Moon center of mass and the problem that re-solves the example with $a_{\text{c}} = v^2/r$ both repeat the comparison.

concepts.name: Tides
concepts.why: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder than it pulls Earth, and it pulls Earth harder than it pulls the water on the far side, so the water rises on both sides at once. The tidal bulge keeps its orientation with the Moon while Earth rotates under it, which is why there are two high tides a day. The Sun has about half the effect of the Moon, so the largest tides, the spring tides, occur when Earth, the Moon and the Sun are aligned, and the smallest, the neap tides, when the Sun is at 90º to that alignment.
concepts.evidence: The section explains both bulges and the two tides a day, Figure 6.21 draws them, Figure 6.22 draws the spring and neap alignments, and the problem comparing the Moon's and the Sun's accelerations at Earth asks why the tides are predominantly due to the Moon in spite of the numbers.

concepts.name: Weightlessness and microgravity
concepts.why: Weightlessness does not mean that an astronaut is not being acted upon by the gravitational force; there is no zero gravity in an orbit. The term means that the astronaut is in free fall, accelerating with the acceleration due to gravity, as the passengers in a lift whose cable has broken are. Microgravity is the name for an environment in which the apparent net acceleration of a body is small compared with the one Earth produces at its surface, and long stays in it have been observed to waste muscle and to lose bone mass.
concepts.evidence: The section makes the point with the broken lift cable and with the astronauts of Figure 6.24, describes what long stays in microgravity do to muscle, bone, the circulation and the immune system, the glossary carries microgravity, and the conceptual question on whether a satellite in orbit is in free fall asks the reader to settle Anna and Tom's disagreement.

concepts.name: The Cavendish experiment
concepts.why: Henry Cavendish measured the tiny gravitational attraction between two ordinary-sized masses hung on a torsion fiber, and so fixed the value of $G$ in 1798, more than a hundred years after Newton published the law; his value differs by less than one per cent from the best modern one. The measurement is important because it determines the strength of one of the four forces in nature and because it made Earth's mass calculable. Experiments of the same design are still run, to ask whether the gravitational force depends on substance as well as mass and whether the inverse square law holds over sub-millimetre distances.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the apparatus and Figure 6.25 draws it, the passage recounts Eötvös's test to five parts in a billion and the modern torsion-balance work at the University of Washington, and the mass of Earth that follows from $G$ is the subject of the section's first problem.

concepts.name: The two conditions for a simple orbit
concepts.why: Kepler's laws and everything derived from them hold for a small mass $m$ orbiting a much larger mass $M$ in a system isolated from other masses. The first condition lets you view the motion as if $M$ were stationary, from an inertial frame placed on it; the second lets you neglect the small effects of everything else. Earth's satellites including the Moon, the objects orbiting the Sun, and the satellites of other planets all satisfy the two conditions to good approximation, which is why so much can be said about them without a computer.
concepts.evidence: The section states the two conditions as a numbered list before any law is stated, names the systems that satisfy them, and repeats at the end of the derivation that Kepler's third law is valid only for satellites of the same parent body.

concepts.name: Kepler's first law: the orbit is an ellipse with $M$ at one focus
concepts.why: The orbit of each planet about the Sun is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse is a closed curve such that the sum of the distances from a point on the curve to the two foci is a constant, and a circle is the special case in which the two foci coincide. The law holds for any closed gravitational orbit, not only for the planets it was stated for.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, Figure 6.26 draws an ellipse being traced with a pin at each focus and then the same ellipse with $M$ at one focus, and the conceptual question on the frames in which Kepler's laws are valid asks what kind of statement they are.

concepts.name: Kepler's second law: equal areas in equal times
concepts.why: Each planet moves so that an imaginary line drawn from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Because the areas are equal, the planet must move fastest when it is closest to the Sun and slowest when it is furthest away. The law was devised for planets orbiting the Sun but has broader validity.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law and Figure 6.27 shades three equal areas swept in equal times, and the conceptual question that asks for a free-body diagram of a satellite in an elliptical orbit asks why its speed increases as it approaches its parent body.

concepts.name: Kepler's third law, $\kTorbone^2/\kTorbtwo^2 = \krone^3/\krtwo^3$
concepts.why: The ratio of the squares of the periods of any two planets about the Sun equals the ratio of the cubes of their average distances from the Sun. It is a descriptive equation only: Kepler found it in Tycho Brahe's twenty years of observations and it gives no information as to the cause of the equality. It is enough, though, to find the period of one orbit from the period of another, which is how the period of a satellite 1500 km up is got from the period of the Moon.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, Table 6.2 shows $r^3/T^2$ to be constant to the third digit for the satellites of the Sun and again for those of Jupiter, the worked example finds a 1.93 h period for an artificial satellite from the Moon's 27.3 days, and the ratio of Jupiter's mass to Earth's and the unreasonable one-hour orbit are both asked from it.

concepts.name: Orbital speed, $GM/\kr = \kv^2$
concepts.why: For a circular orbit gravity is the whole net external force, so $GmM/r^2 = mv^2/r$. The satellite's own mass cancels, leaving $GM/r = v^2$: at a given orbital radius all masses orbit at the same speed. This is the same fact as all masses falling with the same acceleration, seen from further out.
concepts.evidence: The section derives it as the first step of the derivation of Kepler's third law and remarks that the cancelling of $m$ is another aspect of the oft-noted fact that all masses fall alike, and the space-debris problem begins by finding the speed of a satellite 900 km above Earth's surface.

concepts.name: Kepler's third law from gravitation, $\kT^2 = 4\pi^2\kr^3/GM$
concepts.why: Substituting the average speed $v = 2\pi r/T$ into $GM/r = v^2$ gives $T^2 = 4\pi^2 r^3/GM$, and taking the ratio of that expression for two satellites of the same parent body gives Kepler's third law, with $M$ cancelling. The point of the derivation is to demonstrate that the force of gravity is the cause of what Kepler only described, and it also shows why the third law compares satellites of one parent body only.
concepts.evidence: The section carries the derivation through from Newton's second law applied to circular motion and the universal law of gravitation, and closes by saying that Kepler was able to discover what was happening and Newton discovered that gravitational force was the cause.

concepts.name: Weigh a parent body from a satellite's orbit, $\kr^3/\kT^2 = GM/4\pi^2$
concepts.why: Solving $T^2 = 4\pi^2 r^3/GM$ for the ratio $r^3/T^2$ gives a quantity that is the same for every satellite of one parent body and that depends on nothing but $G$ and the parent's mass. So if the radius and the period of one satellite are known, the mass of the body it goes round can be calculated, and this principle has been used extensively to find the masses of heavenly bodies that have satellites.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation and says it has been used extensively, Table 6.2 shows $r^3/T^2$ constant for the Sun's satellites and again for Jupiter's, and the problems ask for the mass of the Sun from Earth's orbit, the mass of Jupiter from one of its moons, and the mass of the Milky Way from a star on its periphery.

concepts.name: A description and a cause
concepts.why: Kepler's laws describe how the planets move; Newton's universal law of gravitation says why, and that single equation describes every situation in which gravity acts. Before these discoveries the solar system was described by the Ptolemaic model, a list of facts with a different rule for each heavenly body and no cause and effect behind any of it, while the Copernican model needs a small set of rules and a single underlying force. The breadth and simplicity of the laws of physics is the argument the section's title makes.
concepts.evidence: The section calls Kepler's third law a descriptive equation only, derives it from gravitation to show the cause, sets the Ptolemaic model beside the Copernican in Figure 6.28, and the conceptual question asks whether Kepler's laws are purely descriptive or contain causal information.

concepts.name: Non-uniform circular motion
concepts.why: Uniform circular motion holds the angular velocity constant, but a skater who pulls in her arms, a merry-go-round a child starts from rest and a hard disk that slows to a halt when the computer is switched off all change their rate of spin. Motion in a circle at a changing angular velocity is non-uniform circular motion, and it is what the rest of this chapter describes.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by recalling that Chapter 6 discussed only uniform circular motion, names the three everyday cases in which the angular velocity is not constant, and asks in its fourth conceptual question whether a piece of food on a microwave plate is accelerated when the plate starts to spin, turns steadily, and slows to a halt.

concepts.name: Angular acceleration, $\kalpha = \frac{\kdw}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: When the angular velocity changes, the faster the change occurs, the greater the angular acceleration. Angular acceleration is defined as the rate of change of angular velocity, exactly as linear acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, and it is measured in radians per second squared. If the angular velocity increases the angular acceleration is positive, and if it decreases the angular acceleration is negative.
concepts.evidence: The section states the definition as its first new equation, the glossary defines it, and the worked example of the bicycle wheel finds the angular acceleration of a wheel spun up from rest and then the time the brakes need to stop it, where the angular acceleration is negative.

concepts.name: Tangential acceleration, $\kat = \frac{\kdv}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: In circular motion the linear acceleration is tangent to the circle at the point of interest, and so it is called tangential acceleration. It is defined as it was for straight-line motion, as the change in the magnitude of the velocity divided by the time taken, and it tells how fast a point on the rim is speeding up or slowing down along its path.
concepts.evidence: The section names the quantity beside the figure of the semicircle with its tangent arrows, defines it with the same equation one-dimensional kinematics used, and the glossary carries it; the third conceptual question asks the reader to explain why a tangential acceleration changes the magnitude of the velocity but not its direction.

concepts.name: Tangential and centripetal acceleration are perpendicular and independent
concepts.why: Centripetal acceleration changes the direction of the velocity but not its magnitude, and tangential acceleration changes the magnitude but not the direction. The two are perpendicular to each other, so a body in circular motion may have either, both or neither, and each may be considered on its own.
concepts.evidence: The section draws both accelerations on one figure and states that they are perpendicular and independent of one another, and the fourth conceptual question asks which of the two a piece of food on a microwave plate has while the plate starts, turns steadily and stops.

concepts.name: Tangential and angular acceleration, $\kat = \kr\kalpha$
concepts.why: Because the radius is constant in circular motion, the change in the linear velocity is the radius times the change in the angular velocity, and so the tangential acceleration is the radius times the angular acceleration. The greater the angular acceleration, the greater the tangential acceleration, and the smaller the wheel, the smaller the tangential acceleration it gives for the same angular acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the definition of tangential acceleration and $v = r\omega$, prints it in both forms, and the worked example of the motorcycle finds the angular acceleration of its wheels from the linear acceleration of the machine and the radius of the tires.

concepts.name: Rotational quantities and their translational analogs
concepts.why: The angle of rotation, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration are the rotational counterparts of position, velocity and acceleration, and each pair is joined by the radius: the angle is the distance divided by the radius, the angular velocity is the velocity divided by the radius, and the angular acceleration is the tangential acceleration divided by the radius. Recognizing the analogy is what lets everything learned about straight-line motion be carried over to rotation.
concepts.evidence: The section gathers the three pairs and the three relationships into a table of its own, and its first conceptual question asks the reader to name the rotational term analogous to acceleration, force, mass, work, kinetic energy, momentum and impulse.

concepts.name: The rotational kinematic equations, $\kw = \kwo + \kalpha\kt$
concepts.why: Substituting $v = r\omega$ and $a = r\alpha$ into each of the four kinematic equations for straight-line motion makes the radius cancel, leaving four equations in the angle, the angular velocity, the angular acceleration and the time. They describe the motion without any reference to the forces or masses that produce it, and they hold whenever the angular acceleration is constant.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the first of them from $v = v_0 + at$ and then prints all four beside their translational counterparts in a table, and every worked example of the section — the fishing reel spun up, the reel braked to a stop, the freight train's wheels — chooses one of them and solves it.

concepts.name: Average angular velocity, $\kwb = \frac{\kwo + \kw}{2}$
concepts.why: When the angular acceleration is constant, the average angular velocity is halfway between the initial and the final value, just as the average velocity is halfway between the initial and the final velocity in straight-line motion. The angle turned through is then simply the average angular velocity multiplied by the time.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the average angular velocity beside the average velocity and prints $\theta = \bar{\omega}t$ as the first row of its table of kinematic equations; the example of the fly on the microwave plate finds the number of revolutions from the average angular velocity and the cooking time.

concepts.name: Linear quantities from angular ones, $\kx = \kr\theta$
concepts.why: Something spinning in place still carries its rim through a distance, and that distance is the radius times the angle turned through, in radians. In the same way the speed of a point on the rim is the radius times the angular velocity. Radians must always be used in these relationships, and because a radian is dimensionless the product of a length and an angle is a length.
concepts.evidence: The section converts revolutions to radians before every such calculation and warns that this must be done; the fishing reel example finds the speed at which line leaves the reel and the meters of line played out, and the fly on the microwave plate travels eleven meters without going anywhere.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational kinematics problem
concepts.why: A rotational kinematics problem is solved the way a straight-line one is: check that rotation is involved and that forces and masses need not be, identify the unknown, list what is given, choose the equation that contains the unknown and nothing else unknown, substitute with units, and ask whether the answer is reasonable. Thinking in terms of the translational analog is useful, because that motion is already familiar.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the six steps as a strategy box of its own and then follows them through three worked examples, and every problem at the end of the section — the gyroscope spun up with a string, the car braking on its tires, the yo-yo unwinding — is solved by choosing among the four equations.

concepts.name: Torque on a point mass, $\ktau = mr^2\kalpha$
concepts.why: A force applied perpendicular to the radius gives a point mass an acceleration $a = F/m$, and since $a = r\alpha$ this is $F = mr\alpha$. Multiplying both sides by the radius turns the left side into the torque, and the result is the rotational analog of Newton's second law for a single point mass, with $mr^2$ standing where the mass stands in $F = ma$.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the figure of a mass on a frictionless table tethered to a pivot, and states that torque is analogous to force, angular acceleration to translational acceleration, and $mr^2$ to mass.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia, $\kI = \sum mr^2$
concepts.why: To rotate anything other than a point mass, the idea of $mr^2$ is extended to a whole body: the moment of inertia is the sum of $mr^2$ over all the point masses of which the body is composed. It plays the part in rotation that mass plays in straight-line motion, it is measured in kilogram meters squared, and because the distance to the axis enters it, a body has a different moment of inertia about every axis.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity, gives the hoop as the one case simple enough to work out by hand, and prints a figure of ten shapes with their moments of inertia that every later section of the chapter sends the reader back to; the glossary carries both rotational inertia and moment of inertia.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia depends on how the mass is distributed
concepts.why: The moment of inertia depends not only on how much mass a body has but on where that mass sits relative to the axis. A merry-go-round full of children is much easier to accelerate when the children stand close to the axis than when they all stand at the rim, although the mass is the same in both cases, because the distance from the axis is squared in every term of the sum.
concepts.evidence: The section states the point directly after defining the moment of inertia, the worked example finds the angular acceleration of a merry-go-round with and without a child sitting on it, and the take-home experiment asks the reader to change the moment of inertia of a cardboard circle and see how much putty is then needed to turn it.

concepts.name: Newton's second law for rotation, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kI\kalpha$
concepts.why: The general relationship among torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration is that the net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. The larger the torque the larger the angular acceleration, and the larger the moment of inertia the smaller it is. The relationship is valid for any torque, applied to any object, about any axis, which makes it the rotational form of Newton's second law.
concepts.evidence: The section states it in both of its forms and says it is very generally applicable, the merry-go-round example uses it twice, and the problems of the section run from a grindstone to Earth's own rotation being slowed by a villain pushing at the equator.

concepts.name: Choosing the moment of inertia for a body and an axis
concepts.why: Calculating a moment of inertia by integration is beyond this text, so the moment of inertia is read from the figure of shapes for the body and the axis at hand: a hoop about its axis, a disk, a rod about its end or about its center, a sphere. Where a system is made of several bodies turning about one axis, the moments of inertia add, since each is a sum of $mr^2$ over the same axis.
concepts.evidence: The section prints the figure of ten shapes for this purpose and says that in all cases but the hoop the reader must consult it; the merry-go-round example adds the child's moment of inertia to the disk's, and later sections of the chapter send the reader back to the same figure for a rod, a sphere and a disk.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational dynamics problem
concepts.why: A problem in rotational dynamics is set up by determining that torque and mass are involved, choosing the system of interest, drawing a free body diagram of the external forces on it, and applying the rotational form of Newton's second law about the point of rotation, with care taken over which moment of inertia belongs to the body and which axis the torques are taken about. As always, the answer is then checked for reasonableness.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the five steps as a strategy box, and the problem about slowing Earth's rotation asks the reader explicitly to show how the steps are followed.

concepts.name: Rotational work, $\text{net}\;\kW = (\text{net}\;\ktau)\theta$
concepts.why: When a net force is kept perpendicular to the radius of a turning disk, the force is parallel to the displacement and the net work is the force times the arc length travelled. Multiplying and dividing by the radius turns the force into a torque and the arc length into an angle, so that the net work is the net torque times the angle turned through. Torque is analogous to force here, and angle to distance.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the expression from the figure of the disk turned by a perpendicular force and says it holds in general although it was derived for a special case; the grindstone example finds the work done through one radian of rotation and confirms that it equals the rotational kinetic energy gained.

concepts.name: Rotational kinetic energy, $\kKErot = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2$
concepts.why: A body has kinetic energy by turning as well as by travelling, and the rotational kinetic energy is half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. The expression is exactly analogous to the translational one, with the moment of inertia standing where the mass stands and the angular velocity where the velocity stands.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity by analogy after deriving the work-energy theorem for rotation, and the glossary carries it; the helicopter example finds that most of a flying helicopter's kinetic energy is in its blades rather than in its motion, and the flywheel bus stores its energy this way.

concepts.name: The work-energy theorem for rotation, $\text{net}\;\kW = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2 - \frac{1}{2}\kI{\kwo}^2$
concepts.why: Substituting the rotational form of Newton's second law into the expression for rotational work, and then using the kinematic relation between the angular velocity and the angle, gives the net work as the change in one half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. Net work changes the kinetic energy of a system, and for a turning body that kinetic energy is rotational.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the theorem step by step and names it, the glossary carries the term, and the grindstone example verifies that the work done by the torque equals the rotational kinetic energy the stone ends with.

concepts.name: A rolling body divides its energy, $\kPEgrav = \kKEtrans + \kKErot$
concepts.why: A body rolling down an incline without slipping converts its gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy of two kinds at once, translational and rotational. The greater its moment of inertia, the more of the energy goes into turning and the less is left to carry it down the slope, which is why a can of thick soup, whose contents turn with the can, loses the race to a can of thin soup, and why a can that slides without rolling wins.
concepts.evidence: The section asks why cans of identical size and mass roll down an incline at different rates, answers it with the figure of the three racing cans, and the example of the solid cylinder shows that the mass and the radius cancel, so that every solid cylinder rolls at the same rate.

concepts.name: Solving a rotational energy problem
concepts.why: Energy problems that involve rotation are solved as other energy problems are: determine that work or energy is involved, choose the system, decide which kinds of work and energy are present, and for a closed system set the initial kinetic and potential energy equal to the final, remembering that the kinetic energy may have both a translational and a rotational part. For an open system the other forms of energy must be accounted for as well.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the seven steps as a strategy box, and the problem about the flywheel bus climbing a hill asks the reader explicitly to show how they are followed.

concepts.name: Angular momentum, $\kL = \kI\kw$
concepts.why: Every rotational phenomenon has a direct translational analog, and angular momentum is the analog of linear momentum: it is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, as linear momentum is the mass times the velocity. It is measured in kilogram meters squared per second. A body with a very large moment of inertia, such as Earth, has an enormous angular momentum, and so does a body turning very fast, such as a centrifuge.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity in its first equation and the glossary carries it; the first worked example calculates the angular momentum of Earth spinning on its axis, and the problems ask for the angular momentum of the Moon, of a skater and of an engine crank.

concepts.name: Torque changes angular momentum, $\text{net}\;\ktau = \frac{\kdLang}{\kdt}$
concepts.why: When you push a merry-go-round, spin a bike wheel or open a door, you exert a torque, and if that torque is greater than the torques opposing it the angular momentum increases. The net torque is the rate at which the angular momentum changes, exactly as the net force is the rate at which linear momentum changes, which makes this the rotational form of Newton's second law.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relationship and calls it very fundamental and broadly applicable; the lazy Susan example finds the angular momentum a partygoer gives a tray by pushing for a seventh of a second, and notes that the angular momentum imparted depends on the torque and the time alone.

concepts.name: Conservation of angular momentum, $\kL = \kLprime$
concepts.why: If the net torque on a system is zero, then its angular momentum does not change: this is the law of conservation of angular momentum, and it stands beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum. It is why Earth keeps on spinning, since only the tides exert any significant retarding torque on it, and why a skater can spin for a long time on ice that opposes her very little.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the law from the relation between torque and angular momentum by setting the net torque to zero, the glossary carries it, and the section's own boxed note places it beside the conservation of energy and of linear momentum as another sign of underlying unity in physical laws.

concepts.name: A smaller moment of inertia means a faster spin, $\kI\kw = \kIprime\kwprime$
concepts.why: Because the angular momentum is conserved when no net torque acts, a body that reduces its moment of inertia must increase its angular velocity to keep the product the same. A skater pulling in her arms and her extended leg spins several times faster, an air mass whose radius narrows becomes a tornado, and the cloud of gas and dust that became the Solar System sped up as gravity drew it together.
concepts.evidence: The section writes the conservation law in terms of the moment of inertia beside the two images of the spinning skater, and the worked example finds that a skater spinning at 0.800 rev/s with her arms out reaches 5.16 rev/s when she pulls them in; the tornado, Earth's formation and the merry-go-round problems all turn on the same step.

concepts.name: Work done in pulling in raises the rotational kinetic energy
concepts.why: The skater's angular momentum is unchanged when she pulls in her arms, but her rotational kinetic energy rises sharply, and the increase comes from the work she does pulling her arms inward against the force needed to hold them on their circles. Conserving angular momentum does not conserve rotational kinetic energy, because energy can be added from within the system while the angular momentum cannot.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds the skater's rotational kinetic energy rising from 29.6 J to 191 J while her angular momentum stays the same, the section says the increase comes from work that depletes some of her food energy, and a conceptual question asks the reader to identify the force she exerts on each arm and the distance it moves.

concepts.name: Angular momentum in a collision, $\kL = m\kv r$
concepts.why: Bowling pins fly and spin when the ball reaches them, and cars spin as they collide on ice, so angular momentum has to be carried into the account of a collision. A body moving in a straight line has an angular momentum about a chosen point, since taking it to be a point mass gives $I = mr^2$ and $\omega = v/r$, and the product is the mass times the velocity times the distance to the point. Where the external force acts at the pivot its lever arm is zero, so it exerts no torque and the angular momentum of the system is conserved through the collision.
concepts.evidence: The section works through a disk that strikes and adheres to a nailed stick on a frictionless surface, states that the force at the nail exerts no torque because its lever arm is zero, and uses the conservation of angular momentum to find how fast the two turn afterward.

concepts.name: Solving a collision of extended bodies, $\kwprime = \frac{m\kv r}{\kIprime}$
concepts.why: A collision in which a body is free to rotate is solved by setting the angular momentum before equal to the angular momentum after, both calculated about the same pivot point. The angular momentum before is that of the incoming body treated as a point mass, and the angular momentum after is the combined moment of inertia about the pivot times the angular velocity, where the combined moment of inertia is the sum of the separate ones about that axis.
concepts.evidence: The section carries the disk-and-stick example through in full and the problems repeat it with the disk striking closer to the nail, with the disk already spinning, and with the stick free to travel as well as turn; the twin skaters who lock hands and the person who catches a ball on ice are solved the same way.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy and linear momentum in a rotational collision
concepts.why: Angular momentum may be conserved in a collision while kinetic energy is not, because the collision is inelastic, and linear momentum need not be conserved either, because the force at the pivot may have a component along the incoming body's path. In the disk and stick the kinetic energy falls from 22.5 J to 1.57 J while the linear momentum rises, which the nail explains: the stick pushes back on the nail and the nail pushes forward on the stick.
concepts.evidence: The example calculates the kinetic energy and the linear momentum before and after the collision as well as the angular velocity, and its discussion works out why the momentum afterward is the greater of the two; the conceptual questions ask which quantities are likely to be conserved when a puck strikes a free hockey stick.

concepts.name: The percussion point
concepts.why: Striking the nailed stick at its far end pushes the nail backward and striking it near the nail pushes the nail forward, so there is a point in between at which no force is delivered to the pivot at all. That point is the percussion point. A tennis racquet and a baseball bat have one too, and a ball met there leaves little force and little vibration in the hand, which is what players call the sweet spot.
concepts.evidence: The section reasons from the two extremes of the disk-and-stick collision to the point between them, names it, and draws the three cases for a racquet: struck near the end, struck far down the shaft, and struck at the percussion point.

concepts.name: The right-hand rule for angular velocity and angular momentum
concepts.why: Angular velocity and angular momentum are vectors, and their direction is found by curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the rotation: the thumb then points along the axis of rotation in the direction of both. Because the angular momentum is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity, and the moment of inertia is a positive number, the two point the same way.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rule beside the figure of the turning disk with its arrow along the axis and the drawn right hand, and the glossary carries it; the direction of a torque is found the same way, by curling the fingers in the direction of the force.

concepts.name: A torque changes angular momentum in its own direction
concepts.why: The net torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so the change in angular momentum points the way the torque points. When the torque is perpendicular to the angular momentum already there, the two add head to tail to give a new angular momentum of the same size pointing in a new direction, and the axis of rotation moves perpendicular to the forces applied rather than the way they push.
concepts.evidence: The section applies the rule to a bicycle wheel with handles that a person tries to tip, draws the vector sum of the angular momentum and its change, and notes that the wheel moves toward the person instead of the way she pushes it.

concepts.name: Gyroscopic precession
concepts.why: The weight of a spinning gyroscope and the force from its stand create a horizontal torque, always perpendicular to the angular momentum, so the direction of the angular momentum changes while its magnitude does not and the gyroscope precesses about a vertical axis instead of falling over. A gyroscope that is not spinning simply acquires angular momentum in the direction of the torque and falls. Earth precesses in the same way, once in about 26,000 years, under the torque of the Sun and the Moon on its nonspherical shape.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the two forces on a spinning gyroscope and the vector diagram of the angular momentum turning, says that Earth's axis points at Polaris and slowly precesses, and the section's one problem finds the torque that produces that precession.

concepts.name: Fluid
concepts.why: A fluid is a state of matter that yields to a sideways, or shearing, force, while a solid resists one. Liquids, gases, and plasmas are all fluids, because in each of them the particles slide past one another and the substance flows. This one property is what the rest of the chapter rests on: because a fluid cannot withstand a shearing force, it cannot exert one either, and so the force it exerts on any surface is perpendicular to that surface.
concepts.evidence: The section states the definition beside the figure of the three phases, the glossary carries the term, and the first conceptual question asks what physical characteristic distinguishes a fluid from a solid.

concepts.name: The common phases of matter
concepts.why: Matter most commonly exists as a solid, a liquid, a gas, or a plasma. A solid has a definite shape and a specific volume, a liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of whatever holds it, and a gas or a plasma has neither, since its particles move to fill the container. Knowing which phase a substance is in tells you at once whether it will flow and whether it can be compressed.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the four phases and names them, its figure draws the atoms of each, and two conceptual questions ask which substances are fluids at room temperature and how gases differ from liquids.

concepts.name: Atomic arrangement explains the phases
concepts.why: The forces between atoms explain what we see. Atoms in a solid are in contact and held near their neighbors, so a solid keeps its shape and resists compression. Atoms in a liquid are also in close contact but can slide over one another, so a liquid flows and yet still resists compression. Atoms in a gas and charged particles in a plasma are far apart and pull on one another only weakly, so a gas both flows and compresses easily.
concepts.evidence: The section devotes a paragraph to each phase, the Connections note names this submicroscopic explanation as a theme of the text, and a conceptual question asks why gases are easier to compress than liquids and solids.

concepts.name: Density, $\krho = m/V$
concepts.why: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object, and it is what the old riddle about a ton of feathers and a ton of bricks turns on: the two have the same mass, but the feathers occupy a far greater volume, so their density is much lower. Density is crucial in determining whether an object sinks or floats in a fluid, which is why the chapter defines it before it defines anything else.
concepts.evidence: The section states $\krho = m/V$ as its first equation and repeats it in a boxed note, Table 11.1 lists the density of solids, liquids and gases, and the problem set asks for the density of a rock, of a full gasoline can and of eighteen-karat gold.

concepts.name: Density identifies a substance
concepts.why: Because every substance has its own density, a measured density helps say what an object is made of. Gold is about two and a half times as dense as iron, which is about two and a half times as dense as aluminum. Density also reveals something about the phase of matter and its substructure: liquids and solids have roughly comparable densities because their atoms are in close contact, while gases are far less dense because their atoms are separated by large amounts of empty space.
concepts.evidence: The section reads Table 11.1 for exactly this purpose, a conceptual question asks for an example in which density is used to identify the substance composing an object, and a problem asks for the density of a nucleus and of a neutron star.

concepts.name: Finding a mass from a density and a volume
concepts.why: Solving $\krho = m/V$ for the mass gives $m = \krho V$, so once the volume of a body is known from its dimensions and its density is looked up, its mass follows. This is how the chapter weighs the water behind a dam, and it is the first step of almost every buoyancy calculation later in the chapter.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds the mass of a reservoir from its surface area and its average depth, and the problem set asks for the volume of a troy ounce of gold, the volume of a flask of mercury, the mass of a deep breath of air and the depth of a gasoline tank.

concepts.name: Pressure, $\kPr = \kF/A$
concepts.why: Pressure is the force divided by the area perpendicular to the force over which the force is applied. A given force can have a very different effect depending on the area it is spread over, which is why being poked with a finger is merely irritating while the same force applied through the sharp end of a needle breaks the skin. Pressure is defined for all states of matter, but it matters most in fluids.
concepts.evidence: The section states $\kPr = \kF/A$ as its first equation and repeats it in a boxed note, the figure of the finger and the needle shows one force over two areas, and the conceptual questions ask about the sharpness of a knife, a dull hypodermic needle, padded shoes and toe dancing.

concepts.name: The pascal, $1\;\text{Pa} = 1\;\text{N/m}^2$
concepts.why: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, which is one newton per square meter. Everyday pressures run to large numbers of pascals, so several other units stay in common use: millibars in meteorology, pounds per square inch for tire pressure, and millimeters of mercury for blood pressure. Knowing what each is worth in pascals is what lets a measurement taken with one instrument be compared with another.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the pascal and then the millibar and the pound per square inch, the summary states the unit again, and a conceptual question asks how to convert millimeters of mercury, centimeters of water and inches of mercury into newtons per meter squared without a table of conversion factors.

concepts.name: Fluid pressure has no direction
concepts.why: A static fluid cannot withstand a shearing force, and so it cannot exert one either. The force a fluid exerts on any surface is therefore perpendicular to that surface, and it is exerted on every surface at once: a swimmer feels pressure on all sides, and the air in a tire pushes outward on every part of it. The pressure itself is a scalar quantity and has no direction; only the forces it produces have one.
concepts.evidence: The section argues this in a paragraph of its own, the figures of the tire and of the swimmer draw the forces perpendicular to every surface, and the conceptual questions ask why the force exerted by static fluids is always perpendicular to a surface and how the outward force on the end of an air tank is balanced.

concepts.name: Finding a force from a pressure, $\kF = \kPr A$
concepts.why: Rearranging the definition of pressure gives the force a pressure exerts on a surface, $\kF = \kPr A$. The force is directly proportional to the area acted upon as well as to the pressure itself, which is why the flat end of a gas cylinder must be strong and why a hammered nail can split wood.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds the force the air in a tank exerts on a disk 0.150 m in diameter, and the problem set asks for the pressure under a high heel, the pressure of a phonograph needle on a record and the force needed on the tip of a nail.

concepts.name: Pressure due to the weight of a fluid, $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$
concepts.why: The bottom of a container supports the entire weight of the fluid in it, because the vertical sides cannot exert an upward force on a fluid. Writing that weight as $\krho A\kh\kg$ and dividing by the area gives $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$, and the area cancels. The result holds even where there is no container: the pressure at any depth in a fluid is the weight of the fluid above a unit area, and it depends on the depth and the density and on nothing else.
