concepts.evidence: The section derives the result step by step from the figure of the container, states it as the section's own equation, and repeats it in the summary; every worked example of the section and most of its problems use it.

concepts.name: Pressure depends on depth, not on the shape of the container
concepts.why: Because $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$ contains no width and no length, the pressure at a point in a fluid does not depend on how much fluid there is or on the shape of what holds it. The pressure on a dam is set by the average depth of the water at the dam, not by how far the reservoir stretches behind it, and a small column of water inside a ring of sandbags can balance a whole flooded river.
concepts.evidence: The discussion after the dam example says that the pressure is completely independent of the width and length of the lake, and a conceptual question asks how the small amount of water held by sandbags balances the much larger body of water behind a levee.

concepts.name: Where $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$ can be used
concepts.why: The result assumes the density is the same everywhere in the fluid. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so it holds in them to great depths. Gases are quite compressible, and their density falls with height, so the result can be applied to a gas only over a depth small enough that the density changes little, or with an average density standing in for the true one.
concepts.evidence: The section states the restriction immediately after deriving the result, the worked example on the density of the atmosphere finds an average density about fifteen times smaller than the density at sea level, and a conceptual question asks why atmospheric pressure decreases more rapidly than linearly with altitude.

concepts.name: Atmospheric pressure, $\kPatm = 1.01\times 10^{5}\;\text{N/m}^2$
concepts.why: Atmospheric pressure is pressure due to the weight of a fluid like any other, in this case the weight of the air above a given height. On average at sea level a column of air standing on one square meter weighs $1.01\times 10^{5}$ N, and that is one atmosphere. It falls as you climb, because there is less air above you, which is why your ears pop on a plane flight.
concepts.evidence: The section states the standard value, draws the column of air over one square meter, and shows that 120 km of air and 10.3 m of water create the same pressure; the conceptual questions ask why you can get up from the beach with ten tons of air on you and why atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.

concepts.name: Average pressure and the force on a wall, $\kF = \kPbar A$
concepts.why: Pressure increases linearly with depth, so the average pressure on a vertical wall is the pressure at its average depth, and the force on the wall is that average pressure times the area of contact. This is how the force on a dam is found, and it is why a dam is built thicker at the bottom, where the pressure is greatest.
concepts.evidence: The worked example finds the average pressure on a dam holding water 80.0 m deep and the force it must withstand, and shows that the force is less than a tenth of a percent of the weight of the water behind it; a problem asks the reader to show that the force on a rectangular dam increases with the square of the water depth.

concepts.name: Finding a density or a depth from a pressure
concepts.why: Because $\kPr = \kh\krho\kg$ ties three quantities together, any one of them follows from the other two. Solving for the density gives the average density of a fluid from the pressure it exerts and the height of its column, and solving for the height gives the depth at which a fluid reaches a stated pressure.
concepts.evidence: One worked example finds the average density of the atmosphere from atmospheric pressure and the 120 km height of the air, and another finds that 10.3 m of water creates a pressure of one atmosphere; the problems ask for the depth of mercury that creates 1.00 atm and for the height of a water tower that creates a stated gauge pressure.

concepts.name: Pascal's principle
concepts.why: A change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid and to the walls of its container. The atoms in a fluid are free to move about, so they carry the change everywhere, and an enclosed fluid cannot flow away from the push as a river would. This experimentally verified fact is what makes pressure so important in fluids, since a pressure applied at one place is then known at every other.
concepts.evidence: The section states the principle in the text and again in a boxed note, the glossary carries it, and every hydraulic calculation of the section begins by setting the pressure at one piston equal to the pressure at the other.

concepts.name: Pressures from different sources add
concepts.why: Because a change in pressure is transmitted undiminished, the total pressure in a fluid is the sum of the pressures from the different sources acting on it. The pressure 10.3 m down in a swimming pool is two atmospheres, half from the water above and half from the air above the water, and the pressure anywhere in a fluid open to the air is the fluid's own pressure plus atmospheric pressure.
concepts.evidence: The section states that Pascal's principle implies that pressures add, 11.4 has already shown the water and the air adding at a depth of 10.3 m, and 11.6 rests the whole distinction between gauge and absolute pressure on it.

concepts.name: A hydraulic system
concepts.why: A hydraulic system is an enclosed fluid system used to exert forces. Pushing on one piston raises the pressure everywhere in the fluid, and that pressure pushes on every other piston in the system. The advantage over a lever is that the pressure can be sent through tortuously curved lines to several places at once, which is what lets one brake pedal work four wheels.
concepts.evidence: The section names the term, draws the simple two-cylinder system and then the automobile brakes with four wheel cylinders, and takes the brake system as its worked example; a conceptual question asks what happens if the pedal cylinder sits higher than the wheel cylinder.

concepts.name: Forces in a hydraulic system, $\kFone/A_1 = \kFtwo/A_2$
concepts.why: The two pistons of a simple hydraulic system are at the same height, so there is no difference in pressure due to a difference in depth and the pressure at one equals the pressure at the other. Writing each pressure as force over area gives $\kFone/A_1 = \kFtwo/A_2$: a force applied to a small piston comes out larger at a large one, in the ratio of their areas. A pedal cylinder five times narrower than a wheel cylinder multiplies the force twenty-five-fold, since the areas go as the square of the radii.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from Pascal's principle, the worked example finds the $1.25\times 10^{4}$ N each wheel cylinder exerts when 500 N is applied to a pedal cylinder five times narrower, and the problems ask for the force needed to lift a car and for the area ratio of a system that multiplies force a hundredfold.

concepts.name: A hydraulic system cannot do more work than is done on it
concepts.why: A hydraulic system increases force the way a simple machine does, and like a simple machine it obeys conservation of energy. Work is force times the distance moved, and the wheel cylinder moves through a smaller distance than the pedal cylinder by exactly the factor the force is multiplied by, so the work output equals the work input. The more wheel cylinders are added, the smaller the distance each one moves.
concepts.evidence: The section says so in the paragraph after the brake example and again in the Making Connections note on conservation of energy, and a problem asks the reader to verify that the work input equals the work output when there are no losses to friction.

concepts.name: Gauge pressure
concepts.why: Pressure gauges are built to read zero at atmospheric pressure, which is why a tire with a gaping hole in it reads zero even though there is air inside. Gauge pressure is the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure: positive for pressures above atmospheric pressure and negative for pressures below it. It is the useful quantity for a tire and for blood, because what matters is how much greater the pressure is than the air outside.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the flat tire, states the definition in the text and again in a boxed note, and explains that atmospheric pressure has no net effect on blood flow because it adds to the pressure coming out of the heart and going back into it.

concepts.name: Absolute pressure, $\kPabs = \kPg + \kPatm$
concepts.why: Because pressures add, atmospheric pressure adds to the pressure in any fluid that is not enclosed in a rigid container. The total, or absolute, pressure is therefore the gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. Fluids push rather than pull, so in most cases the absolute pressure cannot be negative, and the smallest possible gauge pressure is $-\kPatm$; there is no theoretical limit on how large a gauge pressure can be.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation and a boxed note repeats it, a tire gauge reading 34 psi is shown to be 48.7 psi absolute, and a problem asks for the gauge and the absolute pressures in a balloon and in a vacuum-packed peanut jar.

concepts.name: Reading a gauge pressure from a manometer, $\kPg = \kh\krho\kg$
concepts.why: A manometer is a U-shaped tube with one side open to the atmosphere. With both sides open the fluid stands at the same depth on each side, because atmospheric pressure pushes down equally on both. Connect one side to a source of pressure and the levels shift until the height difference balances the difference in pressure, so the gauge pressure is $\kh\krho\kg$ and is found by measuring $\kh$. The height difference is positive when the source is above atmospheric pressure and negative when it is below.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the manometer level, raised by a toy balloon and lowered by a vacuum-packed jar, and reads each; the problems ask for the gauge and absolute pressures in both, and for how tall a water-filled manometer would have to be to measure 300 mm Hg.

concepts.name: The barometer, $\kh\krho\kg = \kPatm$
concepts.why: A barometer is a tube with a nearly pure vacuum above the fluid rather than air, so it measures absolute pressure rather than gauge pressure, and what it measures is the pressure of the atmosphere. The mercury stands at whatever height makes the pressure due to its weight equal to atmospheric pressure, which is why atmospheric pressure is so often quoted in millimeters of mercury and why a barometer also works as an altimeter.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the mercury barometer and states that the atmosphere is able to force the mercury up because the pressure above it is zero, Table 11.2 gives 1.0 atm as 760 mm Hg, and a conceptual question asks why mercury rather than water is used.

concepts.name: Measuring blood pressure
concepts.why: An inflatable cuff on the upper arm is squeezed until the pressure it applies cuts off blood flow below it, and a mercury manometer reads that pressure. As the applied pressure is slowly lowered, the value at which flow first begins is the systolic pressure, the maximum the heart produces, and the value at which blood flows without interruption is the diastolic pressure, the minimum between beats. A young adult's typical reading is 120 mm Hg over 80 mm Hg. Mercury is used because it is 13.6 times as dense as water and so gives a column short enough to read.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the measurement beside the photograph of the cuff, defines systolic and diastolic pressure in boxed notes and in the glossary, and its problems convert a 120 over 80 reading into newtons per meter squared and ask what a cuff on the leg of a standing person would read.

concepts.name: Buoyant force
concepts.why: Pressure increases with depth, so the fluid pushes up on the bottom of a submerged object harder than it pushes down on the top. The horizontal forces cancel, and what is left is a net upward force, the buoyant force. It acts on any object in any fluid, whether the object floats, sinks or hangs suspended, which is why your arms feel strangely heavy when you rise from a warm bath and why a helium balloon tugs upward on its string.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the warm bath and the helium balloons, draws the two unequal forces on the top and the bottom of a cylinder, states the definition in a boxed note and in the glossary, and a problem asks the reader to prove that the difference of the two forces is the weight of the fluid displaced.

concepts.name: Whether an object floats, sinks or stays suspended
concepts.why: The buoyant force competes with the object's weight. If the buoyant force is greater than the weight, the object rises to the surface and floats; if it is less, the object sinks; and if the two are equal, the object remains suspended at that depth. A submarine is built to move between the three by changing what it holds in its ballast tanks.
concepts.evidence: The section states the three cases in the paragraph that defines the buoyant force and again in the summary, the figure of the anchor, the submarine and the balloons shows all three, and the worked example compares the buoyant force with the weight for a block of steel and for the same steel shaped into a boat.

concepts.name: Archimedes' principle, $\kFB = \kwfl$
concepts.why: Take a submerged object out of a fluid and the space it occupied is filled by fluid instead, which the surrounding fluid holds up. The buoyant force must therefore equal the weight of that fluid, which is the weight of the fluid the object displaced. Archimedes stated this long before the concept of force was well established, and it is valid in general, for any object in any fluid, whether partially or totally submerged.
concepts.evidence: The section argues it from the figure of the object and the fluid that replaces it, states it in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, and the worked example uses it to find the buoyant force on ten thousand metric tons of solid steel and on the same steel shaped into a hull.

concepts.name: Average density decides whether an object floats
concepts.why: An object floats when its average density is less than the density of the fluid around it. The fluid, having the higher density, contains more mass and hence more weight in the same volume, so the buoyant force, which is that weight, exceeds the object's own. This is why a lump of clay sinks and the same clay molded into the shape of a boat floats: the shape changes the average density, not the mass.
concepts.evidence: The section opens its discussion of density with the clay and the steel ship, states the rule in a paragraph of its own, and lists oil on water, a hot-air balloon, an iceberg and mountain ranges floating on the denser mantle beneath them as examples of it.

concepts.name: The fraction submerged, $\krhoobj/\krhofl$
concepts.why: For a floating object the volume submerged equals the volume of fluid displaced, and the object's mass equals the mass of that fluid. Putting $\krho = m/V$ into the ratio of the volumes makes the masses cancel and leaves the fraction submerged equal to the average density of the object divided by the density of the fluid. A loaded ship therefore sits deeper than an unloaded one, and the same ship floats higher in sea water than in fresh water.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the figure of the loaded and the unloaded ship, the worked example finds the average density of a woman who floats with 97.0 percent of her volume submerged, and the problems ask what fraction of ice is submerged in fresh water and how a hydrometer reads a fluid's density.

concepts.name: Specific gravity
concepts.why: Specific gravity is the ratio of the density of an object to the density of a fluid, usually water, and it is dimensionless, so it comes out the same whatever units the densities are written in. A substance whose specific gravity is less than one floats, one greater than one sinks, and one exactly equal to one remains suspended, which is the state a scuba diver tries to reach. For a floating object the specific gravity is also the fraction submerged, which is what a hydrometer reads off directly.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, draws the hydrometer floating in a fluid of specific gravity 0.87, and a problem asks for the density of a fluid in which a hydrometer floats with 92.0 percent of its volume submerged.

concepts.name: Finding a density by weighing an object twice
concepts.why: A submerged object appears to weigh less, and the apparent weight loss is exactly the weight of the fluid it displaces; on a balance that measures mass, the apparent mass loss is the mass of the fluid displaced. Weigh an object in air and again submerged in a fluid of known density, and its volume, and so its density, follow. The same two measurements give the density of the fluid instead when the density of the object is already known.
concepts.evidence: The section states both forms and draws the coin weighed in air and then submerged, the worked example finds the density of an ancient Greek coin and identifies it as silver, and the problems do the same for a bird bone, a rock, a chunk of iron in an unknown liquid and a gold-plated tungsten ingot.

concepts.name: Cohesive forces
concepts.why: Cohesive forces are the attractive forces between molecules of the same type. They are what hold a liquid together in an open container, what draw its surface into the smallest area it can take, and what let a column of sap in a tree be pulled upward like a chain held together at every link.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, opens on soap bubbles and an underwater spider's air supply, and a conceptual question asks whether surface tension is due to cohesive or adhesive forces, or both.

concepts.name: Adhesive forces
concepts.why: Adhesive forces are the attractive forces between molecules of different types. They are what make a drop cling to a window pane, what let water spread across bare paint but bead up on wax, and what draw blood into a small-diameter tube that merely touches a drop. The competition between adhesion and cohesion decides how a liquid meets a solid.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, and the conceptual questions ask whether capillary action is due to cohesive or adhesive forces and why water beads up on an oily sunbather but not on her neighbor.

concepts.name: Surface tension, $\kgamma = \kF/L$
concepts.why: Molecules at the surface of a liquid are pulled inward by their neighbors below, while molecules inside the liquid feel no net force at all, so the surface contracts to the smallest area it can. The surface then behaves like a stretched elastic sheet: it dents under an insect's foot and holds up a steel needle although the needle is far denser than water. Surface tension $\kgamma$ is the force per unit length exerted by that stretched membrane, and it is greater for a liquid whose cohesive forces are stronger.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, states $\kgamma = \kF/L$, draws the insect and the needle and the sliding wire device that measures the force, and Table 11.3 lists the surface tension of fourteen liquids.

concepts.name: Pressure inside a bubble, $\kPr = 4\kgamma/r$
concepts.why: Surface tension pulls a bubble into a sphere and squeezes the gas inside, so the gauge pressure within a bubble is $4\kgamma/r$. The smaller the bubble, the greater that excess pressure, which is why opening a valve between a small balloon and a large one empties the small one into the large one rather than the other way about.
concepts.evidence: The section states the result and draws two balloons of unequal size joined by a tube, the worked example finds 740 Pa inside a soap bubble $2.00\times 10^{-4}$ m in radius, and the problems ask for the pressure inside an alveolus and inside bubbles of water, alcohol and soapy water.

concepts.name: Surface tension in the lungs
concepts.why: The lungs end in hundreds of millions of mucus-lined sacs called alveoli, about 0.1 mm in diameter, and surface tension in their lining is enough to push air out without any muscle action at all. Because the pressure rises as a sac shrinks, small alveoli would empty into large ones and collapse; a lipoprotein surfactant in the lining prevents this by raising the wall tension as a sac stretches and lowering it as the sac contracts. An infant born without the surfactant has lungs that are very difficult to inflate.
concepts.evidence: The section devotes three paragraphs to the alveoli, draws them and graphs surface tension against surface area for lung surfactant and for a detergent, and its problems ask for the pressure inside an alveolus and for the surface tension of its fluid lining.

concepts.name: Contact angle
concepts.why: Where a liquid meets a solid, the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface and the solid surface is the contact angle, and it says which of the two kinds of force is winning. A large angle means the cohesive forces are strong relative to the adhesive ones and the liquid draws itself into a droplet; a small angle means adhesion is flattening the drop against the solid. Water on waxed car paint stands at a large angle, water on bare paint at a small one.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, shows water beaded on waxed paint and flattened on bare paint, and Table 11.4 lists contact angles for seven combinations of liquid and solid.

concepts.name: Capillary action, $\kh = 2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$
concepts.why: Surface tension always works to flatten the curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube, and that pull raises the liquid when the contact angle is less than $90^\circ$ and suppresses it when the angle is greater, as it is for mercury in glass. How far the liquid goes is limited by the weight of the column it must lift, and the height works out to $2\kgamma\cos\theta/\krho\kg r$: greater for a stronger surface tension, and greater for a narrower tube and a less dense liquid, since both mean less weight to hold up.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term in the text, in a boxed note and in the glossary, draws mercury suppressed and water raised in glass tubes and then four tubes of decreasing radius, and the worked example shows that capillary action alone cannot be solely responsible for raising sap 100 m to the top of a giant redwood.

concepts.name: Pressures in the body
concepts.why: The pressures measured in the body are gauge pressures, quoted in millimeters of mercury, and they are among the most useful indicators medicine has. Table 11.5 lists them: over a hundred millimeters of mercury in the large arteries at each beat, a few in the large veins, twelve to twenty-four in the eye, and pressures that are negative between the lungs and the ribs and in the esophagus.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on how common a blood pressure measurement is, prints Table 11.5 of typical pressures in humans, and takes each system of that table in turn through the rest of the section.

concepts.name: Blood pressure and height in the body, $\kdPr = \kdh\krho\kg$
concepts.why: Blood is a fluid with weight, so the pressure in it varies with height in the body exactly as it does in any other fluid. Standing up puts the feet about 1.4 m below the heart, which raises the pressure there by 108 mm Hg, and standing still for a long time lets blood accumulate in the legs and the legs swell, which is why soldiers required to stand at attention have been known to faint and why doctors recommend tight stockings for long flights.
concepts.evidence: The section works the 1.4 m calculation in the text and again in a boxed note, the figure of the circulatory system gives typical pressures around the body, and the problems ask what a cuff on the leg would read and what happens to the pressure at the brain when a person sits up.

concepts.name: Pressure in the eye
concepts.why: The shape of the eye is maintained by the pressure of the fluid inside it, normally in the range of 12.0 to 24.0 mm Hg. When the circulation of that fluid is blocked the pressure builds, a condition called glaucoma, and it can reach 85.0 mm Hg, which over the $6.0\;\text{cm}^2$ at the back of the eye is a force of 6.8 N, the weight of about a 680 g mass resting on the eye. That is enough to damage the optic nerve permanently.
concepts.evidence: The section works the force out in the text and again in a boxed note, defines intraocular pressure and glaucoma in the glossary, and describes the tonometer that measures the pressure with a puff of air and a photograph of one in use.

concepts.name: Pressures in the lungs and the chest
concepts.why: The pressure inside the lungs drops below atmospheric pressure when muscle action in the diaphragm and the rib cage expands the chest, and that is what draws air in; it rises above atmospheric pressure when the muscles relax and surface tension in the alveoli contracts them, and that is what forces air out. The liquid attaching the lungs to the inside of the chest wall is at a negative gauge pressure of $-4$ to $-8$ mm Hg, and it is that attachment which keeps the lungs from collapsing; letting air into the chest cavity breaks it and a lung may collapse.
concepts.evidence: The section devotes its passage on the lungs to this and draws inhalation and exhalation side by side, and its problems ask for the force the diaphragm creates during forced exhalation and for the greatest depth from which a person can breathe through a hollow reed.

concepts.name: Bladder pressure and the micturition reflex
concepts.why: Bladder pressure climbs steadily from zero to about 25 mm Hg as the bladder fills to its normal capacity of $500\;\text{cm}^3$. That pressure triggers the micturition reflex, which produces the feeling of needing to urinate and also contracts the muscles around the bladder, raising the pressure to over 100 mm Hg and accentuating the sensation. Coughing, straining, tight clothes and the weight of a fetus all add to the pressure and can trigger the reflex.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the numbers and defines the micturition reflex in the glossary, and a problem asks whether the weight of a full-term fetus resting on an area of $90.0\;\text{cm}^2$ is by itself great enough to trigger it.

concepts.name: Pressures in the skeletal system
concepts.why: The largest pressures in the body are in the joints and between the vertebrae, because large forces are applied over small areas. Lifting an object improperly can create 5000 N between two vertebrae over an area as small as $10\;\text{cm}^2$, which is $5.0\times 10^{6}\;\text{N/m}^2$, about 50 atmospheres, and that is enough to damage the spinal discs and the bony vertebrae themselves.
concepts.evidence: The section works the calculation in the text and says that even under normal circumstances the forces between vertebrae create pressures of several atmospheres, and the problems ask for the pressure a tooth creates on $1.00\;\text{mm}^2$ and for the pressure and the deformation of a spinal disc under a 5000 N compressional force.

concepts.name: Flow rate
concepts.why: Flow rate is the volume of fluid that passes a location through an area during a period of time, and it is the quantity almost every question about a moving fluid is asked in: how much blood a heart pumps, how much water a hose delivers, how much air a duct carries. Because it counts volume rather than distance, it tells you nothing on its own about how fast the fluid is moving or how wide the conduit is, only about the product of the two.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the definition and its equation, the first worked example takes the resting heart’s 5.00 liters per minute and finds the volume of blood pumped in a 75-year lifetime, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Converting flow rate to convenient units
concepts.why: The SI unit of flow rate is the cubic meter per second, but almost nothing is quoted in it: a heart is measured in liters per minute, a fire hose in liters per second, a capillary in cubic centimeters per second. A liter is a thousandth of a cubic meter, and the section says plainly that whatever metric units are most convenient for a given situation are the ones to use, so converting between them is part of working almost every problem in the set.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the liter beside the definition of flow rate, the first worked example carries four conversion factors in a single line, and the problem set asks for the same rate in cubic centimeters per second, in cubic meters per second and in liters per second.

concepts.name: Flow rate from area and speed, $\kQ = A\kvb$
concepts.why: Flow rate and velocity are related but quite different physical quantities. The greater the velocity of a river the greater its flow rate, but flow rate also depends on the size of the river, which is why a rapid mountain stream carries far less water than the Amazon. The shaded cylinder of fluid that passes a point in a time has the volume of its cross-section times its length, and dividing that volume by the time gives the flow rate as the cross-sectional area times the average speed.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the cylinder of fluid in Figure 12.2, the worked example on the garden hose uses it to find the speed of the water in the hose, the example on the aorta uses it again for blood, and the summary states it.

concepts.name: Incompressible fluid
concepts.why: A fluid is incompressible when a given amount of it always occupies the same volume, however hard it is pressed. Since liquids are essentially incompressible, the equation of continuity is valid for all of them; gases are compressible, and the equation must be applied to them with caution if they are subjected to compression or expansion. Every result of this chapter, Bernoulli’s equation and Poiseuille’s law included, is written for an incompressible fluid.
concepts.evidence: The section states the restriction immediately after deriving the equation of continuity, and one of the conceptual questions asks the reader to identify some substances that are incompressible and some that are not.

concepts.name: Equation of continuity, $A_1\kvbone = A_2\kvbtwo$
concepts.why: Because the fluid is incompressible, the same amount of fluid must flow past any point of a tube in a given time, so the flow rate is the same at all points along it. Where the cross-sectional area decreases the velocity must necessarily increase, and where it increases the velocity drops. That is the purpose of a nozzle, and it is why water slows considerably when a river empties into a reservoir and picks up speed again when it leaves.
concepts.evidence: The section states it for points 1 and 2 of the narrowing tube of Figure 12.3, the worked example on the hose and the nozzle uses it to get 25.5 m/s from 1.96 m/s, the summary states it, and most of the problem set turns on it.

concepts.name: Continuity where the flow branches, $n_1A_1\kvbone = n_2A_2\kvbtwo$
concepts.why: In the cardiovascular system and in any other branching network the flow does not stay in one tube. Continuity still holds, but what is maintained is the sum of the flow rates in all the branches in any portion along the tube, so the number of branches enters the equation along with their areas and their speeds. Because the capillaries have an enormously greater total cross-section than the aorta, the blood in them moves at about a millimeter per second, which is slow enough for substances to be exchanged with the cells and still fast enough to avoid clotting.
concepts.evidence: The section states the general form after describing how arteries subdivide into arterioles and then into capillaries, the third worked example uses it to count five billion capillaries in the body, and three problems ask by what factor the blood slows when a vessel branches.

concepts.name: Pressure drops in a rapidly moving fluid
concepts.why: When a fluid flows into a narrower channel its speed increases, so its kinetic energy increases, and that energy comes from the net work done on the fluid to push it into the channel. Pressure times area is a force, so the work is done by a pressure difference, and the result is that the pressure drops in a rapidly moving fluid, whether or not the fluid is confined to a tube. A shower curtain bulges into the stall, a car passing a truck tends to veer towards it, and trains passing in opposite directions were found in the mid-1800s to tip precariously towards one another.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on this argument, draws it as the air between the car and the truck in Figure 12.5, sets a Take-Home Investigation in which the reader blows over a sheet of paper, and returns to it in the conceptual questions about the roof of a house in a tornado and about standing close to a passing train.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation, $\kPr + \frac{1}{2}\krho\kv^2 + \krho\kg\kh = \text{constant}$
concepts.why: Bernoulli’s equation states the relationship between pressure and velocity in a fluid quantitatively: for an incompressible, frictionless fluid the sum of the pressure, the term in the square of the speed and the term in the height is constant along the path a bit of fluid follows. Various quantities in the sum may change as the fluid moves, but the total does not, so a gain in speed or in height has to be paid for out of pressure.
concepts.evidence: The section states it and then restates it for two points along the path, names it for Daniel Bernoulli, and the rest of the chapter is its application: the static fluid and Bernoulli’s principle in this section, Torricelli’s theorem and power in the next, and every worked example of both.

concepts.name: Every term of Bernoulli’s equation is an energy per unit volume
concepts.why: Bernoulli’s equation is a form of the conservation of energy principle. The second and third terms are the kinetic and the gravitational potential energy with the mass replaced by the density, so each is an energy divided by a volume, and the pressure is an energy per unit volume too, since a newton per square meter multiplied by meter over meter is a joule per cubic meter. Bernoulli’s equation is, in fact, just a convenient statement of conservation of energy for an incompressible fluid in the absence of friction.
concepts.evidence: The section proves it for each of the three terms in turn, sets a Making Connections box on conservation of energy that says viscosity is what the equation leaves out, and the first problem of the set asks the reader to verify that pressure has units of energy per unit volume.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation for a static fluid, $\kPrtwo = \kProne + \krho\kg\khone$
concepts.why: When the fluid is not moving, both terms in the speed vanish and Bernoulli’s equation says that pressure increases with depth: going down by a height adds the weight of that column of fluid to the pressure. In the simplest case the pressure at the top is zero and the familiar relationship for the pressure due to the weight of a fluid is recovered. Although Bernoulli’s equation is introduced for fluid flow, it includes much of what was studied for static fluids in the preceding chapter.
concepts.evidence: The section takes the static case first, sets the lower height to zero and reads off the result, and the section’s first AP item asks at what depth beneath the surface of a lake the pressure is twice atmospheric.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s principle, $\kProne + \frac{1}{2}\krho\kvone^2 = \kPrtwo + \frac{1}{2}\krho\kvtwo^2$
concepts.why: When a fluid moves but its depth is constant, the terms in the height subtract out and Bernoulli’s equation becomes a statement about pressure and speed alone. Situations of that kind are so important that the equation has a name of its own. It says what the opening of the section argued: if the speed at one point is greater, the pressure there must be less for the equality to hold.
concepts.evidence: The section names it and derives it from Bernoulli’s equation, the worked example uses it to find the pressure in a hose from the pressure in its nozzle, the summary states it, and every application that follows, entrainment, wings and sails and velocity measurement, is worked from it.

concepts.name: Entrainment
concepts.why: People have long put Bernoulli’s principle to work by using the reduced pressure in a high-velocity fluid to move things about: with a higher pressure on the outside, the fast stream forces other fluids into itself. Entrainment devices have been in use since ancient times as pumps to raise water small heights, and the same trick runs a Bunsen burner, an atomizer, a paint sprayer, an aspirator and the chimney of a water heater.
concepts.evidence: The section names the process and draws four devices that use it in Figure 12.6, and four conceptual questions turn on it: the Venturi constriction, the T-shaped chimney pipe, the limit to the height an entrainment device can raise a fluid, and how the perfume rises in an atomizer.

concepts.name: Lift on a wing and a sail
concepts.why: The airplane wing is a beautiful example of Bernoulli’s principle in action. The wing is tilted upward at a small angle and its upper surface is longer, so air flows faster over the top, the pressure there is reduced, and the difference is a net upward force. A sail has the characteristic shape of a wing too: the pressure on its front is lower than the pressure on its back, which gives a forward force and even allows a boat to sail into the wind. Wings also gain lift by pushing air downward, and the deflected air pushes back on the wing by Newton’s third law.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the wing and the sail in Figure 12.7 and names the pressure on each surface, and the conceptual questions ask why an airplane takes off into the wind and why a sailboat needs a keel; the book’s problem on the force the wind exerts on a square meter of sail turns on the same difference in pressure between the two sides.

concepts.name: Measuring fluid speed with a manometer, $\kvtwo \propto \sqrt{\kh}$
concepts.why: Two tubes small enough not to disturb the flow, joined by a manometer, measure the speed of a fluid. The tube facing the oncoming fluid creates a dead spot with zero velocity in front of it, while the fluid passing the other tube keeps its speed, so the pressure at the second opening is lower by the term in the square of the speed. The manometer fluid rises by a height proportional to that term, and the speed is therefore proportional to the square root of the height. The pitot tube built on this principle is the air speed indicator of an aircraft.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the manometer and the pitot tube in Figure 12.8 and works the proportionality out from Bernoulli’s principle, and three problems use it: by what factor the wind speed must rise to double the height, what a pitot tube reads at 700 km/h given its reading at 200 km/h, and the derivation of the speed from a mercury manometer.

concepts.name: Torricelli’s theorem, $\kvtwo^2 = \kvone^2 + 2\kg\kh$
concepts.why: Water gushing from a tube at the base of a dam emerges at just the speed it would have if it had fallen the distance from the surface of the reservoir, and the speed does not depend on the size of the opening. Both pressures are atmospheric and subtract out of Bernoulli’s equation, and the density cancels because the fluid is incompressible, leaving a kinematic equation for an object falling that height with negligible resistance. As with conservation of energy applied to falling objects, the result does not depend on the direction the water leaves in.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the theorem from Bernoulli’s equation for the dam of Figure 12.11, and the conceptual question about the old boot with two leaks at the same height asks the reader to say how high the water from each can squirt and why.

concepts.name: Applying Bernoulli’s equation where pressure, speed and height all change
concepts.why: Every earlier use of Bernoulli’s equation simplified it first, by holding the height constant or the pressure equal at both points. The general case keeps all three terms at both points: the speeds are found from the flow rate and the two cross-sections, the heights are measured from whichever point is taken as the reference, and the remaining pressure is what is solved for. A fire hose that runs ten meters up a ladder to a narrow nozzle is exactly this case, and its pressure falls for both reasons at once.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the general case before the worked example, and the example on the fire hose nozzle finds the speeds from the flow rate, takes the ground as the zero of height and solves for the pressure at the base of the hose; two of the section’s AP items ask the same of a pipe that rises into a building.

concepts.name: Power in fluid flow, $\left(\kPr + \frac{1}{2}\krho\kv^2 + \krho\kg\kh\right)\kQ = \text{power}$
concepts.why: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is used or supplied. Every term of Bernoulli’s equation is an energy per unit volume, so multiplying the whole equation by the flow rate, which is a volume per unit time, gives a power. Each term then has a clear physical meaning: one is the power supplied to give the fluid its pressure, one the power supplied to give it its kinetic energy, and one the power that goes to gravitational potential energy.
concepts.evidence: The section derives it by considering the units, sets a Making Connections box on power beside it, and the summary states it; the problem on Hoover Dam asks for the power in a flow of 650 cubic meters per second taken from a depth of 150 meters, and the problem on the left ventricle asks for the total power output of a heart that raises pressure, speed and height at once.

concepts.name: Finding the power a pump supplies, $\text{power} = \kPr\kQ$
concepts.why: A pump that takes fluid in and sends it out through a hose of the same diameter at the same height changes neither the speed nor the height of the fluid, so its kinetic and gravitational potential energy are unchanged and the only term left is the pressure. The power the pump supplies is then the pressure it adds multiplied by the flow rate. A pump that raises velocity and height as well, as the heart does, needs all three terms.
concepts.evidence: The worked example on the fire truck finds 36.8 kW from a pressure rise of 0.920 million newtons per square meter at 40.0 liters per second and remarks that this is about 50 horsepower, and the discussion says what would have to change if the pump were a heart.

concepts.name: Laminar flow
concepts.why: Laminar flow is characterized by the smooth flow of a fluid in layers that do not mix. The lines drawn in the figures of this chapter are streamlines, the paths followed by small volumes of fluid, and in laminar flow they are smooth and continuous. The precise definition of viscosity is based on laminar flow, and so is Poiseuille’s law, so the whole of this section assumes it.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term against the photograph of rising smoke, which is laminar at first, draws the layers in Figure 12.15(a), and the glossary carries it; the Take-Home Experiment asks the reader to drop two sticks into a river, one near the edge and one near the middle, and say which travels faster.

concepts.name: Turbulent flow
concepts.why: Turbulence is characterized by eddies and swirls that mix layers of fluid together, and its streamlines break up rather than running smoothly. It has two main causes: any obstruction or sharp corner imparts velocities perpendicular to the flow, and high speeds alone will do it, since the drag between adjacent layers and between the fluid and its surroundings forms swirls if the speed is great enough. Turbulent flow mixes the fluid, heats it more and resists more than laminar flow does.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term against the same photograph of smoke, where the rise slows once the flow becomes turbulent, draws an obstruction making eddies in Figure 12.15(b), and the glossary carries it; the whole of 12.5 is about predicting when it sets in.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.why: Viscosity is fluid friction, both within the fluid and between the fluid and its surroundings: juice pours freely and syrup sticks to the pitcher. It is measured by shearing a fluid between two plates, one held fixed and one moved at a steady speed, and finding the force that keeps the top plate moving. That force grows with the speed, with the area of the plate and with the viscosity, and falls as the plates are moved apart, so the viscosity is the force times the separation divided by the speed times the area. Viscosities vary from one fluid to another by several orders of magnitude, gases being far less viscous than liquids, and most of them depend on temperature.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it from the two plates of Figure 12.16, prints Table 12.1 of the coefficients of viscosity from air to honey, and the glossary carries it; two problems find a viscosity from the force needed to slide one microscope slide over another, and the first conceptual question asks why a liquid’s viscosity falls with temperature while a gas’s rises.

concepts.name: The velocity profile across a tube
concepts.why: If the flow in a tube has negligible resistance the speed is the same all across it. When a viscous fluid flows, the layer in contact with the wall does not move at all, and the speed increases steadily to its maximum at the center of the tube. The shape of a Bunsen burner flame is that velocity profile made visible, even though the viscosity of natural gas is small.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the two profiles side by side in Figure 12.17 and puts the photograph of the flame beside them, and the conceptual question about paddling a canoe, near the shore going upstream and near the middle coming down, is the same profile in a river.

concepts.name: Flow rate from pressure difference and resistance, $\kQ = (\kPrtwo - \kProne)/R$
concepts.why: What causes flow is a pressure difference, and the relationship between the two is very simple: the flow rate is the pressure difference divided by the resistance, and it is in the direction from high to low pressure. The resistance includes everything except pressure that affects the flow rate. It is greater for a long tube than for a short one, greater for a more viscous fluid, greatly increased by turbulence, and decreased by widening the tube; if the viscosity is zero the fluid is frictionless and the resistance is zero as well.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relationship before Poiseuille’s law and discusses each thing the resistance depends on in turn, the summary states it, and the problem on the concrete pump asks for the resistance of a fifty-meter hose from the pressure at the pump and the flow rate.

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law for resistance, $R = 8\keta l/\pi r^4$
concepts.why: For laminar flow of an incompressible fluid through a horizontal tube of uniform radius, the resistance is eight times the viscosity times the length, divided by pi times the fourth power of the radius. Resistance directly proportional to viscosity and to length makes good intuitive sense, since both directly affect the amount of friction encountered. The fourth power of the radius is the surprise. J. L. Poiseuille derived the law in an attempt to understand the flow of blood.
concepts.evidence: The section states it with the tube of Figure 12.18, the summary states it, and the problem set asks what happens to the flow when the length is quadrupled or the radius cut to a tenth.

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law, $\kQ = (\kPrtwo - \kProne)\pi r^4/8\keta l$
concepts.why: Putting the resistance into the relationship between flow rate and pressure difference gives one equation for laminar flow through a tube: the flow rate is the pressure difference times pi times the fourth power of the radius, divided by eight times the viscosity times the length. It is the working equation of the section, and of every medical application in the chapter.
concepts.evidence: The section states it and the summary repeats it; the worked example on plaque deposits uses it to show that halving the flow in a coronary artery takes only a sixteen percent narrowing, the example on the intravenous needle uses it to find the pressure needed at the entrance to the needle, and a dozen problems are worked from it.

concepts.name: Flow is extraordinarily sensitive to a tube’s radius
concepts.why: Because the radius is raised to the fourth power, any change in it has a very large effect on the resistance: doubling the radius decreases the resistance by a factor of sixteen, and reducing a vessel’s radius by only five percent cuts the flow to about eighty-one percent of its original value. This is why the body regulates blood flow mostly by dilating and constricting vessels rather than by working the heart harder, and why plaque in an artery is dangerous out of all proportion to its thickness. The body may compensate by raising the blood pressure, but that puts the heart and any weakened vessel at risk.
concepts.evidence: The section works the arithmetic out twice, once for a doubling and once for a five percent narrowing, and returns to it for the circulatory system of Figure 12.20; six problems turn on it, among them the arterioles that shut an organ down, the angioplasty that restores a tenfold flow, and the penguin standing on ice.

concepts.name: Pressure drop from flow and resistance, $\kPrtwo - \kProne = R\kQ$
concepts.why: Rearranged, the relationship between flow rate, pressure difference and resistance says that flow through a resistance causes the pressure to drop along it. That is why the water pressure in a house is lower on a hot summer day when the neighborhood is drawing heavily: the flow rate in the main is large, so the drop along it is large, and what arrives is what is left. The relationship holds for turbulent as well as for laminar flow, and it can be applied to a system whose radius is not the same everywhere, where the drop is greatest at the narrowest place.
concepts.evidence: The section derives it for the water main of Figure 12.19 and then applies it to an obstructed coronary artery and to the circulatory system as a whole, the summary states it, and the problem about a house whose supply falls from 20.0 to 8.00 liters per minute is worked from it.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for flow in a tube, $N_{\text{R}} = 2\krho\kv r/\keta$
concepts.why: Sometimes it can be predicted whether flow will be laminar or turbulent. Flow in a very smooth tube is laminar at low velocity and turbulent at high velocity, and in between it is more difficult to say. The Reynolds number gathers the four quantities that decide it, the density and the speed of the fluid, the radius of the tube and the viscosity, into one unitless number, and experiments have shown that it is the number, and not any of the four on its own, that the onset of turbulence is related to.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it, the worked example computes 523 for the intravenous needle of the previous section and concludes that the flow there is indeed laminar, the summary states it, and one problem asks the reader to show by substituting units that the number is unitless.

concepts.name: When flow in a tube turns turbulent
concepts.why: For a Reynolds number below about 2000 the flow is laminar, and above about 3000 it is turbulent. Between 2000 and 3000 the flow is unstable: it can be laminar, but small obstructions and surface roughness can make it turbulent, and it may oscillate randomly between the two. Most of the blood flow in the body is quiet and laminar; the exception is the aorta, where the speed rises above a critical value and the flow becomes turbulent.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the two thresholds immediately after defining the Reynolds number and the summary repeats them, and most of the problem set is the same question asked of different fluids: an oil gusher that is barely laminar, a garden hose and its nozzle that are not, concrete in a pump that is, and the greatest speed of blood in an artery that keeps the flow laminar.

concepts.name: Turbulence in the circulatory system
concepts.why: An occlusion or narrowing of an artery is likely to cause turbulence, both because of the irregularity of the blockage and because of the complexity of blood as a fluid. Turbulence in the circulatory system is noisy and can often be heard: the Korotkoff sounds heard through a stethoscope when a blood pressure cuff is released, the sounds of an aneurysm, and the heart murmurs made by damaged valves that do not close. Ultrasound detects the same turbulence in a way analogous to Doppler-shift radar detecting a storm.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the occluded vessel in Figure 12.22 and lists the sounds a physician listens for, and the first conceptual question asks where blood speed is greatest at a constriction and what the two distinct causes of the higher resistance there are.

concepts.name: Chaotic behavior
concepts.why: A system is chaotic when its behavior is so sensitive to some factor that it is extremely difficult to predict. Flow with a Reynolds number between 2000 and 3000 is a good example: whether it is turbulent is difficult but not impossible to predict, and the difficulty lies in the extremely sensitive dependence on roughness and obstructions, where a tiny variation in one factor has an exaggerated effect on the flow. Phenomena as disparate as turbulence, the orbit of Pluto and the onset of irregular heartbeats are chaotic and can be analyzed with similar techniques.
concepts.evidence: The section closes on the topic and names the three examples, and the conceptual question about the decorative wicker reeds on a ceiling fan asks the reader to judge whether such a fan is as quiet and efficient as one with smooth blades.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for an object in a fluid, ${N'}_{\text{R}} = \krho\kv L/\keta$
concepts.why: A moving object in a viscous fluid is equivalent to a stationary object in a flowing stream: riding a bicycle at ten meters a second in still air feels exactly like standing still in a ten-meter-a-second wind. Just as with flow in tubes, it is possible to predict when a moving object creates turbulence, and the indicator is another form of the Reynolds number, built from the fluid’s density and viscosity, the object’s speed and a characteristic length of the object such as a sphere’s diameter.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it against the equivalence of a moving object and a flowing stream, and the worked example computes 2.11 × 10⁵ for a thrown ball 7.40 cm across and concludes that it must have a turbulent wake.

concepts.name: How the flow around an object changes with its Reynolds number
concepts.why: Below about 1 the flow around an object can be laminar, particularly if the object has a smooth shape. Between 1 and about 10 the flow turns turbulent, the exact point depending on surface roughness, and a turbulent wake forms behind the object while some laminar flow remains over its surface. Between 10 and a million the flow may be either and may oscillate between the two, and above a million it is turbulent everywhere, even at the surface. Laminar flow occurs mostly when the objects are small, such as raindrops, pollen and blood cells in plasma, so most large objects, airplanes and sailboats among them, create significant turbulence as they move.
concepts.evidence: The section walks through the ranges in order and draws the three of them around one sphere in Figure 12.24, and the discussion of the worked example notes that Bernoulli’s principle gives only qualitatively correct results once the wake is turbulent.

concepts.name: Viscous drag
concepts.why: One of the consequences of viscosity is a resistance force called viscous drag, exerted on an object moving through a fluid. Unlike simple friction it depends on the object’s speed, and how it depends on it changes with the Reynolds number: for laminar flow the drag is proportional to the speed, while between about 10 and a million it is proportional to the speed squared, which is why even a small headwind costs a bicycle racer so much and why cyclists take turns leading the pack. For laminar flow around a sphere the drag is proportional to the viscosity, the size of the object and its speed, all of which makes sense, since the more viscous the fluid and the larger the object the more drag is to be expected; Stokes’ law gives the constant.
concepts.evidence: The section names the force, gives its dependence on speed in each range, restates Stokes’ law for a small sphere moving slowly, and draws the drag on the sphere at three speeds in Figure 12.24; the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: Sedimentation and the centrifuge
concepts.why: Because the viscous drag grows with speed, an object falling through a fluid does not accelerate indefinitely. The drag increases, the acceleration falls, and at the terminal speed the object continues to fall at a constant speed. This is the case for particles of sand falling in the ocean, cells falling in a centrifuge and sky divers falling through the air, and the terminal speed is greatest for low-viscosity fluids and for objects that are dense and small, which is why a skydiver falls more slowly with outspread limbs than in a pike position. Knowing it is useful for estimating how quickly small particles settle, and a centrifuge speeds that settling by replacing gravitational acceleration with a much greater centripetal acceleration.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the weight, the viscous drag and the buoyant force on a falling object in Figure 12.25 and names the three things terminal speed depends on, the glossary carries the term, the Take-Home Experiment asks the reader to time a marble falling through syrup and through oil and compare the speeds with the viscosities in Table 12.1, and the conceptual questions ask about raindrops in warm and cold air and about marbles of two sizes.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.why: Atoms and molecules are in constant motion at any temperature, and in fluids they move about randomly even where there is no macroscopic flow. That motion is a random walk, and diffusion is the movement of substances that it produces. It explains how an ice cube picks up the odors of a freezer, and fluids can even diffuse through solids. It is a slow process over macroscopic distances, because the densities of common materials are great enough that a molecule cannot travel far before a collision scatters it in any direction, including straight backward.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the fishy ice cube and the sprained ankle soaked in Epsom salt, draws the random walk in Figure 12.26, and the glossary carries the term; the section closes by noting that single-celled organisms rely on diffusion alone while larger organisms had to evolve circulatory systems.

concepts.name: Distance travelled by diffusion, $\kxrms = \sqrt{2D\kt}$
concepts.why: It can be shown that the average distance a molecule travels by diffusion is proportional to the square root of the time, not to the time itself, which is what makes diffusion so slow over any distance worth speaking of. The distance is the root-mean-square distance, the statistical average for the process, and the constant in it is the diffusion constant for that molecule in that medium.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation before the table of diffusion constants, the worked example finds that a glucose molecule needs 21 hours to move a centimeter through water and remarks that this is why sugar is stirred rather than waited for, the summary states it, and every problem of the section is worked from it.

concepts.name: The diffusion constant
concepts.why: The diffusion constant is determined experimentally and gathers into one number most of the things that set the rate: the molecule, the medium, the temperature and the cohesive and adhesive forces. It gets progressively smaller for more massive molecules, because the average molecular speed at a given temperature is inversely proportional to molecular mass, and it is far smaller in water than in air, because a molecule in water makes many more collisions in its random walk. It increases with temperature, since the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to absolute temperature.
concepts.evidence: The section prints Table 12.2 of the constants for hydrogen, oxygen, glucose, hemoglobin and DNA and then reads the table for what it shows, noting that an oxygen molecule moves only about forty micrometers in a second in water; two problems ask for the ratio of the distances oxygen diffuses in air and in water and for the time by which hydrogen outruns oxygen, which is how gas chromatography tells them apart.

concepts.name: The rate and direction of diffusion
concepts.why: A drop of food coloring placed carefully in still water spreads until its concentration is the same everywhere, which is free diffusion, since no barrier inhibits it. Molecular motion is random in direction, so simple chance dictates that more molecules leave a region of high concentration than enter it, and the net rate of diffusion is proportional to the difference in concentration; if the concentrations were the same there would be no net movement at all. The net rate is higher at the start than after the process is partly complete, and it is proportional to the diffusion constant as well.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the concentration difference along a tube in Figure 12.27 and argues the direction and the rate from it, and it names diffusion as the dominant mechanism by which nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissue and between air and blood in the lungs.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membranes
concepts.why: Some of the most interesting examples of diffusion occur through barriers that affect the rates. Membranes are generally selectively permeable, or semipermeable: one type has small pores that allow only small molecules through, and in others the molecules dissolve in the membrane or react with molecules in it while moving across. Because membranes are only a few nanometers thick, diffusion rates through them can be high, and diffusion through membranes is an important method of transport; oxygen moves in, carbon dioxide moves out, nutrients go in and wastes go out.
concepts.evidence: The section draws both kinds of membrane in Figure 12.28, gives the thickness of a membrane in meters, and the glossary carries the term; membrane function is named as the subject of much current research.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.why: Osmosis is the transport of water through a semipermeable membrane from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration, and it is driven by the imbalance in water concentration. Water is more concentrated in the body than in Epsom salt, so soaking a swollen ankle in Epsom salt moves water out of the body into the lower-concentration region in the salt. Both osmosis and dialysis are used by the kidneys to cleanse the blood.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term against the Epsom salt of its opening question, draws two sugar solutions separated by a membrane that passes water but not sugar in Figure 12.29, and the glossary carries it; the second conceptual question asks how osmosis and dialysis are alike and how they differ.

concepts.name: Dialysis
concepts.why: Dialysis is the transport of any molecule other than water through a semipermeable membrane because of its concentration difference. It is the same process as osmosis with a different substance moving, and like osmosis it can create substantial pressures. The kidneys use both.
concepts.evidence: The section defines it immediately after osmosis and pairs the two in every sentence that follows, the glossary carries it, and the second conceptual question asks how the two are alike and how they differ.

concepts.name: Osmotic pressure and back pressure
concepts.why: Osmosis can create a substantial pressure. Water moving through a membrane raises the solution on the low-concentration side, and the movement continues until the pressure created by the extra height of fluid is large enough to stop further osmosis. That back pressure is called the relative osmotic pressure if neither solution is pure water and the osmotic pressure if one of them is, and it can be very large: pure water and sea water separated by a membrane that passes no salt come to equilibrium at 25.9 atmospheres, which would raise the salt water 268 meters above the pure water. Turgor, the pressure of a plant cell’s fluid against its wall, is the same effect holding a plant up. Where the back pressure is sufficient to reverse the normal direction, the process becomes reverse osmosis or reverse dialysis, which is how water is desalinated and how a membrane is used to filter.
concepts.evidence: The section draws the fluid rising until the back pressure balances in Figure 12.29(b), gives the figure for sea water, names turgor, and the glossary carries relative osmotic pressure, osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis and reverse dialysis.

concepts.name: Active transport
concepts.why: Substances sometimes pass through a membrane in the direction opposite to the one expected. Cypress tree roots extract pure water from salt water although osmosis would move it the other way, and this is not reverse osmosis, because there is no back pressure to cause it. What is happening is active transport, a process in which a living membrane expends energy to move substances across it. Many living membranes do this, the kidneys among them, and it is estimated that at least a quarter of the body’s energy is expended on active transport at the cellular level.
concepts.evidence: The section closes on it with the cypress roots and the kidneys, gives the share of the body’s energy it takes, and the glossary carries the term.

concepts.name: The first law of thermodynamics, $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW$
concepts.why: The first law is the law of conservation of energy stated in the form most useful when heat transfer and doing work are the ways energy enters and leaves a system. The change in internal energy of a system equals the net heat transfer into the system minus the net work done by the system, so that positive heat transfer adds energy to the system and positive work takes energy from it, and whatever comes in and is not spent as work is stored as internal energy.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law as its first equation and returns to it in the Making Connections box, Figure 15.3 draws the system with heat in and work out, Example 15.1 applies it twice, and every problem of the section, from the gasoline in the tank to the woman climbing the Washington Monument, is a rearrangement of it.

concepts.name: Sign conventions for heat transfer and work
concepts.why: In the first law, heat transfer is positive when it is into the system and work is positive when it is done by the system. The convention matters because the same physical event, heat leaving a body or work being done on it, enters the equation with a minus sign, and a reader who mixes the two conventions will find the internal energy going the wrong way. Some texts define work against the external pressure and so write the law with a plus sign; this book does not.
concepts.evidence: The paragraph after the first equation spells the convention out, Figure 15.3 draws the in and out arrows for both quantities, Example 15.1 turns heat out and work in into negative numbers before adding, and the keyed AP item on 300 J of work done on a system with a heat transfer of −320 J tests exactly this.

concepts.name: Heat transfer and work are both energy in transit
concepts.why: Heat transfer and doing work are the two everyday means of bringing energy into or taking energy out of a system, and they are different processes: heat transfer is driven by a temperature difference and is disorganized, while work is a macroscopic force exerted through a distance and is organized. Yet both can produce the same result, a warmer tire whether the Sun heated it or the pump compressed it, and once the temperature has risen there is no telling which did it. Neither is stored as such in a system; both change the internal energy, which is a different kind of thing.
concepts.evidence: The section's Heat Q and Work W passage makes the argument with the bicycle tire, Table 15.1 sets the three terms side by side, and three conceptual questions ask the reader to give an example of each kind of energy and to say which can be stored.

concepts.name: Internal energy $\kEint$
concepts.why: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules, which is to say the sum of their mechanical energy. Because no one can keep track of every atom, the section deals with averages and distributions and, macroscopically, with a few quantities such as pressure, volume and temperature that the internal energy turns out to depend on. It is the account that heat transfer and work pay into and draw from.
concepts.evidence: The Internal Energy passage defines it in the atomic and molecular view and then in the macroscopic view, the second Making Connections box says which view is used for what, and the conceptual question on food energy as molecular potential energy tests the atomic picture.

concepts.name: The change in internal energy is independent of path, $\kdEint = \kEinttwo - \kEintone$
concepts.why: Experiment shows that the internal energy of a system depends only on the state of the system and not on how it reached that state. The change in internal energy between State 1 and State 2 is therefore the same for every path between them, while the heat transfer and the work done each depend on the path taken. This is what makes internal energy easier to work with than either heat or work: if the state is known, the change in internal energy follows from a few macroscopic variables.
concepts.evidence: The passage on going from State 1 to State 2 states the result, Example 15.1 produces the same 9.00 J change by two quite different processes and Figure 15.4 draws both, and the conceptual questions on how heat transfer and internal energy differ turn on it.

concepts.name: Find the change in internal energy from the net heat transfer and the net work
concepts.why: A problem gives heat transfer into and out of a system and work done on and by it; the net heat transfer is heat in minus heat out, the net work is work by minus work on, and the first law gives the change in internal energy. The same procedure, run the other way, finds an unknown heat transfer from a known change in internal energy and a known work, which is how the section's problems about the human body are solved.
concepts.evidence: Example 15.1 works the procedure step by step and then as a single sum, and the keyed problems on the gasoline in the tank, the system that does work while heat leaves it, the woman who does 500 J of work and the man who metabolizes 10,500 kJ in a day all use it.

concepts.name: Human metabolism and the first law
concepts.why: Human metabolism is the conversion of food into heat transfer, work and stored fat. Taking the body as the system, heat transfer to the surroundings makes Q negative and the work the body does on the world makes W positive, so the body loses internal energy and food, which enters as chemical potential energy and may be counted as work done on the body, replaces it. Eating too much makes the change in internal energy positive and the surplus is stored as fat; eating too little makes it negative and the body metabolizes its own fat. The body also shows that many thermodynamic processes are irreversible, since fat can be turned into work and heat but work and heat cannot be turned back into fat.
concepts.evidence: The Human Metabolism passage and Figure 15.5 set the body up as a first-law system, the paragraphs on the Calorie and on the basal metabolic rate follow, and the problems on the woman's efficiency, the man's daily metabolic rate, the cup of yogurt and the Washington Monument climb all apply the law to the body.

concepts.name: Heat engine
concepts.why: A heat engine is a machine that uses heat transfer to do work. Car engines and steam turbines are examples. Heat transfer into a gas in a cylinder raises its pressure, the gas pushes a piston through a distance and so does work on the outside world, and to repeat the process heat must leave the gas so that its pressure falls and the piston can be returned. The first law governs every step of it, and the section's simple processes are the pieces every heat engine is built from.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the term, Figure 15.7 draws the engine as a system with heat in and work out, Figure 15.8 walks the piston through its three panels, and the problems on the steam locomotive's piston and on the engine following the path ABCDA compute what such an engine does.

concepts.name: Work done at constant pressure, $\kW = \kPr\Delta V$
concepts.why: A process in which a gas does work on a piston at constant pressure is an isobaric process. The force on the piston is the pressure times the piston's area, the work is that force times the distance the piston moves, and the area times the distance is the change in volume, so the work done is the pressure times the change in volume. A positive change in volume means work done by the gas on the outside world. Pressure is an energy per unit volume, as the fluids chapters noted, and here some of that energy becomes work.
concepts.evidence: The PV Diagrams passage derives the result from W = Fd, Figure 15.9 draws the expanding cylinder with every symbol on it, Table 15.2 lists it as the isobaric entry, and the keyed problem on the steam locomotive's piston asks the reader to find the same work both ways.

concepts.name: Work is the area under the curve on a $PV$ diagram
concepts.why: A graph of pressure against volume shows a process as a path, and the work done on or by a system in going from one state to another is the area under that path. For a constant pressure the area is a rectangle, the pressure times the change in volume; for a pressure that varies, the area is approximated by strips each of average pressure times its small change in volume and the total work is their sum. A path walked toward smaller volume has a negative area, which is work done on the system.
concepts.evidence: Figure 15.10 shades the rectangle under the isobaric line, Figure 15.11 divides a varying-pressure curve into strips and then reverses it, and the keyed AP item asking how much work the system does in process AB reads an area off a diagram in the problems.

concepts.name: The work done depends on the path taken, not only on the endpoints
concepts.why: Two paths between the same two states on a PV diagram enclose different areas, so the work done along them differs, and more work is done along the path that runs at higher pressure. This is the path dependence that the first law's Q and W both have and that the internal energy does not, made visible: the endpoints fix the change in internal energy, and the path fixes how much of it arrives as work.
concepts.evidence: Figure 15.12(a) compares the paths ABC and ADC between the same endpoints, the passage names the greater work along the higher path, and the AP item that asks the reader to sketch a cycle closed by an isotherm or an adiabat and to say which does more net work tests the idea.

concepts.name: Isochoric process, $\kW = 0$
concepts.why: A process at constant volume is isochoric. The volume does not change, so the gas moves no piston and no work is done, and any heat transfer goes entirely into the internal energy. On a PV diagram an isochoric process is a vertical path, and it encloses no area.
concepts.evidence: The passage names the vertical paths of Figure 15.12 as isochoric, Table 15.2 lists the process with W = 0, Example 15.2 sets the work along BC and DA to zero, and the conceptual question asking whether the piston question makes sense for an isochoric process tests it.

concepts.name: The net work of a cyclical process is the area inside its loop on a $PV$ diagram
concepts.why: A cyclical process returns the system to its starting point, and its net work is the area inside the closed loop it forms on a PV diagram, because the positive area under the outward legs and the negative area under the return legs leave only the interior. The loop must be traversed clockwise for the net work to be positive, that is, for the engine to put work out; traversed counterclockwise, the same loop takes work in. The area is often easier to compute than the work along each leg, and comparing the areas of different loops shows which process produces the most work.
concepts.evidence: Example 15.2 finds the work around the rectangle ABCDA leg by leg and then as an area and gets 650 J both ways, Figure 15.12(b) and (c) draw the rectangle and a general loop, the keyed problem on the engine following ABCDA asks for the same calculation on a parallelogram, and three AP items ask which of several loops has the greatest net work.

concepts.name: Isothermal process of an ideal gas, $\kQh = \kW$
concepts.why: An isothermal process is one at constant temperature. For an ideal gas, PV is then constant, and because the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas depends on temperature alone it does not change, so the net heat transfer into the gas must equal the net work done by the gas: just enough heat comes in to replace the work done. An isothermal process is inherently slow, since heat must flow continuously and spread through the gas so that no region is hotter than another.
concepts.evidence: The passage on Figure 15.13(a) defines the process and derives Q = W from the internal energy of a monatomic gas, Table 15.2 lists it, and the conceptual questions on whether the change in internal energy is zero across a phase change and on why an isothermal process must be slow test it.

concepts.name: Adiabatic process, $\kQh = 0$ and $\kdEint = -\kW$
concepts.why: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat transfer takes place, achieved by very effective insulation or by running the process so fast that heat has no time to flow. Because Q is zero, the work the gas does comes entirely from its internal energy, so the temperature falls during an adiabatic expansion and the pressure with it. The adiabatic path from a point therefore lies below the isothermal path from the same point, and less work is done along it.
